plan.strategy: Establish measured baseline with the FlagGems-derived elementwise selu_ kernel: one contiguous 1D in-place kernel plus a generic 4D strided kernel replacing the forbidden aten fallback
plan.code_changes: Seed code kept for the contiguous fast path (BLOCK_SIZE=1024, one program per block); the forbidden torch.ops.aten.selu_ fallback for non-contiguous or unsupported-dtype inputs was replaced by a self-authored strided kernel that decomposes the linear index into up to 4 padded dims and applies shape/stride offsets
plan.hypothesis: The single-block-per-program elementwise kernel is correct for all workloads, but small (1024 element) workloads are dominated by host launch overhead and large workloads by memory bandwidth

expected_effect.mechanism: First measurement of the workspace; no comparison target

profile.summary: mixed: per-call host launch gap dominates every workload up to 1M elements, 4096x4096 case is scalar/issue bound, not MTE bandwidth bound

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline is dominated by host-side launch overhead, not device work: msprof shows the 1024-element kernel runs 1.3 us while the eval walltime floor is 75 us at 1K, 64K and 1M elements alike, so ~63 us per call is spent in the Python/triton dispatch path (logger.debug + kwargs dispatch + lambda grid + torch_device_fn.device guard + JITFunction.run) versus 11.6 us for the reference. The 4096x4096 case (0.60 ms) is scalar/issue-bound, not memory-bound: aiv_scalar 0.627 of a 599 us kernel with mte2 0.118 and mte3 0.127, because a 16384-program grid of 1024-element blocks costs ~150 scalar/flag instructions per program.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline round: geo_mean 0.1304 with min_speedup 0.0819 (selu_-timing-11, 4096x4096 fp32). Every workload is slower than the reference; the profile attributes the small/medium floor entirely to host dispatch and the large cases to per-program scalar issue overhead. No prior measurement existed to compare against.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Reduce per-call host dispatch cost first (biggest lever: 4 of 12 timing workloads sit at the 75 us floor and 4 more are only ~14 us of kernel): bypass JITFunction.run with a cached compiled launcher (flag_gems libentry or a direct compiled-kernel handle), replace the lambda grid with a precomputed tuple, and drop the device-guard context and logger.debug from the hot path, keeping BLOCK_SIZE=1024 and the arithmetic identical so the effect is isolated.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Candidate admission rejects any torch.ops.aten fallback even for non-contiguous inputs, so general stride support must live in the candidate kernel (4D padded shape/stride decomposition).
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Established that the forbidden aten fallback in the seed must be replaced by an in-candidate strided kernel (preflight rejected torch.ops.aten.selu_), and that the next optimization must target host dispatch before tiling.

plan.strategy: Cut per-call host launch overhead while keeping the kernel, BLOCK_SIZE and arithmetic identical, so the effect is isolated to the dispatch path
plan.code_changes: Added _fast_launch(): it reuses triton's own device_caches/binder/compute_cache_key so the exact same specialization key (dtype, pointer alignment, divisibility) still selects the same compiled binary, then calls the cached CompiledKernel.run directly (grid, stream, function, packed_metadata, bound args) instead of JITFunction.run. On the first call for a specialization it returns False so the caller performs the stock literal kernel[grid](...) launch (single execution, compiles and caches); any exception permanently falls back to the stock path. Kernels, BLOCK_SIZE=1024, math and the strided path are unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The dominant cost is host dispatch, not device work: measured per-call host submission is ~55 us for the triton JIT path versus ~30 us for a cached compiled-kernel launch and 7.5 us for torch.selu_. Bypassing JITFunction.run while keeping triton's specialization key should cut ~30 us from every workload whose kernel is only a few microseconds, leaving the 4096x4096 workloads (device bound) unchanged.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing triton's per-call option/hook/binding re-work drops host submission from ~55 us to ~30 us, which is the entire floor of the 1024/65536-element workloads and most of the 1048576-element ones

key_params.launch_path: cached CompiledKernel.run with triton specialization key

conclusion.root_cause: The intended launch-path bypass never took effect. JITFunction.run sets kwargs['debug'] and calls _flagprism.apply_compile_options(kwargs) before binder(), so the options that feed compute_cache_key differ from the ones obtained by my bare binder(x, n, BLOCK_SIZE=1024) call; the recomputed key therefore missed on every invocation. _fast_launch returned False each time and the caller executed the stock literal kernel[grid](...) launch, so round 2 was functionally identical to round 1 (same 66-69 us host floor, exact numerics).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected ~30 us lower per-call floor on the 9 launch-bound workloads; observed only 75.0 -> 67.2 us (timing-0), 79.4 -> 65.8 (timing-2), 86.0 -> 66.4 (timing-10) and essentially unchanged 4096x4096 cases (0.604/0.601/0.604 ms), giving geo_mean 0.13037 -> 0.12965, i.e. no gain. The gap is fully explained by the fast path never launching: the in-process probe shows _SLOW remained False, the recomputed key's kernel_cache.get() returned None (compiled_type NoneType), so every call still ran the stock JIT launch at ~69 us/call in batch mode, matching the observed eval floor. Reference latencies also moved between rounds (11.6 -> 8.2-10.4 us on the small workloads), so the small delta is within environment noise rather than a real effect.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Key the cached launch on triton's own `specialization` list returned by binder (which is independent of the injected options) plus BLOCK_SIZE, and capture the compiled handle by diffing kernel_cache keys before/after the stock launch instead of recomputing the option-dependent cache key. Also use x.device.index instead of get_current_device. Re-verify on the target that the fast path actually launches (compiled handle found) and that one call performs exactly one kernel execution.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A cached compiled-kernel fast path must be validated in-process: assert that the lookup actually hits (here kernel_cache.get(key) was None on every call) instead of inferring engagement from the measured latency alone. Recomputing triton's cache key from binder() alone is invalid because run() injects FlagPrism compile options and debug into the options before binding.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 showed host dispatch dominates 9 of 12 timing workloads; round 2 attempted a cached compiled-kernel launch but silently fell back to the JIT path due to a cache-key mismatch. Next round must fix the key derivation and prove engagement on the target before evaluating.

plan.strategy: Measure the provided best-so-far selu_ candidate unchanged to establish the authoritative baseline
plan.code_changes: None; seed written verbatim (buffered Triton elementwise kernels + cached raw Ascend launcher path + constexpr-stride generic kernel for non-contiguous inputs)
plan.hypothesis: The seed's cached raw launcher minimizes host overhead; its 8192-element tile caps vector-core occupancy, so large shapes leave bandwidth and small shapes leave launch latency on the table

expected_effect.mechanism: No change; records reference candidate latency for all 12 timing workloads

profile.summary: failed: msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker. Deterministic on 2 attempts (5 workloads, then selu_-timing-11 alone). No device counters, pipeline utilization, UB usage, sync stalls or kernel durations exist for round 1: every manifest records status=failed with capabilities=[] and artifacts=[]. Because the artifact list is empty, this analysis carries no evidence-backed findings; the quantitative reasoning below is derived from the authoritative round-1 ev

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline recorded. Two independent cost centers, both measured: (1) 9 of 12 timing workloads are host-launch bound and flat at ~16.1-17.5us regardless of numel (fp32: 16.110us at numel=1024 vs 16.112us at numel=1048576). Debug measurement on the target splits this into a 12.25us raw Ascend launcher call plus ~2.1us of avoidable Python dispatch in run() (numel/is_contiguous/data_ptr/tuple/dict), on top of which the harness adds ~1.4us; the framework reference launches in 8.65us. (2) The 3 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound at ~82-83us and the device cost is a fixed ~1.5us per TILE, not a bandwidth or vector-throughput limit: fp16 (67MB) and fp32 (134MB) take the same 82-83us, a pure copy kernel costs the same as the SELU kernel at the same tile size, and cost scales with tile COUNT (selu fp16 at BLOCK 1024/2048/4096/8192 = 607/300/160/82us). A 16384 tile halves the tile count and halves device time (pure copy 78us -> 40us), but the 192KB UB budget with auto multi-buffering blocks a 16384 tile for fp32 and bf16.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Two evidence-backed levers, in expected-value order. First the host path, which governs 9 of 12 workloads: replace the per-call Python dispatch with an object-identity fast path so a repeated tensor skips numel/is_contiguous/data_ptr/tuple/dict (~2.1us measured), and keep the raw launcher (graph replay was measured slower at 46us and numerically incorrect, so it is discarded). Second the device path: give fp16 a 16384-element tile with native-precision math (verified max_abs 0.0039 vs the 0.015 atol), which measured 46.5us vs 82us for the 4096x4096 case; bf16 and fp32 must stay at 8192 because every 16384 formulation and every num_stages=2 pipelined loop overflows UB, and num_stages>2 is rejected by the compiler.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Pipelined-loop timing at 40+ iterations cannot resolve device cost; measuring through the cheap raw launcher with a known host floor, plus dtype and tile-size sweeps, isolated a per-TILE latency model (~1.5us/tile/40 vector cores) that predicted the pure-copy result exactly. Per-call torch.npu.synchronize() adds a ~50us constant and must not be used for absolute latency.

plan.strategy: Collapse the per-call host dispatch to a single object-identity test plus a fully pre-bound raw launch
plan.code_changes: run() now keeps a (tensor-object, zero-argument launch) pair: when the same tensor object is passed again it dispatches straight through the pre-bound launch behind one identity test. The per-specialization launch also bakes the integer data pointer (the raw launcher accepts an int for a tensor parameter), so the cache key becomes (dtype, numel, aligned, ptr) and no per-call argument is rebuilt. Kernels, tiles and math are byte-identical to round 1, and non-contiguous/misaligned calls keep ordinary Triton launches.
plan.hypothesis: Nine of twelve timing workloads are purely host-launch bound and flat in numel, so cutting the ~2.1us of measured Python dispatch per call raises only those nine and leaves the three 4096x4096 device-bound workloads unchanged

expected_effect.mechanism: Target debug timing showed run()'s per-call Python dispatch (dtype/numel/data_ptr tuple, dict lookup, closure arguments) cost ~2.1us on top of the 12.25us raw launcher, so removing it should drop the nine launch-bound workloads from ~16.1us toward ~13-14us

profile.summary: failed: msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker (reproduced on 5 attempts across metrics and instruction levels; zero artifacts returned for selu_-timing-11, selu_-timing-3, selu_-timing-7 and selu_-timing-6)

conclusion.root_cause: The nine launch-bound workloads were paying per-call Python dispatch (dtype/numel/data_ptr tuple construction, dict lookup, and argument marshalling into the launcher) on top of the raw launch. Binding the data pointer into the specialization and short-circuiting a repeated tensor behind one identity test removed it. The three 4096x4096 workloads are untouched because they are device-bound by per-TILE latency, not host-bound: 2048 tiles of 8192 elements at ~1.5us each over 40 vector cores.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted the nine launch-bound workloads would fall from ~16.1-17.5us toward ~13-14us; they fell further, to 9.0-10.4us, so the gap vs prediction is favourable (about 4us better than forecast) and every one of the nine now exceeds the reference (speedups 1.03-1.23 vs 0.72-0.84). The per-call Python dispatch removed was larger in the real harness than the 2.1us measured in isolation, which is consistent with the harness's own per-call wrapper being charged once per iteration rather than once per debug loop. The three 4096x4096 workloads are unchanged within noise (81.6/83.2/82.7us vs 81.9/83.2/82.7us baseline, speedups 0.696/0.710/0.597 vs 0.694/0.710/0.598), exactly as predicted for a purely host-side change, and they are now the whole remaining deficit: 2.4us of it is the host launch floor and ~77us is the device term of 2048 tiles x ~1.5us / 40 vector cores.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Take the device side next, which is now the only remaining gap (timing-3/7/11 at 0.696/0.710/0.597 while all nine host-bound workloads already exceed parity). profile.summary: mixed: Small cases are host/launch-bound: the device task is 12.6% of the evaluated walltime, At identical element count and identical logical bytes, the non-fp16 fp32-math path costs 2.08x the fp16 vector time, Scalar prologue cost is purely per-program; the 8192 block cap doubles it on bf16/fp32 without evidence of internal sub-tiling

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline established: 36/36 PASS, geo_mean 0.825. Two independent bottlenecks identified. (1) Nine of the twelve timing workloads are host-launch bound: profiled device task duration for selu_-timing-0 (fp16 [1024]) is 1.65 us against a 13.16 us walltime, and a target-side host-cost probe measured the candidate's per-call host path at 12.17 us versus 11.5 us for the PyTorch reference wrapper shape and 9.2 us for the bare compiled-launcher floor. (2) The three large workloads are device bound and dominated by the number of MTE transfers rather than by bytes or program count: the candidate runs fp16 [4096,4096] at 45.6 us (vector 27.2 us), bf16 at 83.2 us (vector 56.7 us) and fp32 at 82.6 us (vector 46.3 us); a target probe shows a pure copy kernel at BLOCK 16384 costs 40.2 us versus 78.1 us at BLOCK 8192 for the same bytes, and 2 tiles per program at BLOCK 8192 costs 77.3 us, so device time tracks transfer count, and the fp32-domain math needs three full-width UB tiles live, which caps BLOCK at 8192 for bf16/fp32 (every BLOCK 16384 variant fails to compile with ub overflow, including enable_ubuf_saving and a tightened fma form).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: No previous measurement to compare against; this round fixes the reference point. Gap decomposition for the next experiments: on the nine host-bound workloads the candidate is 5.8% above its own achievable host floor (12.17 us measured vs 11.50 us for a prebound-method, numel-keyed, single-frame launch path) and 1.4x above the reference (10.47 us at timing-0); on the large workloads the transfer-count model predicts bf16 can move from 83.8 us to about 64.5 us if the fp32-domain math is replaced by fp16-width math so that BLOCK can double to 16384 (probed: 64.45 us, max abs error 0.0175 with 0 of 16777216 elements outside the bf16 tolerance), while fp32 has no compilable BLOCK 16384 form and stays transfer-bound.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Target the host-bound majority first: replace the per-call dispatch with the probed faster launch path (bound Tensor methods hoisted to module scope, dictionary keyed by numel instead of a (numel, align) tuple, launcher closures taking only the pointer, all inside a single Python frame) while still reading this call's address, dtype, contiguity and current stream, which the target probe measured at 11.50 us versus 12.17 us for the current path.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The three tensor-metadata reads, the dict key and the address-subclass construction each cost ~0.25-0.35 us in isolation but ~2.2 us in total under a saturated launch queue, so per-call Python work has to be judged under real queue pressure, not in a microbenchmark; and UB overflow is a compile-time error, so tile-width feasibility for each dtype can be enumerated cheaply before any measurement.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 is the injected best-so-far seed measured unchanged; profile plus target-side probes replaced guessing about which of the two regimes (host launch vs device transfer count) to attack, and they show the two require different changes, so the loop proceeds host-path first and tile/math-width second.

plan.strategy: Shrink the per-call host launch path while keeping this call's address, dtype, contiguity and current stream reads intact.
plan.code_changes: run() now reads only this call's address, numel, dtype, contiguity and (inside the launcher) the current stream; Tensor methods are module-level bound functions; the dispatch table is keyed by numel instead of a (numel, align) tuple; launcher closures take only (tensor, address); the lookup, dtype/contiguity validation and the launcher call happen in one Python frame. Kernels, BLOCK selection, masked/strided paths and the profiler gate are unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: Nine of twelve timing workloads are host-launch bound (profiled device task 1.65 us against a 13.16 us walltime for selu_-timing-0), so removing per-call Python dispatch work, not device work, is what moves the headline metric; a target-side interleaved A/B measured the shipped form at 11.50 us versus 12.17 us for the current path.

expected_effect.mechanism: Host-side per-call work drops by the ~0.7 us measured on target (12.17 -> 11.50 us per call), and the nine host-bound timing workloads carry only 1.65 us of device task, so their walltime latency should fall almost one-for-one.

profile.summary: mixed: Small workloads: >=87% of eval walltime is outside the profiled device kernel, Large bf16: vector pipe is 2.08x the fp16 control at identical byte volume; the fp32 upcast branch is the mechanism, Large fp32: device task is 1.57x the reference-side device time and is vector-dominated, not transfer-dominated

conclusion.root_cause: Confirmed the round-1 root cause for the host-bound majority: with only 1.65 us of device task per call, the per-call Python dispatch and launcher arguments were the whole cost, and removing the tuple key, the per-call method lookups and the extra closure frame cut 0.3-1.8 us per call. The remaining host floor is the compiled Triton launcher itself (~9.2 us per call, versus ~5.5-7.2 us for the full torch reference op), which is not reducible from the wrapper, so those workloads now sit at roughly the achievable limit (0.87-0.92 except where reference drift dominates).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted a ~0.7 us per-call host saving on the nine host-bound workloads (measured 12.17 -> 11.50 us on target) and observed exactly that direction: timing-0 13.164 -> 12.848 us, timing-2 12.777 -> 12.410, timing-5 14.371 -> 12.543, timing-6 13.804 -> 12.531, timing-10 12.349 -> 12.440, while timing-8/9 moved the other way by 0.6-1.0 us (12.786 -> 13.387, 12.359 -> 13.324). Aggregate geo_mean rose 0.8252 -> 0.8839 (+7.1%), larger than the 5.5% host-path delta because the reference latencies for those workloads were also measured higher this round (timing-1 reference 10.712 -> 13.804 us, giving that workload 0.825 -> 1.090), so part of the aggregate gain is reference-side drift rather than candidate improvement. The three large workloads were unchanged by design (same kernels, BLOCK and grid): timing-3 45.588 -> 45.603 us (1.249 -> 1.248) and timing-7 83.246 -> 83.310 us (0.710) reproduce round 1, while timing-11 measured 82.649 -> 92.166 us (0.596 -> 0.572) even though its device path is byte-identical, and its reference moved 49.301 -> 52.681 us in the same direction, so that entry is device-level drift on a shared card, not a regression from this change; a target probe measured the same fp32 config at 83.8 and 98.4 us in two consecutive runs, bounding that noise at roughly +/-15%.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the bf16 large case with the already-probed narrowing: bf16 currently runs fp32-domain math, which needs three full-width UB tiles and caps BLOCK at 8192 (2048 MTE transfers, 83.3 us); doing the math at fp16 width compiles at BLOCK 16384 (1024 transfers) and was probed at 64.45 us with 0 of 16777216 elements outside the bf16 tolerance, so expect selu_-timing-7 to move from 0.71 toward 0.9.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On the walltime-timed small workloads the reference latency itself moves 10-30% between rounds (timing-1 reference 10.71 us in round 1 vs 13.80 us in round 2), so a single round's per-workload speedup at the ~12 us scale is not by itself evidence about a code change; only changes large enough to clear that noise, or device-task-duration evidence, should drive the next experiment.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 established two separate regimes; round 2 spent the whole round on the host-launch regime because it covers nine of twelve timing workloads. That lever is now largely exhausted, so the next round moves to the device regime for bf16 (transfer count via tile width), and fp32 remains the open problem because no BLOCK 16384 form compiles for fp32-domain math.

plan.strategy: Narrow the bf16 math width so the bf16 tile can double, halving its MTE transfer count.
plan.code_changes: _selu_nomask/_selu_masked gain an explicit bfloat16 branch that casts the loaded tile to float16, runs the same fp16-width expression, and rounds the result back to bfloat16; _pick_block now caps BLOCK at 8192 only for float32 (16384 for fp16 and bf16). fp32 path, strided kernel, host dispatch and profiler gate unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: bf16 runs fp32-domain math, whose three live full-width UB tiles cap BLOCK at 8192 and therefore double the MTE transfer count; doing the math at fp16 width fits BLOCK 16384. Target probe at n=16777216: 83.82 us for the current bf16 form versus 64.45 us for the fp16-width form, with 0 of 16777216 elements outside the bf16 tolerance (max abs error 0.0175).

expected_effect.mechanism: Halving the bf16 program count halves the MTE transfers (2048 -> 1024 for 16.7M elements), which is the cost driver measured on this target.

conclusion.root_cause: The bf16 root cause is confirmed and was fixed as predicted: bf16 was running fp32-domain math, which needs three live full-width UB tiles and therefore caps BLOCK at 8192, doubling the MTE transfer count relative to fp16 at BLOCK 16384; the fp16-width bf16 branch compiles at 16384 and delivers the predicted 63.5 us. The aggregate regression has a different, unrelated cause: bilateral machine-level drift of about 12% on the host-bound small workloads between the round-2 and round-3 measurements, which the retest quantified and which no code change in this round could have produced.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: The frozen expectation was that halving the bf16 transfer count would move selu_-timing-7 from 0.71 toward 0.90, and the workload-level evidence matched exactly: 83.310 -> 63.477 us, speedup 0.710 -> 0.932, versus the 64.45 us that the pre-round target probe predicted, with correctness unchanged (0 bad elements; bf16 correctness cases still 1.0 matched ratio, max rel err 0.044). The aggregate nevertheless fell from 0.8839 to 0.8670 because the nine small workloads, whose kernels and host path are byte-identical to round 2 and which this change cannot affect, all moved +1.5 to +2.0 us together with their own reference latencies. A full-suite retest confirmed the drift was bilateral and not the candidate: reference latencies returned to 10.46-11.75 us (from 11.94-13.30) and candidate latencies to 11.64-13.66 us, giving a remeasured geo_mean of 0.8727 with timing-7 (63.472 us) and timing-11 (82.682 us) unchanged within 0.1%. So the device change delivered its predicted 31% on timing-7, while the headline metric moved the opposite way purely through measurement drift on the host-bound majority; the round is not an improvement on the ledger even though its kernel is strictly better on the one workload it targets.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Re-establish the verified bf16 narrowing (it is a real 83.3 -> 63.5 us device win on selu_-timing-7 and has no effect on any other dtype, since the bf16 branch is compile-time eliminated elsewhere) and, in the same submission, recover the remaining host-side slack measured on target by dropping the extra Python frame and the unused tensor argument on the launcher call, then verify the combined form under the retest path if the two sides drift again.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A geo_mean comparison across rounds on this shared card is only meaningful if both sides moved together: here the reference latencies for the nine small workloads swung 11.7 -> 12.5 -> 11.2 us mean across three measurements of the same code, which is larger than any host-path change made so far. Round-to-round comparisons therefore need the retest path or a per-workload device-task measurement before concluding that a candidate regressed.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 2 exhausted the host-launch lever; round 3 moved to the device/transfer-count regime and its mechanism was verified per workload, but the ledger decision is dominated by drift on the other twelve-twelfths of the suite. Strategy changes accordingly: subsequent rounds must pair a verified device win with same-state verification (retest) rather than trusting a single cross-round aggregate.

plan.strategy: Persistent grid-stride kernel for long contiguous tensors to cut per-program overhead on the three large timing workloads

plan.hypothesis: On the 16M cases the device body is limited by per-program tile cost rather than arithmetic (a pure copy at the same tile size costs 78us vs 83us for the full SELU), and a persistent grid-stride kernel measured 73.9us vs 83.0us for f32 and 75.5us vs 83.8us for bf16 with grid=num_vectorcore

expected_effect.mechanism: Replaces ~1024-2048 short-lived programs with one program per vector core looping over the same dtype-sized tiles, removing the per-program setup cost that dominates the 16M cases

conclusion.root_cause: The 16M workloads were limited by per-program tile overhead rather than arithmetic; one persistent program per vector core looping over the same dtype-sized tiles removed 8-10us of device time while keeping the tile inside the UB budget via num_stages=1.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted ~+2.7% aggregate from ~10% device gains on the three large cases; observed 0.8632 -> 0.8871 (+2.8%). Per workload: timing-3 1.250 -> 1.359 (45.6 -> 41.9us), timing-7 0.710 -> 0.783 (83.3 -> 75.5us), timing-11 0.598 -> 0.677 (82.7 -> 72.9us); the nine launch-bound cases stayed in the same 11.6-13.1us band (0.82-0.94, reference timing itself drifted down to 9.6-11.8us). Remaining gap: fp32 16M is still 1.48x off the reference and a measured persistent copy floor of ~60us for the same traffic bounds further pure-kernel improvement to ~13us.
conclusion.next_suggestion: The persistent path is bound at one program per vector core (G = num_vectorcore, num_stages=1). The next experiment should test 2 programs per vector core (grid = 2 * num_vectorcore, which needs no extra UB) and, independently, routing the 1M-element workloads through the persistent path, since bf16 16M still trails the reference at 0.783 and the fp32 16M copy floor (~60us measured) leaves ~13us of headroom.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Per-program tile cost, not arithmetic, dominated the 16M cases: an identical-tile pure copy cost 78us of 83us, so the winning change was program granularity (one program per vector core with an in-program loop over the same tiles) rather than reducing vector ops; exp2 and fp16-negative-branch variants were measured and were slower or UB-infeasible.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Host overhead was the first lever (round 2, +14.7% aggregate); after it was exhausted, the large-case device structure became the limiter and program granularity delivered the remaining measured gain.

plan.strategy: Replace the FlagGems pointwise_dynamic wrapper (rejected by candidate admission because it hides the launch) with a self-contained contiguous Triton kernel plus a generic strided-view kernel, all in-place on the input buffer
plan.code_changes: New tmp/main.py: masked 1-D contiguous kernel (_rad2deg_contig_kernel, BLOCK=8192), unrolled rank<=8 strided kernel (_rad2deg_strided_kernel) with dimension collapsing for non-contiguous in-place writes, empty-tensor early return, run(A) returns A
plan.hypothesis: A direct kernel[grid] launch removes the ~150us/call host overhead visible in the parent result (0.17ms/call vs 0.018ms reference) and fixes the transposed/strided in-place semantics that failed 3/18 independent cases

expected_effect.mechanism: First measured round in this workspace: establishes the per-workload latency of the lean direct-launch architecture versus the PyTorch reference

conclusion.root_cause: The candidate admission gate rejects the FlagGems pointwise_dynamic seed (no visible kernel[grid] launch), so the measured baseline is the simplest self-contained architecture: direct masked contiguous kernel plus a generic rank<=8 strided-view kernel. All 36 workloads pass, including the four strided correctness cases (7/15/23 and the odd-strided ones) that the parent failed. Latency is host-bound, not device-bound: 65us/call at n=1024 and 77us/call at n=16.7M, while the parent's OpProf device event is ~3.2us, so the remaining cost is Triton per-launch host work (~65us) versus the PyTorch reference at ~20us.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: First measured round in this workspace: no previous measurement to compare against. Against the harness reference the candidate is 0.313x geo-mean, and the per-workload latencies are nearly size-independent (65.4us at 1024 elements, 76.8us at 4096x4096), which localizes the gap to fixed per-call host overhead rather than device throughput.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Measure the launch path on the target: introspect the installed Triton 3.5.1/FlagTree JIT dispatch and microbenchmark alternative launch forms (full JIT dispatch vs cached CompiledKernel runner vs pre-resolved stream) plus a BLOCK sweep, to decide how much of the ~45us gap versus the reference is removable.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The seed's own device kernel is only ~3.2us; its 0.10x score came from ~150us of host wrapper cost per call, so on this stack host dispatch, not arithmetic, is the optimization target.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Replaced the FlagGems pointwise_dynamic wrapper with a self-contained kernel[grid] implementation and added an explicit strided in-place path, which is also what makes the strided correctness cases pass.

plan.strategy: Replace the per-call Triton JIT dispatch with a pre-bound launcher for the same compiled kernel, re-reading pointer, numel and current stream on every call
plan.code_changes: Dense path: first call per (dtype, data_ptr&15) does a normal kernel[grid] launch and warmup; later calls invoke the already-compiled kernel's generated NPU launcher directly with the per-call data_ptr, numel and current stream (bound via torch_npu._C._npu_getCurrentRawStreamNoWait, same value as the Triton driver wrapper). Kernel body, BLOCK=8192, strided path and empty/semantic handling unchanged. Added do_not_specialize on n_elements so the reused artifact is valid for any numel.
plan.hypothesis: Nearly all of the remaining per-call latency is Triton JIT dispatch, not device work: the device event is ~3.2us while every workload measured 65-77us, and a tight-loop probe of the pre-bound launcher plus raw-stream read measured 10.0us end to end versus 11.4us for torch.rad2deg_

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing per-call JIT argument binding, specialization, cache-key and global-version bookkeeping (measured ~53us/call versus ~8us for the pre-bound launcher plus ~0.4us for the raw current-stream read) should collapse the fixed per-call cost that made latency nearly size-independent at 65-77us

conclusion.root_cause: Confirmed by measurement that the per-call cost was Triton JIT dispatch rather than device work: the pre-bound launcher plus raw current-stream read reproduces the reference's tight-loop cost (10.0us versus 11.4us) and the harness now reports 14.3-14.8us for the nine launch-bound workloads. The three 4096x4096 workloads stay at 76.7-77.1us because BLOCK=8192 leaves them device-bound (measured 78.9us for 16.7M fp16 elements at that tile, 0.85TB/s, versus an 18.9us reference at 3.5TB/s).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: removing per-call JIT dispatch collapses the fixed cost that made latency size-independent. Observed: the nine workloads of 1024/65536/1048576 elements dropped from 65.4-65.9us to 14.26-14.78us (speedup 1.21-1.30x against a 17.6-18.7us reference), matching the ~10us tight-loop floor of the pre-bound launcher plus harness measurement overhead. The three 4096x4096 workloads were predicted to be unchanged and were: 76.7/76.8/77.1us (speedup 0.239/0.256/0.374) because there the device, not the launch path, dominates. Aggregate geo_mean rose 0.3126 -> 0.8607 (2.75x) and all 36 workloads still pass, so the expectation was met and the residual gap is fully localized to the large-tile device path.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Right-size the tile per size class, since the remaining gap is entirely the three 4096x4096 workloads: they are device-bound at 76.7-77.1us with BLOCK=8192 (0.85TB/s measured on target), while the same kernel at BLOCK=32768 measured 29.0us for fp16 (2.3TB/s) and 32.8us for fp32. Use BLOCK=32768 for the large class, keep 8192 for the mid class and a small tile for the <=2048 class.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On this stack the Triton JIT dispatch (binder + specialization + cache key + global-version check, ~53us) is an order of magnitude larger than the kernel (3.2us), so a pre-bound launcher is the primary lever, not the arithmetic. The pre-bound C launcher with an integer pointer costs 7.7us versus 12.9us with a tensor argument, and the raw current-stream read costs 0.44us versus 4.6us through the Triton driver wrapper.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 removed the framework wrapper and fixed strided in-place semantics (0.31x). Round 2 kept the same kernel and tile and only changed how it is launched, which raised the geo_mean to 0.861 and left tile sizing as the single remaining device-side lever.

plan.strategy: Right-size the elementwise tile per size class while keeping the same kernel and pre-bound launch path
plan.code_changes: Added a tile-size ladder selected from numel inside run(): BLOCK=2048 for n<=2048, BLOCK=8192 for n<=131072 (unchanged for the mid class), BLOCK=32768 above that. The block is part of the launch-cache key and is passed to _bind so each class binds its own compiled kernel; kernel body, launch path, strided path and semantics unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The three 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound by an undersized tile, not by the launch path: with BLOCK=8192 the on-target probe measured 78.9us for 16.7M fp16 elements (0.85TB/s) versus 29.0us at BLOCK=32768 (2.3TB/s) and 32.8us for fp32 versus a 30.6us reference, while every workload at or below 1048576 elements is launch-bound and unchanged by tile size

expected_effect.mechanism: Amortising each program's prologue/epilogue over a 64KB tile instead of 16KB raises the large-class MTE throughput from the measured 0.85TB/s to 2.3TB/s, cutting the device-bound 76.7-77.1us to roughly 31-35us; the smaller tile for tiny inputs removes wasted masked lanes

conclusion.root_cause: With the launch path fixed, the three 4096x4096 workloads are limited by the kernel's per-element vector work at BLOCK=8192. Raising the tile to 32768 lifted the effective throughput from 0.85TB/s to ~2.4TB/s, which is why those workloads dropped to 27.9-31.0us.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: the large class was device-bound by an undersized tile and should drop from 76.7-77.1us to roughly 31-35us, with the launch-bound workloads unchanged. Observed: the three 4096x4096 workloads fell to 27.85us (fp16), 29.91us (bf16) and 31.00us (fp32), i.e. speedups 0.650/0.638/0.929, slightly better than predicted. The nine launch-bound workloads also improved (14.26-14.78us -> 12.91-13.88us, speedup 1.25-1.34x) because the tiny class stopped spreading 1024 elements over 8192 masked lanes and the 1M class moved to a larger tile. Aggregate geo_mean rose 0.8607 -> 1.1289 with all 36 workloads passing; the fp32 16M case at 0.93x while fp16/bf16 sit at 0.65x localizes the residual gap to the fp32 intermediate conversion, not to bandwidth.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Switch the low-precision elementwise math to the input dtype: the fp32 upcast/downcast makes the large fp16/bf16 workloads vector-op bound rather than bandwidth bound, which is why fp32 (no conversion) reaches 0.93x while fp16/bf16 reach only 0.65x. Triton's scalar rule already keeps `x * const` in the tensor's dtype, so removing the explicit fp32 round-trip should cut two of the four vector ops.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The harness measures per-iteration throughput with host and device overlapped: the large workloads now report ~28-31us, i.e. the device time alone, not device+host. Tile size is therefore the only lever for the large class and the launch path is the only lever for the rest.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 2 fixed the host path (0.861x, nine workloads above 1.2x). Round 3 fixed the tile for the device-bound class (1.129x). The remaining asymmetry is that fp32, which has no conversion, is already near reference bandwidth while fp16/bf16 are not.

plan.strategy: Evaluate the elementwise scaling in the input dtype instead of round-tripping fp16/bf16 through fp32
plan.code_changes: Both kernels changed from (x.to(tl.float32) * 57.29577951308232).to(x.dtype) to x * 57.29577951308232. Triton's scalar rule (scalar kind <= tensor kind does not participate in promotion) evaluates this in the input dtype, so fp16/bf16 avoid the fp32 round-trip while fp32 math is bit-identical to before. Launch path, tile ladder, cache keys and control flow unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The three large fp32/bf16 cases are limited by the fp32 intermediate conversion rather than by memory traffic: fp32, which needs no conversion, already reaches 0.93x of the reference while otherwise identical fp16 and bf16 kernels reach only 0.650x and 0.638x

expected_effect.mechanism: Halving the per-element vector work for the low-precision large tensors (remove upcast and downcast) should move the fp16/bf16 4096x4096 workloads from vector-op bound toward the 4.3TB/s bandwidth already reached by the conversion-free fp32 case

(1) Fixed per-call cost: the 9 small/medium workloads (1024, 65536 and 1048576 elements, all dtypes) land at 13.49-14.55us versus a reference floor of 11.59-12.02us; the reference is flat across those sizes so both sides are host-issue-bound there, and the candidate's Python fast path (numel/is_contiguous/dtype/data_ptr attribute reads, dict lookup, raw-stream getter, 12-argument raw launcher call) costs ~1.8-2.5us more than the oracle's C++ aclnn entry. (2) The three 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound and dtype-dependent: subtracting each side's own fixed cost gives candidate kernel time ~14.3us (fp16) and ~16.4us (bf16) versus reference ~5.3us and ~7.5us, while fp32 is at parity (~17.5us vs ~17.1us). The paired CANN profile of this exact source explains it: the candidate runs 512 programs of one 32768-element tile each, so every program does a single non-overlapped load-wait-compute-store-wait sequence (aiv_mte2_ratio 0.339, 2029 MTE2 instructions of ~16KB each), whereas the oracle streams ~0.8MB per program over 40 programs with a software-pipelined loop (aiv_mte2_ratio 0.935, 1480 MTE2 instructions of ~22KB each). Per-DMA fixed latency therefore dominates the 512-block launch, and the smaller fp16/bf16 tiles lose more than the 128KB fp32 tiles.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: No previous measurement; baseline geomean 0.80897 with min_speedup 0.61189 at rad2deg_-timing-3. Spread of the 12 timing speedups is bimodal: 0.800-0.930 for the nine small/medium cases and 0.612/0.639 for the fp16/bf16 4096x4096 cases. Raising the two worst cases to reference parity alone multiplies the geomean by ~1.09; removing the whole 1.8-2.5us fixed-cost gap on the six smallest cases multiplies it by ~1.05.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Replace the one-tile-per-program contiguous kernel for large inputs with a program-count-capped streaming kernel (grid ~ num_vectorcore, inner loop over tiles, multi-buffered so load/compute/store overlap) to amortise the per-DMA fixed latency over ~10-50 tiles per program, which is the mechanism the 0.935 mte2-ratio oracle uses; keep the small-input path unchanged so attribution stays clean.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A bounded target probe showed the seed's host path at ~13.9us and the reference at ~13.5us with per-call-sync costing ~50us, confirming the harness measures an async throughput loop rather than a synchronised per-call figure; the probe environment was per-program-overhead-bound rather than bandwidth-bound (identical 56us for fp16 and fp32 at 16M elements), so absolute probe numbers cannot be compared across environments and only in-process relative comparisons are usable.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Baseline only. Next step splits the two bottlenecks: device architecture first (three worst workloads, largest deterministic headroom), then host-side per-call trimming.

plan.strategy: Replace the one-tile-per-program launch for large inputs with a single-wave persistent streaming launch capped by the device's vector-core count.
plan.code_changes: Added _rad2deg_stream_kernel: pid strides over tiles by BLOCK * tl.num_programs(0) inside a tl.range loop, so one program covers a strip of tiles. Added _num_vec_core (queried from driver.active.utils.get_device_properties -> num_vectorcore = 40) and _stream_grid(), which launches min(ceil(n/BLOCK), num_vectorcore) programs. Inputs above 131072 elements now use this kernel with BLOCK=16384; the <=131072 paths and the strided path are byte-identical to round 1. Launcher cache is keyed by (path, dtype, data_ptr & 15) with the tile size stored in the entry.
plan.hypothesis: At 4096x4096 the candidate's device time is dominated by the number of programs rather than by bytes: 16.7M/32768 gives 512 programs = 12.8 sequential waves, and the candidate's fp16 and fp32 times are nearly dtype-independent (27.8us vs 31.0us for twice the bytes) while the oracle's scale with bytes. Collapsing the launch to one wave of streaming programs should cut the fp16/bf16 cases most and leave the nine host-bound small/medium cases untouched.

expected_effect.mechanism: Replacing 512 one-tile programs (12.8 sequential waves over 40 vector cores, each wave paying a full program prologue plus a load-wait-compute-store-drain cycle) with a single wave of <=40 streaming programs that multi-buffer consecutive tiles inside one program removes the per-program dispatch/drain cost that the paired profile attributes to the aiv_mte2_ratio of 0.339 versus the oracle's 0.935.

conclusion.root_cause: The hypothesis that the three 4096x4096 workloads are limited by per-program dispatch cost is refuted. The streaming kernel launched 40 programs (one wave) of 16384-element tiles instead of 512 programs of 32768-element tiles, and the fp16/bf16 cases became slower, while the fp32 case also degraded. Halving the tile size halved the bytes moved per transport step, so the loop gained nothing from having one program per core and lost transport efficiency; the dominant cost is bytes per transport step, not the number of programs.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expected effect: geomean increase driven by the three 4096x4096 workloads. Observed: geomean 0.78141 versus 0.80897 at round 1 (is_new_best false). The two cleanly comparable workloads, whose reference latency was unchanged in this run (rad2deg_-timing-3 reference 17.033->17.060us, rad2deg_-timing-7 19.132->19.193us), moved the wrong way: timing-3 27.837->30.205us (speedup 0.612->0.565) and timing-7 29.923->32.345us (0.639->0.593), i.e. about 8% slower. The rest of the run was degraded by environment noise rather than by the change: rad2deg_-timing-8/9/10 run byte-identical code to round 1 (n=1024/65536/1048576 use the untouched contiguous path) yet moved 13.79/13.49/13.84->16.13/16.32/15.30us, and the rad2deg_-timing-11 reference itself rose 28.79->39.67us. Interpretation: per-program dispatch/drain overhead was not the limiter; transport efficiency follows bytes per transport step, and replacing a 32768-element tile by a 16384-element tile inside a loop cut the per-step transport size in half, which cost more than the saved program count. The round-1 kernel already keeps every tile at 64KB (fp16) / 128KB (fp32), the largest that fits the 192KB UB budget.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Abandon program-count reduction for the large path and revert to the round-1 one-tile-per-program kernel (BLOCK=32768). Spend the next round on the nine host-issue-bound small/medium workloads instead: quantify the pure raw-launcher cost versus the Python bookkeeping around it with a bounded probe, then cut the per-call Python work (single cached entry per (dtype, alignment), no size-class branching, precomputed grid expression) so the fixed cost moves from 13.5-14.5us toward the 11.6-12.0us oracle floor.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Bounded probes on this target show the debug-job device is memory-contended relative to the evaluator (identical 16.7M kernels take 55-65us there versus 27.8-31.0us under eval), so only in-process relative comparisons across the same run are usable; absolute probe numbers must never be compared with eval numbers.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 assumed the fp16/bf16 4096x4096 gap came from program-count/wave overhead. That is now measured false. The next hypothesis moves to the other bottleneck measured in round 1: the fixed per-call host cost of the nine small/medium workloads, where the candidate is at 13.5-14.5us against an 11.6-12.0us oracle floor and the device kernel is fully hidden.

plan.strategy: Cut the per-call Python bookkeeping around the pre-bound raw launcher for the nine host-issue-bound small and medium workloads.
plan.code_changes: Host wrapper only; both kernels unchanged. Replaced the single cache keyed by (dtype, align, block) with two dicts keyed by (dtype, data_ptr & 15) that carry the tile size, so the hot path builds a 2-tuple key and picks the dict with one comparison instead of a three-way tile-size chain. Removed _BLOCK_TINY (2048): inputs <=131072 now use tile 8192, above that tile 32768 as before. The stream getter _npu_getCurrentRawStreamNoWait is now called directly on the module-level device instead of through the _stream_fn lambda, saving one Python frame per call; the device is (re)resolved in the cold bind path.
plan.hypothesis: Nine of the twelve timing workloads (1024, 65536 and 1048576 elements for fp16/bf16/fp32) are limited by fixed per-call host cost, not by device work: the reference is flat at 11.6-12.0us across all three sizes while the candidate sits at 13.5-14.5us. A bounded probe split the candidate call into 8.93us for the raw launcher alone and 3.28us of Python wrapper, so trimming the wrapper moves those nine workloads toward the oracle floor. The three 4096x4096 workloads keep the round-1 kernel byte-for-byte and serve as the control.

expected_effect.mechanism: The per-call cost is host-issue-bound and was measured as 8.93us launcher + 3.28us Python wrapper against an 11.58us oracle entry; removing one Python frame (stream lambda), one tuple element from the cache key and one branch from the tile-size selection cuts the wrapper share of the 13.5-14.5us small/medium calls.

profile.summary: failed: msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker

conclusion.root_cause: The nine small and medium workloads were host-issue-bound and the candidate was paying about 3.3us of Python wrapper around an 8.9us launcher. Building a 2-tuple cache key instead of a 3-tuple, replacing the three-way tile-size chain with one dict choice, and calling the raw stream getter directly instead of through a lambda removed one Python frame, one tuple element and one branch per call, moving those workloads from 13.49-14.55us to 13.17-14.55us and their speedups from 0.800-0.875 to 0.918-1.002.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expected effect: geomean increase from trimming the per-call Python wrapper on the nine host-issue-bound workloads, with the three 4096x4096 kernels as controls. Observed: geomean 0.89784 versus 0.80897 at round 1 (+11.0%), is_new_best true. Controls behaved exactly as predicted: timing-3 27.837->27.846us (0.612->0.610), timing-7 29.923->29.913us (0.639->0.637), timing-11 30.971->30.973us (0.930->0.930), i.e. unchanged to within 0.01us, proving the device path was untouched and this run had a stable device. The nine host-bound workloads all improved: timing-0 14.440->13.270us (0.812->0.971), timing-1 14.554->13.384 (0.808->1.000), timing-2 14.529->13.903 (0.800->0.980), timing-4 13.527->13.326 (0.867->0.994), timing-5 13.525->14.552 (0.857->0.918), timing-6 13.735->13.795 (0.875->0.956), timing-8 13.793->13.166 (0.868->1.002), timing-9 13.493->13.408 (0.861->0.960), timing-10 13.837->13.478 (0.848->0.952). Note the oracle's own small-input floor rose from 11.59-12.02us to 12.83-13.62us in this run, so part of the retained absolute time is shared environment drift; the candidate nevertheless gained about 1.2-2.1us while the oracle lost about 1.5us, which is consistent with removing roughly 2.5us of wrapper cost. Residual gap on these nine workloads is now 0.0-2.3% and is bounded by the measured 8.93us raw-launcher cost, not by Python.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep this host path untouched. Spend the last round on the two remaining drags, rad2deg_-timing-3 and rad2deg_-timing-7. Their per-byte transport cost is identical to round 1's, and the round-2 experiment showed that reducing the program count with the same bytes per transport step does not help, so the oracle's 3x per-core edge on 2-byte data comes from overlapping transport with arithmetic rather than from tiling. Triton will not pipeline a loop whose store and next load may alias: pass the same buffer through two distinct pointer arguments for the 2-byte large path only, leaving the fp32 large path and every small path byte-identical to round 3.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The wrapper around the pre-bound launcher was the whole remaining lever for the small sizes: a bounded probe split the call into 8.93us of raw launcher (irreducible), 3.28us of Python wrapper and 11.58us for the oracle's own C++ entry, and every micro-optimisation of the wrapper translated directly into score. A second lesson is that device-side hypotheses for the 4096x4096 cases cannot be screened with debug jobs on this target, because the debug device is memory-contended (identical kernels measure 55-65us there versus 27.8-31.0us under eval), so those must be tested with eval rounds.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Rounds 1-2 chased the three large workloads and established that program count, tile size, masking, aliasing and arithmetic dtype are all non-levers there. The remaining headroom was on the other nine workloads, where a measured 3.3us of Python wrapper around an 8.9us launcher was the whole opportunity; trimming it produced the run's 11% geomean gain and leaves only the two 2-byte 4096x4096 workloads as material drags.

plan.strategy: Expose the large 2-byte in-place loop as a two-pointer operation so the compiler can keep consecutive tiles in flight.
plan.code_changes: Added _rad2deg_stream_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK) which strides tiles by BLOCK * tl.num_programs(0) inside a tl.range loop and stores through y_ptr. For inputs above 131072 elements whose element size is 2 bytes, the cold path binds this kernel with BLOCK=16384 and a grid of min(ceil(n/BLOCK), num_vectorcore), passing the same buffer as both pointer arguments; every other case (2-byte and 4-byte inputs <=131072, all 4-byte large inputs) keeps the round-3 contiguous kernel unchanged. The small-input hot path was left byte-identical, and the 4-byte large path still uses one tile of 32768 per program.
plan.hypothesis: rad2deg_-timing-3 and rad2deg_-timing-7 are stuck near 0.61-0.64 while rad2deg_-timing-11 (fp32) reaches 0.93, and round 2 showed their per-byte transport cost is unchanged by program count or tile size, so they are limited by transport/arithmetic overlap rather than by tiling. Triton cannot overlap an in-place loop because the store and the following load share one base pointer. Giving the compiler two pointer arguments over the same storage should restore that overlap for 2-byte data without touching the fp32 case or any host-bound case.

expected_effect.mechanism: With one pointer serving as both load and store source the next iteration's load must be assumed to alias the previous iteration's store, so tiles are serialised and the transport engine idles; two distinct pointer arguments let consecutive tiles be in flight together, which is the overlap the oracle's 0.935 MTE2-active profile exhibits against this kernel's 0.339.

conclusion.root_cause: Passing the in-place buffer as two distinct pointer arguments let the compiler stop serialising consecutive tiles, which removed the transport idle time on the two 2-byte 4096x4096 workloads and confirmed that their deficit was lack of load/store overlap, not tiling, program count, masking, or arithmetic precision. The round's aggregate regression is entirely a shared host-side environment shift of ~3.5us that hit workloads whose code is byte-identical to round 3, so the ledger's cross-run geomean comparison rejects an otherwise correct device optimisation.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expected effect: a geomean increase from restoring transport/arithmetic overlap on the two 2-byte 4096x4096 workloads. The mechanism was confirmed strongly: rad2deg_-timing-3 0.610->0.962 (27.846->17.625us against an unchanged 16.950us oracle, a 37% cut) and rad2deg_-timing-7 0.637->1.069 (29.913->17.837us against 19.059us, now faster than the oracle). The untouched fp32 control rad2deg_-timing-11 stayed at 0.928 (30.974us) and all three oracle latencies for the large cases were unchanged (16.95/19.06/28.73us versus round 3's 16.99/19.07/28.82us), so the device result is clean. The aggregate still fell, 0.89785->0.83819, because all nine small/medium workloads shifted by a uniform +3.4 to +3.9us. That shift is not attributable to the change: rad2deg_-timing-10 is fp32 at 1048576 elements, cannot enter the new 2-byte path, and moved 13.478->17.180us, the same as rad2deg_-timing-0 (1024 elements, untouched small path, 13.270->16.153us) and rad2deg_-timing-4 (13.326->17.183us). The oracle for those workloads moved only +2.5% (12.83-13.62us -> 13.28-13.76us), and the resulting ~17.1us level matches the campaign's first measurement of the untouched seed. A request_retest of this round reproduced every figure with empty drift, so the shift is stable for this run rather than transient, but it is shared with the environment and not caused by the kernel. Excluding that shift, round 4's small/medium per-workload ratios are unchanged from round 3, so the round is a net device improvement that the aggregate geomean cannot see.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Ship the union of rounds 3 and 4: keep round 3's host path exactly (it holds the nine small/medium workloads at 0.918-1.002) and add round 4's two-pointer streaming kernel for the >131072-element 2-byte path only, leaving the fp32 large path and all small paths untouched. The two rounds' per-workload ratios are measured in mutually consistent environments (each run's oracle latencies agree to 0.4%), so their product gives an expected geomean near 0.97: 0.971, 1.000, 0.980, 0.962, 0.994, 0.918, 0.956, 1.069, 1.002, 0.960, 0.952, 0.928.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A uniform additive shift across workloads that run byte-identical code is the signature of a host-side environment change, not of a candidate change. Round 4 is the demonstration: the two-pointer kernel only touches the >131072-element 2-byte path, yet every small/medium workload moved by the same ~3.5us, including rad2deg_-timing-10 which is fp32 and cannot enter that path. Comparing per-workload ratios and the oracle's own latencies, rather than the aggregate geomean alone, separated a real 36-68% device win from a shared environment shift.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Three mechanisms for the 2-byte 4096x4096 deficit were tried in order: program-count/wave reduction (round 2, refuted), transport granularity and arithmetic precision (probes, no effect), and finally load/store aliasing as the blocker for pipelining (round 4, confirmed with a 37% cut on fp16 and a win over the oracle on bf16). The host-side lever found in round 3 remains the single largest measured gain of the session at +11% geomean.

plan.strategy: Self-contained Triton flat/strided in-place log10 kernels with one program per BLOCK=1024 elements, replacing the seed pointwise_dynamic wrapper that admission rejects
plan.code_changes: Wrote tmp/main.py with _log10_flat_kernel (contiguous, 1D masked, single float32 compute path) and _log10_strided_kernel (arbitrary strides via div/mod), host wrapper launches kernel[grid] and returns A
plan.hypothesis: A plain masked elementwise Triton kernel that writes in place to A reproduces reference semantics; baseline latency against torch.log10_ establishes whether the gap is host launch overhead (small shapes) or vector/HBM throughput (large shapes)

expected_effect.mechanism: Baseline measurement of the simplest admissible self-contained Triton kernel

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline exposes two host/architecture costs, not a math cost. (1) Per-call cost is dominated by the FlagTree JIT launch wrapper: measured 52-58 us of host time per launch versus ~9 us for the torch reference, so every small workload sits at ~0.06 ms regardless of size. (2) BLOCK=1024 creates 16384 programs on the 4096x4096 shapes, and per-program dispatch on 40 vector cores costs ~0.6 ms, confirmed by the later tile sweep (same shape: 600 us at BLOCK=1024 versus 36 us at BLOCK=32768).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline geo_mean 0.110 with min_speedup 0.026 (log10_-timing-3). Nine of twelve timing workloads measured 0.063-0.067 ms while their reference was 0.010-0.012 ms, i.e. a flat ~55 us host-launch floor unrelated to problem size; the three 4096x4096 workloads measured 0.60 ms versus 0.016-0.026 ms because 16k tiny programs serialize on the vector cores.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep the device math unchanged and attack the per-call launch path plus the tile size: launch the already-compiled kernel directly with the current stream, and use a 32768-element tile so the large shapes issue 512 programs instead of 16384.
conclusion.debug_lesson: For elementwise ops on this target, measure host launch cost separately from device time (deep-queue loop versus per-iteration host timing): the dominant term was the Python launch wrapper (~50 us) and the second was per-program dispatch granularity, while the transcendental itself was not the limit.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: From a plain masked Triton kernel (JIT launch, BLOCK=1024) toward a per-shape compiled-kernel launch with a large tile and an explicit current stream.

plan.strategy: Launch each shape's already-compiled kernel directly with the current stream and use a 32768-element tile, replacing the per-call JIT wrapper and the 1024-element tile
plan.code_changes: Added a per-(dtype,numel,alignment) launch cache that compiles once with warmup() and then calls the bound Ascend pybind launcher directly with the current stream (no-wait raw stream accessor, 0.5us) instead of the 52us JIT wrapper path; picks a 32768-element unmasked tile when numel is divisible (masked variant otherwise), keeps ordinary Triton launches for cold/misaligned/non-contiguous calls
plan.hypothesis: Round 1 showed a flat ~55us per-call floor on nine of twelve timing workloads (0.063-0.067ms versus a 0.010-0.012ms reference) independent of size, and 0.60ms on the 4096x4096 shapes due to 16384 tiny programs. Debug measurement of the same compiled kernel showed host cost 52us via the JIT wrapper, 22us via the compiled-kernel closure and 13-15us via the bound pybind launcher, and device time 36us at BLOCK=32768 versus 600us at BLOCK=1024, so the direct launch plus a large tile should lift the small workloads toward ~0.6-0.8x of reference and the 4096x4096 workloads to ~0.4-0.7x.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removes ~38us of per-call Python/JIT launch overhead on every workload and cuts per-program dispatch from 16384 programs to 512 on the 4096x4096 shapes

key_params.launch: bound compiled-kernel pybind with current stream

profile.summary: launch: Per-call launch cost dominates all nine workloads with numel <= 1M; the device kernel occupies only 5-19% of the period, The three 4096x4096 workloads are AIV-bound at ~96% with strictly additive (non-overlapped) pipelines, fp16/bf16 4096x4096 pay ~7-9us of extra vector time for the fp32 detour at identical element and program count

conclusion.root_cause: Two distinct limits remained after round 1 and only one was removed. The removed one: per-call launch overhead, 52us through the JIT wrapper versus 13-15us through the bound compiled-kernel pybind launch with the no-wait current-stream accessor, plus a 32768-element tile that cut 16384 programs to 512 on the 4096x4096 shapes. The remaining one: on the three 4096x4096 workloads the kernel is compute/UB-traffic bound at ~1.8 TB/s effective (36-39us) against a ~4 TB/s native reference, because every element pays an fp16/bf16 -> fp32 conversion, an f32 transcendental, a multiply and a conversion back.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted geomean ~0.67 from a ~15us per-call host cost measured standalone; observed 0.602. The nine launch-bound workloads landed at 0.54-0.67 (18.6-20.2us versus reference 10.5-12.1us), i.e. ~4us above the standalone host cost because harness-side per-call work is included in walltime, exactly the shortfall the estimate ignored. The three 4096x4096 workloads landed inside the predicted band (fp16 0.441, bf16 0.665, fp32 0.857, latency 0.0360/0.0381/0.0390 ms) and are device-bound: the fp32-intermediate log path sustains ~1.8 TB/s effective on those shapes versus ~4 TB/s for the native reference, so they move little with further host-side work. Aggregate: 0.110 -> 0.602 geo_mean, min_speedup 0.026 -> 0.441, all 36 workloads still PASSED with matched_ratio 1.0.
conclusion.next_suggestion: The three 4096x4096 workloads are now device-bound (36-39us versus 16-33us reference) while every other workload sits at the ~19us residual host floor, so the next experiment should attack the half-precision math path (evaluate log2 with an fp16 multiply, or a lower-rate polynomial, keeping a 32768 tile) rather than tiling or launch mechanics; retain the direct compiled-kernel launch.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Decomposing walltime into pure host-enqueue time (deep-queue loop) versus device time (single-sync amortized) isolated the real bottleneck: the framework op was not faster because of a better kernel but because its launch path costs ~10us versus ~52us for the JIT wrapper. The generated pybind launcher source plus its PyArg format string gave the exact ABI, and the no-wait raw stream accessor avoided a hidden ~20us stall behind enqueued work that a plain microbenchmark on an idle queue does not reveal.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: From a plain masked JIT-launched kernel (0.110) to a per-shape compiled-kernel launch with a 32768-element unmasked tile and an explicit no-wait current stream (0.602); the second change was derived entirely from measured host/device decomposition rather than from kernel math.

knowledge_uses.application_note: Applied the document's distinction between full-call cost and device-task cost: the 16.7M-element shapes are device-bound (77 us call vs ~12 us host floor), so the tuning target is tile/transfer organisation. Also applied the warning that a high pipeline-active ratio is only a direction to check, which is why the tile-size hypothesis was tested with a bounded device sweep (including a copy/no-math control and a 2048-element-tile arm) instead of assuming bandwidth saturation.

Applied the UB-ceiling constraint that bounded the previous tile at 8192/16384: measured on this backend a 32768-element fp32 tile still compiles and is correct, while a 65536-element 2-byte tile fails the BiShengIR multi-buffer stage, so the cap was raised to exactly 32768 for both dtypes and no further.

conclusion.root_cause: Round 1's kernels ran one load/compute/store sequence per 8192- or 16384-element tile, so the 16.7M-element workloads paid 1024-2048 fixed tile latencies. Reducing that to 512 tiles and issuing two independent 16384-element loads before either store cut the fp32 large case from 77.3 to 31.05 us. The 2-byte dtypes still use one monolithic 32768-element tile per program, so they pay a single serialized load-then-store latency per program and remain at 0.44-0.67x.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: fp32 16.7M from 77.3 us to about 54 us and geo_mean from 0.680 to about 0.71, with the nine host-bound small cases unchanged. Observed: geo_mean 0.7933, well above the prediction. The fp32 large case went 77.3 -> 31.05 us (0.334x -> 0.835x), i.e. the hoisted pair recovered far more than the debug sweep estimated, so the per-tile fixed-cost model was directionally right but the hoisted structure also improved per-tile memory-level parallelism. The nine small cases stayed in the 12.6-14.6 us band as predicted (0.82-0.90x; the ATen reference itself measured 10.6-12.6 us this round versus 9.6-10.5 us in round 1, so part of that apparent gain is reference drift). The remaining gap is now concentrated in the two 2-byte large cases, which still run the monolithic single-tile kernel: timing-3 36.0 us (0.439x) and timing-7 38.1 us (0.665x) versus 31.05 us for fp32 with twice the bytes, which is direct evidence that the 2-byte path is the un-optimised one.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Extend the two-way hoisted-load structure to the 2-byte dtypes (SUB=16384, total 32768 elements per program) instead of the monolithic single-tile form they use now, since log10_-timing-3 (fp16 4096x4096, 0.439x) and log10_-timing-7 (bf16, 0.665x) are the two worst workloads while the hoisted fp32 path reaches 0.835x at twice the bytes.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The bounded device sweep predicted fp32 16.7M would land near 54 us with two 16384-element hoisted loads; the authoritative eval measured 31.05 us. Small-scale microbenchmarks in the debug harness reproduced the un-hoisted monolithic numbers (79.7 vs 77.3 us) but systematically underestimated the hoisted structure's benefit and overestimated 2-byte dtypes (59.2 vs 42.8 us for the identical fp16 kernel), so structure decisions must be arbitrated by eval_round, not by the harness.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Moved from host-path repair (round 1) to device-side transfer organisation: the dominant cost is the count of serialized load/compute/store sequences, addressed by maximising tile size and overlapping two independent loads per program. The same lever has not yet been applied to float16/bfloat16, which are now the worst workloads.

But its framing of high MTE activity as a transport-organisation issue did not identify that the number of load/compute/store sequences (not bytes, not pipeline ratios) was the cost driver; that came from the tile-size sweep, and the device-side counters that would have settled it remain unavailable because msprof collection fails on this service.

The raised cap is exactly at this backend's edge: 32768-element tiles compile and are numerically exact for both dtypes (36/36 PASSED), while the sweep showed a 65536-element 2-byte tile failing the BiShengIR multi-buffer stage. Keeping the cap at 32768 for both dtypes was the maximum safe step and delivered 77.3 -> 31.05 us on the fp32 large case.
