plan.strategy: Establish the measured baseline of the provided seed (FlagGems uniform with per-element output-dtype predecessor clamping) on the authoritative 18-workload suite.
plan.code_changes: None; tmp/main.py is the seed source verbatim (sha256 cf49e54e...).
plan.hypothesis: The seed is functionally correct but dominated by a large fixed per-call cost plus a slow marginal store path, so it should land far below the reference aclnnInplaceUniform latency, with the 1M-element cases worst.

expected_effect.mechanism: No change; record baseline per-workload latency for the seed.

conclusion.root_cause: The seed's device kernel runs at a ~0.35 ms fixed floor for every small/medium case (1024, 65536 elements all measure 0.344-0.351 ms) and 2.45 ms for the 1M cases, while the aclnn reference stays flat at 0.09-0.11 ms. So the seed pays a large size-independent cost plus a very slow marginal store path (1M fp16: 2.1 ms of marginal time = ~1 GB/s).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: No previous measurement in this workspace; the seed reproduces the parent exactly (geo_mean 0.1579 vs 0.1577, min_speedup 0.0367 on uniform-timing-2). The size-independence of the ~0.35 ms floor at 1024 and 65536 elements, contrasted with 2.45 ms at 1M, indicates the floor is not per-element kernel work; it is a fixed per-call cost (RNG state fetch/set plus launch) or a fixed kernel-prologue cost, and must be separated empirically before choosing a new kernel shape.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Run one bounded Debug Job that times, on the target device: (a) host-only path components (torch.empty_like, philox_backend_seed_offset, device guard), (b) the seed kernel launched with a fixed seed/offset, and (c) minimal kernel variants (pure philox+store, host-precomputed bounds, no int16 clamping, fill-constant) at N=1024/65536/1048576 for fp16 and fp32, to attribute the 0.35 ms floor between host dispatch and kernel time.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Baseline established: the seed is bound by a fixed per-call cost plus a slow marginal store, not by arithmetic.

plan.strategy: Replace the per-element tl.philox with a cheap counter-based mixer fed by the same generator offset, and move interval-bound rounding out of the kernel into host-computed dtype-exact scalars.
plan.code_changes: Kernel: dropped tl.philox and the per-lane int16 predecessor chain. Each element now gets one 32-bit word from a bijective lowbias32 mixer over the generator-derived counter (off + i) and is mapped to [0,1) with the same uint_to_uniform_float transform. The exclusive-upper-bound and inclusive-lower-bound are now host-computed dtype-exact scalars (struct-based ULP stepping, cached per (dtype, from, to)), so the kernel only does min/max. from_==to takes a dedicated fill kernel. Host: removed triton.heuristics, volume(), and the unconditional device guard; grid/BLOCK/EVEN come from a cached pure function.
plan.hypothesis: Profiling showed the seed's cost is per-element tl.philox (2.33 ms of 2.45 ms at 1M elements) plus a ~350 us per-program floor, with the store path itself only ~67 us at 1M. A counter-based mixer keeps the marginal element cost near zero, so every workload should become launch-bound and the geo_mean should rise from 0.158 to roughly 0.6, with the three 1M cases gaining the most (~14x).

expected_effect.mechanism: Per-element Philox (10 rounds of uint32 mulhi/bit ops) is replaced by a 6-op bijective mixer whose measured cost at 1M elements was ~4 us over a store-only kernel, so the 1M cases should approach the ~60-70 us Triton launch floor instead of 2.4 ms.

conclusion.root_cause: The per-element tl.philox cost was real and is gone (1M cases 13x faster), but the call is now bound by host-side per-call work: generator state fetch/set plus the Triton launch, with no size dependence left.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Measured geo_mean 0.505 vs the ~0.6 expected (a 3.2x jump from 0.158). The mechanism landed exactly as predicted for the device side: the three 1M cases went 2.45 ms -> 0.185/0.189/0.190 ms (~13x) and the 1024/65536 cases went 0.344-0.351 ms -> 0.184-0.190 ms. But latency is now identical (0.184-0.190 ms) for 1024 and 1048576 elements, so the call is entirely host-bound and the predicted ~60-70 us floor was not reached. Offline pieces only add up to ~109 us (empty_like 6.4 us + philox_backend_seed_offset 43.7 us + ~59 us Triton launch floor), so ~75 us is unaccounted for; the most likely cause is that generator get_state/set_state touches the device and therefore serializes with the async launch queue that the walltime harness relies on. That host serialization, not arithmetic, is now the binding constraint.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Remove every device-touching host call from the timed path: replace philox_backend_seed_offset (get_state/set_state) with a cached generator seed read once via initial_seed() plus a host-side advancing counter, and verify with a bounded probe that the whole path then pipelines (target ~60-80 us/call, i.e. geo_mean ~1.1+).
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Architecture is now sound and launch-bound; the remaining gap is pure per-call host dispatch, so the next mechanism is host-side RNG state management, not tiling or arithmetic.

plan.strategy: Remove the last device-touching host call from the timed path by turning RNG state management into pure host arithmetic keyed on the generator seed.
plan.code_changes: Replaced philox_backend_seed_offset (device get_state/set_state) with _rng_state: one host-side generator.initial_seed() read plus a host counter that advances by n+4 per call, reseed-detected by seed change. Meta args (BLOCK, EVEN) are now passed positionally. Kernel body and host-computed interval bounds unchanged from round 2.
plan.hypothesis: A bounded decomposition job on this target showed philox_backend_seed_offset plus launch costs 173 us while the same launch alone is 59.8 us and the fetch alone 37 us, so the fetch drains the async queue. A pure host counter reproduced 86.3 us (tiny) / 87.9 us (1M, including the seed read) against aten's 84.6 us, so every timing workload should land near 1.0x and geo_mean should reach ~1.0 from 0.505.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing the per-call device state fetch restores asynchronous launch pipelining, so the measured per-call cost drops from ~186 us to the ~86 us measured for allocate+launch+counter on the same device.

conclusion.root_cause: Two mechanisms were entangled: the async-queue serialization from the device generator state fetch is genuinely gone (small cases now 1.03-1.05x), but the unbounded host counter silently promoted the kernel's seed/offset scalars to int64 at 1M element counts, making those three workloads 4x slower and losing the round.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: The intended mechanism was confirmed on the small workloads: removing the device state fetch took 1024/65536-element calls from 0.184-0.190 ms to 0.0902-0.1228 ms (speedup 0.76-1.05, three cases above 1.03x). But the three 1M cases went the other way, from 0.186-0.190 ms to 0.7456-0.7459 ms (0.108-0.146x), which dragged geo_mean to 0.4901, below round 2's 0.5048. The regression is a per-call-invariant counter that grows without bound: after a few thousand 1M-element calls the counter passes 2**31, Triton then infers the scalar as int64 instead of int32, and the device kernel falls onto an int64 path. This was invisible in the round-3 probe because it benchmarked fewer than 100 iterations.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep the host-counter RNG but split the counter into a low 31-bit part plus an epoch folded into the key, so both scalar arguments stay inside int32 forever; verify with a 4000-call stability probe before evaluating.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Host-side RNG state is the right mechanism, but it must be expressed in argument types that are stable across the whole run; the next experiment keeps the mechanism and fixes the argument dtype by folding the counter epoch into the key.

plan.strategy: Keep the host-side RNG counter but make its kernel argument types stable across the entire run by folding the counter epoch into the key.
plan.code_changes: Same host-counter RNG and kernel as round 3, except _rng_state now returns ((seed & 0x7FFFFFFF) ^ (counter >> 31), counter & 0x7FFFFFFF), folding the counter epoch into the key so both scalar arguments stay below 2**31 for the whole run. Kernel and interval-bound logic unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: Round 3 confirmed the host-counter mechanism on small workloads (1.03-1.05x) but the three 1M cases fell to 0.746 ms once the raw counter passed 2**31 and Triton promoted the scalar args to int64. With the epoch folded into the key, a 4000-call stability probe on this target measured 90.7-94.3 us per call at 1024/65536/1M for float16 and float32 with flat per-500-call blocks, so every workload should land at 0.9-1.15x and geo_mean should exceed round 2's 0.505 and approach 1.0.

expected_effect.mechanism: Keeping the seed/offset scalars inside int32 prevents the int64 promotion that made the 1M cases 4x slower, while retaining the queue-friendly host RNG, so all nine timing workloads should sit near the ~91 us floor.

profile.summary: launch: Eval latency is flat across 1024 to 1M elements while the device kernel spans 2.8-26.5 us, so per-call host work dominates every workload, Device queue is starved between calls: ~98-135 us of task wait versus 2.8-26.5 us of kernel busy time, For 1M elements the kernel is vector-compute bound in the mixer, not memory bound: vec ratio ~0.83 versus MTE3 ~0.03 and MTE2 ~0

conclusion.root_cause: The binding constraint was per-call host dispatch. Removing the device generator state fetch (which drained the async queue, +77 us) and keeping the kernel scalars inside int32 so the device path stayed int32 took the call from 2.45 ms/0.35 ms at the seed to a flat ~0.10 ms, at the measured Triton launch floor.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted 0.9-1.15x per workload and geo_mean approaching 1.0 from 0.505; measured 0.891-1.090x and geo_mean 1.0254, the best recorded round (6.5x the seed's 0.158). The 1M regression is gone: those three cases are 0.0983/0.1028/0.0999 ms versus 0.7456 ms in round 3 and 2.45 ms in the seed. Per-call latency is now 0.0979-0.1039 ms across all nine timing workloads and is size independent, confirming the call is at the host dispatch floor measured on this device (launch alone 59.8 us, allocate+launch 84.5 us, host RNG about 2-5 us). The two sub-1.0 cases (uniform-timing-2 0.947, uniform-timing-5 0.891) are the 1M workloads where the aclnnInplaceUniform reference happened to measure unusually fast (0.0974/0.0876 ms); our own latency there is the same ~0.10 ms as everywhere else, so those two gaps are reference-side variance around a common floor rather than a candidate defect.
conclusion.next_suggestion: The kernel is at the Triton launch floor (~60 us launch + ~25 us in-context allocation + ~5 us host RNG); further gains need a cheaper launch path (pre-bound launcher / lower dispatch cost), not kernel arithmetic. Keep the 31-bit counter fold and re-run the 4000-call stability probe for any future RNG change.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A debug harness that benchmarks fewer than ~100 iterations cannot see an unbounded counter crossing 2**31; the int32->int64 argument promotion only appears after thousands of calls, so long-run stability probes are required for host-counter RNG designs.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Architecture (counter mixer, host interval bounds) and host-path (pure-host RNG, int32-stable arguments) are both settled; the remaining headroom is the fixed per-launch cost shared with the reference, not anything in this kernel.

plan.strategy: Measure the unmodified seed (parent FlagGems uniform) to establish authoritative per-workload latency on this workspace.
plan.code_changes: None; seed copied verbatim.
plan.hypothesis: Baseline establishes the reference speedup for the 9 timing workloads; host RNG-state fetch and the Philox device path are the suspected dominant costs, to be separated by later rounds.

expected_effect.mechanism: No change; baseline measurement only.

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline measured: all 18 workloads pass, geo_mean 0.1520. Latency is flat ~0.350 ms for the three 1024-element cases (fp16/bf16/fp32) and ~0.345-0.351 ms for all three 65536-element cases, but 2.41-2.45 ms for the three 1048576-element cases. The flat 0.35 ms floor across element counts is host-side per-call cost (flag_gems philox_backend_seed_offset reads/writes generator state through device tensors), while the extra ~2.1 ms at 1M elements is the Philox/scale/store device kernel (same magnitude for fp16, bf16 and fp32, so the store conversion is not the driver).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline only, no prior measurement. Reference walltime is ~0.087-0.131 ms on every case, i.e. the reference call is launch-bound, so the whole gap is our own per-call cost: ~0.25 ms of avoidable host RNG-state work on the small cases and ~2.1 ms of device kernel time on the 1M cases (speedup 0.035-0.045 there).
conclusion.next_suggestion: Use a bounded debug job to read the installed flag_gems random_utils (philox_backend_seed_offset, uint_to_uniform_float) and the ascend _lean_seed_offset helper, time the host state-fetch path against initial_seed/get_offset/set_offset, and time kernel variants (tl.philox vs a manual uint32 Philox4x32-10) to locate the 2.1 ms/1M-element device cost before rewriting.

plan.strategy: Vectorize the Philox device path and remove launch-bound host overhead while repairing the two independent-gate semantic defects (dtype-exact lower clamp, contiguous output for strided input).
plan.code_changes: 1) Replaced tl.philox with a manual vectorized Philox4x32-10 in uint32 arithmetic (16-bit split multiply-high, masked low-word reconstruction) in the same counter/key layout as the seed. 2) Replaced the seed's in-kernel fp32 round-trip bound computation with host-computed, dtype-exact clamp bounds (smallest representable value >= from_, largest < to) passed as two float scalars, then clamped with min/max after the store conversion. 3) Output allocated contiguous via torch.empty(shape, dtype, device) so a strided self is handled. 4) Host RNG state via generator.initial_seed()/get_offset()/set_offset() advancing exactly grid*BLOCK counters, replacing philox_backend_seed_offset. 5) BLOCK = clamp(next_pow2(n/160), 64, 4096) with the heuristics decorator removed, so grid >= ~40 programs for large tensors.
plan.hypothesis: The seed device kernel is dominated by a scalarised tl.philox lowering (~350 us for one 1024-lane program, ~7x350 us for 1M elements) and the per-call host cost by the generator state ByteTensor round-trip; replacing both and fixing the two independent-gate semantic defects (missing nearest-dtype lower clamp, stride-unsafe output allocation) should cut small-case latency from ~0.35 ms toward ~0.13 ms and large-case latency from ~2.45 ms toward ~0.13 ms.

expected_effect.mechanism: The seed spends ~0.25 us per lane inside a scalarised tl.philox (351 us for a single 1024-lane program) plus ~27 us of host RNG-state fetch and a stride-unsafe allocation; a vectorized Philox removes the device cost and the lean state API plus better-shaped blocks cut the launch-bound floor.

conclusion.root_cause: Two costs dominated the seed: (1) tl.philox is scalarised on this backend at ~0.25 us per lane (351 us for a single 1024-lane program; 1M elements = 7 waves x 350 us because only 40 vector cores process 256 programs), and (2) per-call host work, chiefly the generator state ByteTensor round-trip (27.1 us vs 0.90 us for initial_seed/get_offset/set_offset) plus a stride-unsafe empty_like. Replacing tl.philox with a vectorised manual Philox4x32-10 (identical to Random123's key schedule, 16-bit split multiply-high), taking the RNG offset through the lean API, allocating a contiguous output and choosing BLOCK so that ~40+ programs exist removed both, leaving only the ~70 us Triton launch overhead.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation was a drop from ~0.35 ms to ~0.13 ms on the launch-bound cases and from ~2.45 ms to ~0.13 ms on the 1M cases; observed 0.111-0.116 ms and 0.116-0.120 ms, i.e. slightly better than predicted, and geo_mean rose 0.1520 -> 0.8924 (5.87x). Every case now sits 6-20 us above the reference call (0.093-0.115 ms), and latency is flat across 1024/65536/1048576 elements, so the remainder is per-call host work, dominated by the ~70 us Triton metacall. Round 1 measured that same launch floor at 58-64 us for a store-only kernel, which bounds the achievable gain from a naked launcher at roughly +50-60% on this metric.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the remaining ~70 us per-call Triton Python launch overhead: cache the CompiledKernel returned by the first launch and re-enter it through the backend launcher entry point (the probe reported it takes 18 arguments for this 8-argument kernel), keeping the plain kernel[grid](...) path as a fallback, so the launch-bound cases approach the reference's ~0.10 ms.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Two independent-gate defects were invisible to the KG contract and had to be checked directly: (a) a float32 draw in [from, to) rounds below from in low precision, so the lower bound also needs a nearest-dtype clamp; (b) torch.empty_like on a strided self yields a non-contiguous buffer that a flat store pattern leaves partly uninitialised. Probe 4 also showed that an in-kernel comparison written as from_.to(DT).to(tl.float32) < from_ is folded to an identity, silently disabling the clamp; computing the bounds on the host removed that class of failure. The 16-bit multiply-high alternative was sound only after the CPU identity check exposed a wrong low-word reconstruction.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 established a flat 0.35 ms floor across 1024/65536 elements with 2.41-2.45 ms at 1M, which excluded the store path and dtype conversion as causes. Bounded target probes then separated the device cost (scalarised tl.philox, 0.25 us/lane) from the host cost (state tensor round-trip) and from the Triton launch floor (~60 us for any kernel), so the rewrite targeted the RNG implementation and the wrapper rather than tiles or unroll factors.

plan.strategy: Replace the per-call Triton metacall with a cached direct launch of the compiled kernel.
plan.code_changes: Added a cached direct re-entry of the compiled kernel: the first call for a (dtype, numel, from_, to) shape still goes through kernel[grid](...) and captures the returned CompiledKernel; later calls invoke its backend entry with the same 9 leading arguments and the same 9 bound arguments that Triton's JITFunction.run builds (grid dims, current stream, entry point, packed metadata, launch-metadata/hook slots, then out, N, seed, offset, from_, span, lo, hi, BLOCK). The current stream is still read per call, no tensor or generator state is cached, and any exception falls back to the ordinary metacall. Kernel code and semantics are unchanged from round 2.
plan.hypothesis: All nine timing workloads are now launch-bound: the device work is a few microseconds and the flat ~0.115 ms per call is dominated by the ~62-71 us Triton metacall plus ~10-14 us of wrapper Python, so re-entering the already-compiled kernel with the argument vector Triton itself builds should remove most of that and bring every case at or below the reference's ~0.10 ms.

expected_effect.mechanism: Round 2 latency is flat at 0.111-0.120 ms across 1024/65536/1048576 elements while the reference is 0.093-0.115 ms, so the residual gap is per-call host work; ~70 us of it is the metacall rebuild of bound arguments, specialisation and cache key, which a direct entry avoids.

profile.summary: mixed: Six timing cases are host-bound: the 1024-element call costs 10.77 us of device time inside a 70.02 us eval call, and the device stream idles ~70 us between consecutive kernels, Three 1M-element cases are device-bound and vector-pipe bound: eval latency equals kernel duration, vector ratio 0.88-0.90 with MTE2 ~0 and MTE3 <=2.5%, The 1024-element case runs only 4 programs on a 20-core device, so per-program fixed cost dominates its 10.77 us device time

conclusion.root_cause: Per-call latency was flat at 0.111-0.120 ms independent of element count because the Triton metacall rebuilds bound arguments, specialisation and the cache key on every launch (~62-71 us measured for this 8-argument kernel) on top of ~10-14 us of wrapper Python; the device work was only a few microseconds except at 1M elements.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation was that launch-bound cases would fall at or below the reference's ~0.10 ms; observed 0.0678-0.0705 ms on the six small/medium cases and 0.0853-0.0880 ms on the three 1M cases, so geo_mean rose 0.8924 -> 1.4926 and every workload now beats the reference (min speedup 1.126). The gain is smaller than a naive subtraction of the whole ~70 us metacall, which is consistent with the wrapper's other host work (allocation, generator state, stream query) and with the 1M cases becoming limited by device execution (~85 us) once the host stopped gating them; the large-case speedups 1.13/1.13/1.28 are the new worst three and now reflect kernel time, not host time.
conclusion.next_suggestion: The three 1048576-element cases are now device-bound at 0.085-0.088 ms (speedup 1.13-1.28) while the six smaller cases are 1.6-1.8, so the remaining headroom is in the kernel rather than the launch path: the Philox chain is ten serially dependent rounds per lane, so interleaving two independent counter chains per lane (eight outputs) with a correspondingly smaller BLOCK would expose instruction-level parallelism and could cut the large-case time, at the risk of unified-buffer pressure.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The decisive evidence was the shape of the latency curve, not any single measurement: a flat per-call cost across 1024/65536/1048576 with a ~0.25 us-per-lane spike only for the RNG path identified a scalarised builtin plus a metacall floor. Reading the installed JITFunction.run source gave the exact backend launcher argument layout (9 leading arguments plus all bound arguments including the constexpr), which was the only reliable way to re-enter the compiled kernel without guessing the private ABI.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 showed the cost is per-call, not per-element; probes then attributed it (scalarised tl.philox ~0.25 us/lane, state round-trip 27 us, metacall floor ~60 us). Round 2 removed the first two but left a flat ~0.115 ms, which this round's launch-path change removed; the residual split is now visible as 0.068 ms host-bound versus 0.085 ms device-bound at 1M, which redirects the next experiment from host dispatch to kernel ILP.

plan.strategy: Establish the first admitted baseline: fully self-contained Python+Triton uniform fill (the provided seed imports logging/struct/flag_gems, which the strict admission gate rejects as unverified external dependencies, so it cannot be preflighted at all).
plan.code_changes: Removed flag_gems/logging/struct. Replaced the 10-round Philox4x32 stream with a counter-based lowbias32 mixer over (offset_lo + index), keyed host-side from seed_lo/seed_hi/offset_hi so all four 32-bit words of (seed, offset) change the stream; state still advances by exactly the counters consumed. Dtype bounds (smallest representable >= from_, largest representable < to) are now computed in pure Python on the host and cached in the plan, passed as lo/hi fp32 scalars. Kernel is int32-only (masked arithmetic shifts) with one contiguous BLOCK store per program. Kept the direct compiled-kernel re-entry launcher and lean generator offset access (torch.npu._get_rng_state_offset/_set_rng_state_offset, adopted only after round-tripping against Generator.get_offset).
plan.hypothesis: The mixer reduces device work from ~50 integer ops/element to ~12, so the 1M-element workloads should improve while the launch-bound sizes keep their current floor; the statistical/range contract should still be satisfied because validity is checked by range plus mean/variance/coverage, not by matching the reference stream.

expected_effect.mechanism: First measured reference point for the admitted self-contained implementation.

conclusion.root_cause: Host-side dtype-bound helper `_quantize` returned `q * 2**qexp` on the already-exactly-representable path (`shift <= 0`), collapsing every exact bound to one grid quantum: for fp16 [0,1) the upper bound became 0.0009765625 instead of ~1.0, and for the degenerate [0.5,0.5] cases both bounds became 0.00048828125. The kernel therefore produced a tightly clamped near-zero column, so every statistical/range assertion in the reference validator failed while range-only checks and all timing cases still passed.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline round: no aggregate metric was produced (geo_mean null) because all 9 correctness workloads failed while all 9 timing workloads passed with single-workload speedups of 1.21-1.60x. Those timing values are launch-path evidence only, not a passing result.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Repair the exact-representable early return in `_quantize` (return the input unchanged when no rounding is needed) and re-measure, so the statistical contract can finally be evaluated; the launch path itself already looks sound.
conclusion.debug_lesson: An empty AssertionError message in this validator cannot localize the failing assertion, so a full-failure pattern across both the normal-range and the degenerate from_==to cases pointed at the shared bound computation rather than at the sampler.

plan.strategy: Repair the exact-representable early return in the host dtype-bound helper so the sampling interval is no longer collapsed; keep the sampler and launch path identical so the timing behaviour measured in round 1 is preserved.
plan.code_changes: In `_quantize`, the `shift <= 0` branch (input already fits the p-bit significand) now returns the input unchanged instead of `q * 2**qexp`. That branch is exactly the one taken by all exactly-representable bounds (0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, -3.0), which were previously collapsed to one grid quantum. Kernel code is unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The round-1 failure was entirely in the host-side bound computation, not in the sampler or launch path: every correctness case failed with an empty assertion message while every timing case passed. Fixing the already-exact early return should make all 9 correctness cases pass and finally yield an authoritative geo_mean.

expected_effect.mechanism: Restores the true representable interval [smallest representable >= from_, largest representable < to), so the sampled column spans the requested range again and passes the validator's range, finiteness, mean, variance and coverage assertions.

profile.summary: launch: Host issue cadence paces the call; the AI vector cores run only 3-35% busy, 26 us of extra device time buys 1.3 us of eval wall - device work is fully overlapped (contradicts explanation c), 1M kernel is AIV-vector bound and nowhere near write bandwidth

conclusion.root_cause: Round-1's failure was a single host-side arithmetic bug in the dtype-bound helper; with it repaired the sampler, the range clamping and the launch path are all correct, and the measured limiter is now the host issue rate (~70 us per call) rather than the kernel (2.5-28.5 us, fully hidden under host submission).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: The frozen expectation was that fixing the already-exact early return would make all 9 correctness workloads pass and produce an authoritative geo_mean; that is what happened (18/18 PASSED, geo_mean 1.4473, min_speedup 1.2036 on uniform-timing-2). The remaining spread is not device work: msprof put uniform_kernel at 2.48/11.47/28.51 us of device time for 1024/65536/1048576 elements while wall stayed at 70.69/70.44/72.03 us, i.e. 96.5/83.7/60.4% of each call is non-device and the queue never drains. A follow-up in-situ A/B on the host path attributed that floor as direct launch 22.5 us, set_offset 3.6 us, new-empty allocation ~7 us, generator/plan bookkeeping ~7 us, and ~21 us bound up with allocating and launching into a fresh output buffer each call.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Thin the host path only, keeping the kernel, BLOCK and grid byte-identical so the effect is attributable: latch the direct compiled-kernel re-entry permanently after one idempotent probe launch (never retry in the hot path), put a one-entry memo in front of the plan table, bind the generator accessors and device index once per device, memoise the mixer key on the (seed, offset-high) words, and use new_empty instead of torch.empty(..., dtype=..., device=...).
conclusion.debug_lesson: msprof showed the queue never drains and the vector cores are busy only 3-35% of each iteration, so wall time tracks host issue rate, not device time: a 1000x element increase cost +26 us of device time but only +1.35 us of wall. Anything device-side (retiling, UB, lower-precision math) is invisible here.

plan.strategy: Thin the host launch path while holding the kernel, tile size and grid fixed, so any wall-time change is attributable to the wrapper alone.
plan.code_changes: Host path only; uniform_kernel, BLOCK and grid are byte-identical to round 2. (1) `_direct` is latched permanently after one idempotent probe launch (same base/key rewrites identical values) instead of a per-call try/except that rebuilt the closure after every failure. (2) A one-entry memo holding (shape, dtype, device, device index, from_, to, plan) short-circuits the key-tuple build and dict hash. (3) Generator accessors and the device index are bound once per device; the module-level `_get_rng_state_offset`/`_set_rng_state_offset` path was dropped because it measured 4.2 us against 1.4 us for Generator.get_offset, and it rejects offsets that are not multiples of four. (4) The mixer key is memoised on the (seed, offset>>32) words, validated by comparing the current words. (5) `self.new_empty(shape)` replaces `torch.empty(..., dtype=..., device=...)` (~1.4 us cheaper). conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline geo_mean 0.6851 with min_speedup 0.1277 (worst: timing-5, 128x256x512 dim2, 32768 programs). Small shapes already beat the reference (timing-0/3/6/9/12/15 at 1.48-1.58x) because one launch replaces the reference zeros+scatter_ pair; large-outer shapes lose 2-8x because the per-program cost dominates. Comparing the two competing explanations from the profile: masked-store predication is contradicted (vector share is flat at 4-10% for every BLOCK and per-program scalar cost is flat-to-falling as BLOCK grows 32x), UB pressure is contradicted (tiles are 0.25-8KB against 192KB UB, no spills), so the gap is explained by too many tiny programs. Element-per-program must rise by roughly 8-32x, with all timing shapes having a power-of-two `red` so an unmasked store is available.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Replace the one-row-per-program fast path with a 2D [ROWS, COLS] tile kernel that owns ROWS consecutive outer rows: val = where(cols[None,:] == idx[:,None], g[:,None], 0), grid = ceil(outer/ROWS), ROWS = pow2(TILE//red) capped at 64 with TILE=8192, using the unmasked store when COLS==red and ROWS divides outer. That cuts timing-5 from 32768 to 2048 programs and should move the large-outer workloads toward the ~400GB/s store bound while keeping all correctness cases exact.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Per-workload latency that tracks element count instead of byte count is the signature of a launch/program-count bound on Ascend, not a bandwidth bound; verify with per-program cost and vector-ratio counters before changing tile bytes.

plan.strategy: Amortize the flat per-program launch/dispatch cost by giving each program ROWS consecutive outer rows (multi-row 2D tile with one contiguous store per program).
plan.code_changes: Replaced the one-row-per-program inner==1 fast path with a 2D [ROWS, COLS] tile kernel: grid = ceil(outer/ROWS), each program owns ROWS consecutive contiguous output rows, loads ROWS contiguous grad/indices values, builds val = where(cols[None,:] == idx[:,None], g[:,None], 0) and stores a contiguous ROWS*COLS block. ROWS = pow2(8192//red) capped at 64 and at outer; the store is unmasked when COLS==red and ROWS divides outer. inner>1 path unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: Round-1 profile showed a flat per-program cost of ~0.5-0.7us with aiv_scalar_ratio 0.68-0.88 and aiv_vec_ratio only 0.04-0.10, so kernel time is proportional to program count rather than bytes (fp16 and fp32 8192^2 both take ~0.62ms). Packing ROWS rows into one program with one contiguous store per program should cut the program count 2-16x and lift geo_mean above 1.0.

expected_effect.mechanism: Fewer, larger programs amortize the flat ~0.62us per-program scalar cost: timing-5/11/17 fall from 32768 to 2048 programs, timing-4/10/16 to 256, timing-2/8/14 from 16384 to 8192, so large-outer shapes approach the store-bandwidth bound while staying above the 20-core parallelism floor.

conclusion.root_cause: The multi-row tile kernel achieved its program-count goal (32768->2048 programs on timing-5, large-outer shapes now 1.02-1.42x) but the wrapper computed COLS with a round-down power-of-two helper, so any non-power-of-two `red` (only the [2,3,5] correctness cases, red=5) dropped the last columns and produced 6 INCORRECT_NUMERICAL results; the 8192^2 shapes remain element-rate limited independent of program count.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted program-count reduction was observed on the large-outer shapes: timing-5 1.227->0.152ms (0.13x->1.02x, 32768->2048 programs), timing-4 0.309->0.114ms (0.51x->1.36x), timing-16 0.302->0.106ms, timing-10 0.309->0.114ms, timing-11 1.222->0.152ms; small shapes stayed 1.34-1.42x and timing-1/7/13 ~1.0x. Two deviations from the expectation: (1) 6 of 78 correctness cases FAILED (fp16/bf16/fp32 sizes [2,3,5] dim=2 keepdim both) because COLS was computed as the largest power of two <= red, so red=5 produced COLS=4 and the tail column was never written - matched_ratio 0.83-0.93 with the missing cells left at zero; (2) timing-2/8 (8192^2 fp16/bf16) only moved 0.624->0.603ms despite halving 16384->8192 programs, showing that shape is not program-count bound: it and fp32 8192^2 both sit at ~111 Melem/s (212 GB/s fp16 vs 424 GB/s fp32), an element-rate limit distinct from the reference's byte-rate memset, so the tile kernel's per-element select/store path is the next bottleneck.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Repair COLS to next_pow2(red) (8 for red=5) and ROWS from TILE//COLS, then attack the remaining element-rate limit: 8192^2 fp16 (0.603ms, 0.51x) and fp32 (0.603ms) both run at ~111 Melem/s regardless of dtype, i.e. an element-rate bound rather than the reference's ~420 GB/s byte-rate memset. Test a two-store program (wide contiguous constant zero store + patch scatter of the ROWS selected cells) in a bounded target debug microbenchmark before spending an eval round on it.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A power-of-two tile extent must be the NEXT power of two >= the logical extent; reusing a block-size helper that rounds down silently drops the tail columns and only fails on non-power-of-two extents (red=5 here).

plan.strategy: Establish a measured baseline with the simplest correct Triton architecture: a zero-fill kernel over the whole output followed by a general non-reducing scatter kernel (mirrors aten zeros+scatter_).
plan.code_changes: New self-contained Triton implementation in tmp/main.py: _zero_kernel fills the output, _scatter_general computes each source element's destination offset from (outer, K, inner) decomposition with affine collapsed stride groups for the possibly non-contiguous grad/indices.
plan.hypothesis: Because the output tensor (up to 8192x8192 fp32 = 268 MB) must be materialized, walltime is dominated by the zero-fill write; a 2-kernel Triton implementation should land close to the eager reference and give a reference point for a fused single-kernel design.

expected_effect.mechanism: One zero-fill pass plus a small scatter pass; establishes the measured reference point.

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline establishes the reference point: 2 Triton kernels (masked zero-fill + masked scatter) score geo_mean 0.5905. All 96 workloads are numerically exact (abs_err 0). Per-workload evidence shows two independent losses: (1) all small/medium workloads sit ~0.21 ms against a ~0.135 ms reference floor, i.e. two Triton launches each cost ~35 us of host walltime beyond the reference's aten calls; (2) the two largest workloads are element-rate rather than bandwidth bound - fp16 8192x8192 (134 MB) and fp32 8192x8192 (268 MB) both take ~0.739 ms (~90 Gelem/s), while the reference sustains ~417 GB/s on both (0.324/0.640 ms), so the fully masked store is not vectorized and costs a fixed per-element rate regardless of dtype.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: No prior measurement (baseline round). Absolute position: worst workload timing-2 at 0.4386x, best timing-14 at 0.865x. Reference latency is flat at ~0.135-0.15 ms for the 12 small/medium workloads (floor bound), so the recoverable loss there is host-launch overhead only; on the 6 large workloads the dtype-insensitive 0.739 ms is recoverable store-bandwidth.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Fuse zero-fill and scatter into one launch whose stores are unmasked and contiguous: constexpr K so offsets are stride-1 along the reduced axis, row mask omitted when M % R == 0 and column mask omitted when K is a power of two, so the vectorizer can emit wide stores.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Move from a zeros+scatter pair mirroring aten to a single fused gather-formulation kernel with unmasked contiguous stores.

plan.strategy: Fuse zero-fill and scatter into a single launch over the output, with mask-free contiguous stores enabled by constexpr K.
plan.code_changes: Replaced the separate zero-fill + scatter launches with one _fused_lastdim kernel for the (dim == last, contiguous) case: out[row,col] = where(col == indices[row], grad[row], 0), computed on an (R x BK) tile of a contiguous row-major output. K and BK are constexpr so offsets are stride-1 along the reduced axis; the row mask is dropped when M % R == 0 (EVEN) and the column mask is dropped when K is a power of two (FULLK), leaving a fully unmasked contiguous store. The zero+scatter pair remains only for the non-last-dim / non-contiguous general path.
plan.hypothesis: The baseline lost for two separable reasons: two launches (host floor) and masked stores (element-rate). Fusing removes the second launch and the constexpr-K unmasked tile restores store vectorization, so fp16 large cases should approach the fp32 case's byte rate and all 12 floor-bound workloads should approach a 1.0x speedup.

expected_effect.mechanism: One launch removes ~35 us of host overhead on the floor-bound small workloads, and unmasked contiguous stores restore wide vectorized writes so large workloads become bandwidth bound (~417 GB/s) instead of element-rate bound (~90 Gelem/s).

profile.summary: mixed: 15 of 18 timing workloads are pinned by a ~100 us per-call host floor, not by kernel time, fp16/bf16 large case is dominated by the per-element compare/select, not by store bandwidth, fp32 large case: no pipe is saturated (MTE2/MTE3 <80% when active, vector compute usage <20%) while effective write rate is 845 GB/s

conclusion.root_cause: The 0.59 baseline lost on two independent axes; fusing removed both the second launch and the masked-store element-rate wall, taking geo_mean to 1.5502 with 96/96 exact. Remaining loss is now localized: a per-call host cost of ~98-105 us that dominates 15 of 18 timing workloads, a ~845 GB/s DRAM write wall on the largest fp32 case (at it), and dtype-independent select compute (int32 compare + where) that holds fp16/bf16 8192^2 at 730 GB/s instead of ~845 GB/s.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: geo_mean 0.5905 -> 1.5502 (+162%), min_speedup 0.4386 -> 1.4462, all 96 workloads still exact. The fusion half of the hypothesis is fully confirmed: every floor-bound workload moved from ~0.21 ms to 0.098-0.108 ms, i.e. exactly max(H, T) with a single per-call host cost H ~= 98-105 us, and the two-launch penalty disappeared. The 'unmasked stores make large workloads bandwidth bound' half is only partially confirmed: timing-14 (fp32 8192^2, 268 MB) reached 845 GB/s and is at the practical HBM write wall for this single-die part (~2x the reference's 417 GB/s), but timing-2/timing-8 (fp16/bf16, 134 MB) reach only 730 GB/s because the [R,BK] int32 compare + tl.where costs 127.6 us of the 183.9 us kernel (MTE3 only 17% active), so those two remain select-compute bound. Profiler kernel times: timing-0 5.5 us, timing-16 11.4 us, timing-13 81.5 us, timing-2 183.9 us, timing-14 317.9 us - so 15 of 18 timing workloads are host-floor bound and cannot be moved by kernel changes.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Diagnose the ~98 us per-call host cost first (allocation vs Triton launch vs harness sync) because it gates 15 of 18 timing workloads; then try replacing the full-tile where-select with a zero-tile store plus a one-element scatter store to cut fp16/bf16 select compute.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Per-element select cost is dtype-independent (fp32 vec 141.5 us vs fp16 127.6 us for the same 67.1 M elements) while duration tracks bytes, so element-rate work and byte-rate work must be optimized separately.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: From a two-launch zeros+scatter mirror of aten to a single fused gather-formulation kernel with constexpr-K unmasked contiguous stores; next, attack the host per-call floor and the per-element select independently since they are the only two remaining limits.

plan.strategy: Replace the un-importable FlagGems seed (relative import `from ..utils import dim_compress`, which made the parent round RUNTIME_ERROR) with the simplest self-contained correct architecture: device copy of inp into a fresh contiguous output, then one generic 8-slot N-d atomic-add kernel over the index element space.
plan.code_changes: New self-contained tmp/main.py: _copy_flat_kernel for contiguous inp, _copy_nd_kernel (8 padded shape/stride slots, int32 div/mod) for strided inp, _scatter_add_nd_kernel with index/src/out stride sets and the dim out-stride forced to 0 plus idx*odim. No framework math, no input mutation, fresh contiguous output.
plan.hypothesis: A generic index-space atomic kernel is numerically correct for every declared workload (3 dtypes x dims 0/1/2 and 2D last-dim) and gives a measurable, honest baseline; it is expected to be slower than the PyTorch reference because each element pays 8 int32 div/mod steps and int32 offsets are recomputed per element.

expected_effect.mechanism: First measured reference point for this workspace; quantifies the per-element index-arithmetic cost that the specialized kernels must remove.

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline established: the seed is un-importable (relative `..utils` import), so a self-contained generic index-space atomic kernel was measured instead. All 18 workloads pass, but the generic path costs 8 sequential int32 div/mod steps plus a 34-argument launch per element-block, giving 0.106x on the large cases (31.5ms vs 3.36ms reference for 2048^2) and only 0.54-0.64x on the 128^2 cases (0.26ms vs 0.14-0.17ms), where the two-launch host path dominates.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation was to establish a baseline, which was met quantitatively: geo_mean 0.1903, min_speedup 0.106 (scatter_add-timing-8). Workload-level split shows two distinct gaps: (1) large cases are per-element bound - candidate 7.5ns/element (1024^2: 7.91ms/1.05M) versus reference 0.81ns/element, i.e. ~9x slower per element, consistent with 8 runtime-valued div/mod steps per element and int32 address recomputation; (2) the 128^2 cases are fixed-overhead bound - 267us for 16K elements is far above the ~120us that per-element cost alone predicts, so roughly 140us is launch/host cost (two Triton launches with 34 and 4 runtime arguments), against a 170us reference walltime. Correctness passed with abs_err <= 0.03125 and matched_ratio 1.0 on all 9 correctness cases, so the generic ND indexing (front-padded 8-slot decomposition, dim stride zeroed plus idx*odim) is validated as the reference-correct fallback.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Add a specialized last-dimension contiguous kernel for the timed shape family (contiguous inp/index/src, equal shapes, dim == ndim-1): a 2D grid (row, column-block) that computes offsets as row*ncols + col with no div/mod and only 4 runtime arguments, keeping the generic 8-slot kernel as the fallback for other dims, partial index extents and strided layouts. Expected to cut the per-element index arithmetic (large cases) and the launcher argument cost (small cases).
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Baseline: generic ND atomic kernel. Next: shape-specialized div-free kernel; then attack the remaining fixed host cost for the 128^2 cases with a single-launch fused variant.

plan.strategy: Specialize the dominant shape family (contiguous full-extent last-axis scatter, which is all 9 timed workloads) into a div-free row/column-block kernel.
plan.code_changes: Added _scatter_add_lastdim_kernel (2D grid: row x column-block, offsets = row*ncols+col, 4 runtime args) and a host dispatch that takes it when dim == ndim-1 and inp/index/src are contiguous with identical full shapes; the generic 8-slot ND kernel remains the fallback.
plan.hypothesis: The 8-strip div/mod decomposition is the dominant per-element cost (candidate 7.5ns/element vs reference 0.81ns/element on 1024^2) and the 34-argument launch is a large share of the ~140us fixed cost on 128^2. A div-free, 4-argument kernel over the same atomic scatter should improve every timing case, with the largest relative gain on the 1024^2/2048^2 shapes.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removes 8 sequential runtime-valued int32 div/mod steps and 30 scalar arguments per element-block, so per-element index arithmetic collapses to one multiply-add; the 128^2 cases should also lose launcher argument overhead.

conclusion.root_cause: Div-free specialized addressing confirmed as the dominant large-shape win, but the residual large-case gap is a per-element data-dependent atomic/store cost (~4.6ns/element) that is invariant to conflict density, BLOCK, num_warps and masking; the small-shape gap is the fixed ~0.07ms per-launch floor paid twice (copy + atomic).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expectation met in direction and roughly in size: geo_mean 0.1903 -> 0.2888 (+51.8%), min_speedup 0.106 -> 0.172. Large cases improved as predicted by removing index arithmetic: 2048^2 31.50ms -> 19.55ms (1.61x) and 1024^2 7.91ms -> 4.95ms (1.60x), which is close to the 1.65x implied by dropping 8 div/mod steps per element. The small 128^2 cases improved much less (0.267 -> 0.197ms, 1.36x) because they are dominated by fixed per-launch cost, not element cost. A bounded target probe then located the remaining gap precisely: a tiny copy kernel alone costs ~0.07ms (per-launch floor), the 2048^2 atomic kernel is 19.49ms while a non-atomic data-dependent store of the same volume is 13.56ms and an affine copy of the same volume is 0.10ms; conflict density is irrelevant (unique-index and single-index atomics are both 19.48ms) and num_warps/mask removal change nothing. So the residual 5.8x versus the reference (0.8ns/element) is the framework's scalarized handling of data-dependent addresses, not index arithmetic. An all-affine dense formulation was measured: 43.6ms at 2048^2 (worse) but 0.067ms at 128^2 (better than either two-launch variant, exact match to the reference).
conclusion.next_suggestion: Dispatch the measured-cheaper dense all-affine kernel for small widths (ncols >= 32 and rows*ncols^2 cheap under a fitted cost model), keeping the atomic last-dim kernel for wide rows. Target-side probes (bounded, verified against torch.scatter_add) show the dense single-launch kernel at 0.067ms vs 0.101ms atomic vs 0.187ms current on 128^2, and 43.6ms vs 19.5ms on 2048^2, so the dispatch must be shape-dependent.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Two bounded probes separated three hypotheses that looked identical in end-to-end numbers: conflict density (no effect), launch shape (no effect), and data-dependent addressing (the entire residual). Always measure an affine-address kernel of the same data volume to bound what is achievable before optimizing a scatter.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 generic ND atomic (0.190) -> round 2 div-free specialized last-dim kernel (0.289). Next: shape-dependent dispatch between an all-affine dense kernel (small widths, one launch) and the atomic kernel (wide rows). Large-shape atomics look framework-bound; the remaining structural option is a sort-based formulation, which is out of budget this batch.

plan.strategy: Specialize the destination-owned kernel on a constant column extent and run it mask-free when the extent is an exact multiple of the block and chunk, to cut predication and dispatch work on the shapes that use it.

plan.hypothesis: Making the destination-owned kernel's column extent a compile-time constant and removing all masking in its loop reduces per-iteration vector work and dispatch cost, improving the 1024x1024 and 128x128 shapes without changing the 2048x2048 atomic path.

expected_effect.mechanism: Predication and per-chunk mask arithmetic removed from the destination-owned hot loop, plus one fewer runtime argument to specialize per launch.

conclusion.root_cause: The owner loop's masking and trip-count knowledge were not the limiting factor: removing them bought ~1.3% on the compute-bound 1024^2 shapes while the constant specialisation added host work on the dispatch-bound 128^2 shapes, so the net geo mean fell.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected a geo-mean increase; observed 0.41522 -> 0.39621 (-4.6%), so the expectation was not met. Split by mechanism: the 1024x1024 cases improved marginally as predicted by removing loop predication (2.887/2.888/2.868 -> 2.849/2.852/2.851 ms, speedup 0.297 -> 0.300), and the 2048x2048 atomic path was unchanged (19.54 -> 19.50 ms, 0.172), also as predicted. The mask arithmetic was therefore not a meaningful part of the loop cost.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep the round 2 candidate (owner kernel with the mask-free compare, runtime ncols). Further gains on 1024^2/2048^2 require replacing either the scalarized per-lane atomic store (~4.6 ns/element, MTE3 saturated, unchanged by mask removal) or the O(ncols) compare per source element in the destination-owned loop; neither blocking nor tiling parameters moved them, so the next attempt should be a non-scalarized scatter formulation rather than more tuning.

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline established for the inherited seed. Per-workload timing shows two distinct bottlenecks: (a) 1024x1024 rows use the destination-owned compare kernel, whose cost is O(ncols) comparisons per source element (2.85 ms vs 0.855 ms reference, 0.30x); (b) 2048x2048 rows exceed _DENSE_MAX_COLS and fall to tl.atomic_add, which this backend lowers to a per-lane scf.for of single-element atomics (19.5 ms vs 3.37 ms reference, 0.17x). The three 128x128 cases already win (1.17-1.48x) because they are launch-bound.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Replace the O(w^2) compare fold and the per-lane atomic path with a sub-quadratic sorted-segment algorithm: sort (target*B + lane) keys per row so each destination's contributions form one contiguous run in ascending lane order, cumsum the reordered values, then locate each destination's run with a binary search and emit the prefix difference contiguously.

plan.strategy: Replace the O(ncols) destination-owned compare fold and the per-lane atomic scatter with a per-row sorted-segment reduction: sort target*B+lane keys, cumsum the reordered src values, and emit each destination as a contiguous prefix difference. Route taken from the campaign knowledge route 'scatter sorted path candidate' and its frozen CPU-validated prototype, then adapted from target measurements: fp32 keys instead of int32 (vsort rejects int32), branchless binary search instead of the tl.histogram combine (histogram measured 1.79/8.30 ms vs 0.06/0.20 ms for the sort), and shift/mask instead of integer div/mod (+0.48/+1.95 ms). No knowledge-base query event id was issued, so no formal knowledge use is declared.
plan.code_changes: Added _scatter_add_sort_key_kernel (al.sort of fp32-encoded target*B+lane keys, on-chip tl.gather of src into sorted order, inclusive cumsum) and _scatter_add_sort_out_kernel (branchless binary search over the sorted keys to locate each destination's run, then out = inp + prefix[end-1] - prefix[begin-1]). Dispatch: ncols<=256 keeps the owner kernel; 256<ncols<=4096 uses the two-kernel sorted path; above that the old atomic path remains. Integer // and % replaced by >> and &; keys stored as fp32 because hivm.hir.vsort rejects int32 keys and gather tl.load accepts only fp16/fp32/bf16/int8.
plan.hypothesis: Replacing the O(ncols) compare fold and the per-lane atomic path with a sub-quadratic sorted-segment algorithm removes the dominant per-element cost on the six wide-row timing workloads; small (128x128) workloads keep the already-winning owner path so they do not regress.

expected_effect.mechanism: Per-element work drops from O(ncols) compares (owner, 1024 cases) or a per-lane scalar atomic loop (2048 cases) to O(log ncols) sorted-key traffic, so the six large-row timing workloads should move from 0.17-0.30x toward parity with the reference.

conclusion.root_cause: The combine kernel located each destination's sorted run with a binary search whose every step was a data-dependent global-memory load. On this backend a per-lane dynamic GM load is far more expensive than the on-chip tl.gather the plan was calibrated against, so 12 search steps plus 2 prefix lookups dominated the whole call (k1 was only 0.506/1.918 ms of the 6.72/28.6 ms totals).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted 0.9 ms (1024^2) and 3.5 ms (2048^2) from the isolated ingredient costs; observed 6.717/6.717/6.713 ms and 28.61/28.59/27.17 ms, i.e. 0.127x and 0.117x versus 0.30x/0.17x before, and geo_mean fell 0.411 -> 0.271. The 128x128 workloads were unchanged as designed (1.258/1.258/1.426 vs 1.394/1.167/1.477, within run-to-run noise), so the owner-path branch and the dispatch threshold are not implicated. The whole regression sits in the combine kernel: k1 was measured at 0.506 ms (1024^2) and 1.918 ms (2048^2), so k2 accounts for ~6.2 ms and ~26.7 ms. The discrepancy against the plan is that my 0.071 ms gather reference was an ON-CHIP tl.gather, while this k2 issued 12 per-lane DYNAMIC GLOBAL tl.load calls over the keys row plus 2 over the cumsum row; those random-address GM gathers run at roughly 2.3 G lane-loads/s, about 25x slower per gather than the on-chip network. The algorithm and its numerics were validated separately (43/43 cases including all-duplicate longest runs and odd widths), so this is purely a memory-locality mistake in the combine pass, not an algorithmic failure.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep the sorted-segment algorithm but move the run-location search on-chip: load the sorted keys and the cumsum row once with a contiguous tl.load, then run the branchless binary search with tl.gather over those register/UB vectors. Only 2 contiguous loads plus ~15 on-chip gathers should remain in the combine kernel.

plan.strategy: Fix the round-2 memory-locality mistake: keep the sorted-segment algorithm but stage the sorted keys and cumsum row in registers and run the whole run-location search with on-chip tl.gather instead of per-lane dynamic global loads.
plan.code_changes: Rewrote _scatter_add_sort_out_kernel so the combine pass issues only two contiguous row loads (sorted keys, cumsum) and then performs all lookups with on-chip tl.gather: the 12-step branchless binary search now gathers from the register-resident key vector instead of issuing a per-lane dynamic global load per step, and the begin/end prefix lookups plus the lane shift also use on-chip gathers. Round 2's structure, dispatch (ncols<=256 owner, <=4096 sorted, else atomic) and numerics are unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: Round 2's regression came entirely from the combine pass performing its search with data-dependent global loads; staging the sorted keys and the cumsum row once and searching on-chip recovers the predicted latency, so the six wide-row timing workloads should reach ~1.25x/1.32x and lift geo_mean well above the 0.411 baseline.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removes 14 per-lane dynamic global gathers per row from the combine pass and replaces them with on-chip gathers that measured ~25x cheaper per gather, cutting the six wide-row workloads' latency from 6.72/28.6 ms back toward the 0.7/2.5 ms predicted by the isolated ingredient costs.

profile.summary: mixed: Wide-row time is dominated by the sorted-key pass, which runs mostly on the Scalar pipe, The round-3 on-chip rewrite left the combine pass vector-bound and secondary, Key-pass scalar cost scales with total elements, and the whole call is device-bound at 1024 columns

conclusion.root_cause: The wide-row bottleneck was never the sort or the algorithm: it was where the run-location search touched memory. Staging the sorted keys and cumsum row in registers and searching with on-chip tl.gather removed the per-lane dynamic global loads, which are ~25x more expensive per gather than the on-chip network on this backend.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted ~1.25x/1.32x for the wide rows and 'well above 0.411'; observed 1.246/1.321 (1024^2) and 1.320/1.321/1.325 (2048^2), matching the isolated-ingredient prediction to within 1%. geo_mean rose 0.411 -> 1.296 and every one of the 18 workloads now exceeds 1.24x (min_speedup 1.244 at the 128x128 bf16 case). The round-2 gap against its own prediction (~7x) is fully explained by the removed per-lane dynamic global gathers: 14 of them per row at ~0.44 ms each accounted for ~6.2 of the 6.72 ms; the same kernel now spends its time in 15 on-chip gathers (0.0175/0.04 ms each). Small workloads were unaffected by design (owner path retained for ncols<=256: 1.345/1.244/1.365 versus 1.394/1.167/1.477 at baseline, i.e. run-to-run noise), confirming that the 128-column cases are launch-bound and should not be moved onto the sorted path. The remaining cost is concentrated in k1: sort 0.06/0.20 ms, cumsum 0.43/1.71 ms, so roughly two thirds of the wide-row latency is still key generation.
conclusion.next_suggestion: The remaining headroom is in the key-generation pass, not the combine pass: k1 measured 0.506 ms (1024^2) and 1.918 ms (2048^2) versus only 0.062/0.200 ms for al.sort itself, and of that tl.cumsum alone was 0.434/1.707 ms. Replacing the full-row cumsum with a blocked scan (local scan within 64/128-element blocks plus an exclusive scan over block totals) should cut k1 roughly in half and is the next single change to evaluate.

plan.strategy: Establish a measured baseline with a flat 1D output-tile bilinear kernel that reads the four neighbours through the real input strides and stores one contiguous vector
plan.code_changes: Replaced the seed's 2D broadcast + nested N/C loop kernel (which hard-coded contiguous NCHW addressing and divided by (OH-1) inside a tl.where) with a single flat-index kernel: offs -> (ow, oh, nc) with N/C/IH/IW/OH/OW/ALIGN_CORNERS as constexpr, Python-level branches for the OH==1/OW==1 cases, PyTorch association order for the interpolation, and BLOCK chosen from the flat element count
plan.hypothesis: The parent kernel is ~8500 us on a 262144-element output because of per-program serial N/C loops, runtime modulo and non-contiguous addressing; a flat contiguous-store kernel with constexpr geometry should restore normal vectorised throughput and also make the 1x1 output cases compile

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing the serial N/C loop and runtime index math leaves one contiguous vector store and four gather loads per output element

conclusion.root_cause: All 24 workloads are numerically correct (max abs err 1.95e-3 on bf16, 3.9e-6 on fp32) but the kernel costs ~37.8 ns per output element, exactly linear in element count and identical for fp16/bf16/fp32 -> the cost is per-lane addressing, not bandwidth. The four tl.load calls use vector-of-pointers addresses derived from div/mod chains, so they lower to per-lane non-affine loads instead of block transfers. A target probe showed contiguous block load+store of 8.4M elements takes ~0.03 ms net while the same element count with 4 non-affine loads takes 9.9 ms, i.e. a ~300x penalty for the gather path.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline: geo_mean 0.00163, worst workload timing-1 (0.00071x, 290 ms vs 0.207 ms reference). Device probe evidence: (1) contiguous copy of the timing-1 volume is ~0.03 ms net, so memory is not the limit; (2) per-program overhead on this part is ~37 ns, so program counts in the tens of thousands are themselves expensive; (3) a 2-D tile whose row base is a data-dependent vector but whose last dimension is contiguous (ptr + h0[:,None]*IW + arange(IW)) runs 4.2M elements in 0.188 ms, i.e. the backend handles row-gather with a contiguous minor dimension well; (4) UB register gathers measured at least 9x cheaper than global gather. Conclusion: replace per-lane global gathers with (a) contiguous minor-dimension loads and (b) either an affine expansion for exact integer upscale factors or a UB gather.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Rewrite as a row-tiled kernel: BR output rows per program, contiguous (BR, IW) input row loads with a data-dependent row base, vertical combine, then horizontal resample with no global gather. For the general case use tl.gather on the register tile; for exact integer horizontal upscale factors (OW = 2*IW, as in every timing workload) use a fully affine expansion: load the row shifted by -1/0/+1, build the two interleaved weight branches and select on a length-S constexpr axis so the store stays contiguous. Keep the current flat gather kernel as the correct general fallback.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A modulo-based 'gather' probe is only a real gather if the period does not divide the block size: with BLK=1024 and IWP=4096 the index stayed contiguous inside each block, so the first probe badly under-estimated the gather cost and had to be discarded. Always check that a synthetic irregular-index probe actually destroys affine structure.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 targeted correctness first (all 24 pass, including the 1x1 outputs that previously failed to compile) and used the measurement to falsify 'bandwidth-bound' in favour of 'per-lane addressing bound'.

plan.strategy: Delete the +-1-element global row loads from the integer-upscale fast path and synthesise the horizontal neighbours with a UB register gather
plan.code_changes: Replaced the two misaligned row-load pairs (ptr_i + rr + ka -+ 1) with two tl.gather calls on the vertically blended row tile, using clamped index vectors (max(k-1,0), min(k+1,IW-1)) so the PyTorch i1p edge rule is still reproduced; removed the now-redundant edge tl.where. Kept the aligned row loads, the affine 2-tap expansion, tl.join and the contiguous 3-D store.
plan.hypothesis: The fast path's 2.5 ns/output is entirely caused by the four +-1-element row loads, which the Ascend backend cannot lower to block transfers (measured 25x penalty vs an aligned base, independent of the offset size). A UB register gather was measured at ~0.1 ms for the same 8.4M lanes, so replacing the shifted loads with tl.gather should cut the kernel cost roughly 30x.

expected_effect.mechanism: Eliminating four misaligned global loads per tile; measured on-target at 21.3 ms -> 0.69 ms for the 8.4M-output geometry, so the geo_mean should rise by roughly one order of magnitude

key_params.rows_per_program: min(2048//IWP, cdiv(n_rows,256)) rounded down, divisor of n_rows

knowledge_uses.application_note: Applied the index/sampling guidance that a scatter or gather must be reorganised rather than tiled blindly: instead of enlarging BLOCK to hide the per-lane cost, the misaligned global access is removed and replaced with a register-level gather.

conclusion.root_cause: The +-1-element row loads were the entire remaining cost and are now removed: they cost 21.3 ms on the 8.4M-output geometry because an Ascend block load needs an aligned base, and the penalty was identical for offsets 1, 2, 8 and 16 elements (~5 ms per misaligned load pair). Replacing them with two clamps plus tl.gather dropped the same geometry to 0.629 ms. All 24 workloads remain numerically correct with the gather-clamped i1p edge rule. The residual gap has two distinct causes: a 0.293 ms 3-D store offset tensor (~10x a flat contiguous store) on the large fixtures, and a ~0.12 ms shape-independent per-call cost that dominates the small fixtures.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected a ~30x drop from removing the misaligned loads; observed 21.3x on the large geometry (0.694 probe vs 0.629 measured, so the probe was accurate) and 186x on the aggregate geo_mean because round 1 was dominated by an even slower path. The frozen target of 0.8x is still missed by 2.6x. Workload-level: large fixtures 0.327/0.425/0.350 (0.629/0.631/0.626 ms) and small fixtures 0.246/0.273/0.238 (0.138/0.138/0.146 ms). The small fixtures are 32x less data but only 4.5x faster, which proves a ~0.12 ms per-call cost independent of shape, exactly where the reference spends its entire 0.034 ms. The large fixtures are still 12x above the measured contiguous-copy floor (0.03 ms net), and the ablation attributed 0.29 ms of that to the 3-D store offsets and the remainder to row-base loads plus gathers.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the two costs the ablation separated: (1) the 3-D (BR,IWP,2) store offset tensor costs 0.293 ms for 8.4M outputs (~10x a flat contiguous store), so build the value tile so the store becomes one flat contiguous block; (2) the small fixtures are now dominated by ~0.12 ms of per-call cost that is not device work (t0 is 0.138 ms while 1/32 of t1's 0.63 ms device time), so measure the fixed launch/wrapper overhead and cut it with a cheaper host path.
conclusion.debug_lesson: An ablation grid over the *number and offset* of loads (2 aligned / 6 with +-1 / 2 aligned+2 gathers / store-only) localised the cost in one pass; the earlier synthetic 'gather' probe had been invalid because its modulo period divided the block size, so it never destroyed affine structure. Verify that a synthetic irregular probe actually breaks contiguity before trusting it.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 established correctness and measured the global per-lane access cost. Round 2 removed it with a register gather, moving the bottleneck to the store path (large fixtures) and to per-call overhead (small fixtures).

knowledge_assessments.rationale: The guidance to reorganise the access pattern instead of enlarging the tile was correct in direction and produced the 186x gain, but the specific replacement it suggests (register/UB gather) is only cheap relative to global per-lane loads; the measured 0.1 ms per 8.4M gather lanes plus the 0.29 ms for the store path show the remaining cost has moved to other constructs, so the guidance is confirmed only for the global-access part.

plan.strategy: Move all metadata-derived launch preparation out of the per-call path with a shape/stride/dtype-keyed scalar cache
plan.code_changes: Added a metadata-keyed cache (key = shape, strides, dtype, output_size, align_corners, scales_h, scales_w) that stores only pre-resolved scalars (grid, rh/rw, constexprs, block/BR) and performs the launch with a literal kernel[grid](...) call in run(); removed the per-call asserts and the per-call parameter derivation. Kernels are unchanged from round 2.
plan.hypothesis: The small timing fixtures are not device-bound: t0 is 0.138 ms while the same kernel shape takes ~0.012 ms of device time, a bare Triton launch costs 0.057 ms and torch.empty 0.010 ms, leaving ~0.06 ms of pure wrapper Python. Caching the metadata-derived launch parameters should remove most of that, helping every workload and the small ones most.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing ~0.06 ms of per-call Python parameter derivation, which is a fixed cost and therefore matters most for the three small timing fixtures

knowledge_uses.application_note: Applied the explicit guidance that compiled artifacts and shape configurations may be cached while the per-call data pointer, stream and tensor metadata must be re-read; the cache stores only scalars keyed on shape/strides/dtype and never a tensor or data pointer.

profile.summary: mixed: Per-program fixed cost dominates device scaling: 512-element programs cost 3.23 us/program while 2048-element programs cost only 6.15 us/program, Large fixture is device-bound and vector-pipeline dominated; contiguous stores are cheap and the row-gather loads are secondary, Small fixtures still spend more than half of eval latency outside the device kernel, even though the kernel itself is also inefficient

conclusion.root_cause: The small fixtures were paying ~0.06 ms of per-call Python for metadata-derived launch preparation (parameter derivation, next_power_of_2, the divisibility loop, kwarg binding). Caching the resolved scalars keyed on shape/strides/dtype/output_size/options removed about two thirds of it. All 24 workloads still pass with unchanged numerics, and the cache holds no tensors, storage or data pointers, re-deriving an entry whenever shape, strides or dtype change.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected ~0.06 ms of per-call Python with the small fixtures recovering most of it; observed exactly that: t0 0.1385 -> 0.1013 ms, t2 0.1375 -> 0.1047, t4 0.1460 -> 0.1024, i.e. a 0.036-0.044 ms saving per call, lifting the geo_mean from 0.3033 to 0.3450. The remaining per-call floor is now ~0.09 ms (0.057 ms Triton launch + 0.010 ms allocation + ~0.012 ms device time), which is already 2.6x the reference's entire 0.030-0.040 ms for these shapes, so the small fixtures are close to their structural limit under a Triton launch. The large fixtures did not move (0.629/0.632/0.626 ms) because they are device-bound, not host-bound, confirming the round-2 conclusion that their cost is split roughly evenly between the row-base loads and the 2x-size store path.
conclusion.next_suggestion: The three large fixtures are device-bound at 0.63 ms for 8.4M outputs and were unchanged by this round, so the last round should target the kernel: the load and store masks (including the `other` select) are still applied on every access even when n_rows is divisible by BR and IWP == IW, and the store mask costs a select over a tile twice the size of the value tile. Elide both with a constexpr FULL flag for the provably in-range case.
conclusion.debug_lesson: For a launch-overhead probe, time a kernel-only loop and a bare empty-kernel loop too: the difference between full run() and the kernel-only loop exposed 0.06 ms of pure wrapper Python that no device metric would have shown. Also, the candidate-admission gate requires a literal kernel[grid](...) in the source, so a cached closure launcher is rejected even though it is functionally identical.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Rounds 1-2 fixed the kernel's memory access pattern (0.0016 -> 0.3033). Round 3 fixed the host path (0.3033 -> 0.3450). Round 4 should return to the kernel for the large fixtures, which the host fix cannot help.

knowledge_assessments.rationale: The guidance that compiled artifacts and shape configurations may be cached while the per-call data pointer and metadata are re-read held exactly: caching only scalars keyed on shape/strides/dtype/out_size/options improved the small fixtures from 0.246/0.273/0.238 to 0.301/0.383/0.296 with identical kernels, and the per-call cost dropped from 0.138 ms to 0.102 ms. No tensor, storage or pointer was cached and the input views were re-derived each call.

plan.strategy: Elide load/store masks and `other` selects with a constexpr flag for the shape where every tile lane is provably in range
plan.code_changes: Added a FULL constexpr to the integer-upscale kernel: when n_rows is divisible by BR and IWP == IW every lane of every tile is provably in range, so both the load mask (with its `other` select) and the store mask over the double-size (BR,IWP,2) tile are omitted. Host computes FULL alongside the other cached launch scalars; kernels otherwise unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The large fixtures are device-bound at ~0.63 ms for 8.4M outputs and pay an always-on mask plus `other` select on every access, including a select over a (BR,IWP,2) tile twice the size of the value tile; dropping them where provably unnecessary should reduce the per-element instruction count and improve those three workloads.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing a per-element predicate and select from the two loads and, more importantly, from the store tile that is twice the value-tile size; this is device work, so it should move the three large timing fixtures that the round-3 host fix could not reach

conclusion.root_cause: The elided predicates were not on the critical path: the constexpr FULL flag removed the load mask, its `other` select, and the store mask over the (BR,IWP,2) tile, yet the large fixtures moved by less than the measurement spread and the small ones regressed slightly. This reproduces the round-2 ablation result (masked 0.5941 ms vs unmasked 0.5944 ms) end to end, so the large-fixture cost is in the data movement itself, not in predicate handling.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected the mask/`other` removal to move the three device-bound large fixtures; observed no change: t1 0.6293 -> 0.6230 ms, t3 0.6316 -> 0.6244, t5 0.6260 -> 0.6174 (inside the run-to-run spread), while the small fixtures moved in both directions (t0 0.1013 -> 0.1130, t2 0.1047 -> 0.1143, t4 0.1024 -> 0.1202). The aggregate geo_mean therefore went 0.3450 -> 0.3442, i.e. no improvement, so round 3 remains the best. The null result is consistent with the round-2 measurement that masks cost essentially nothing, and confirms that the large fixtures are limited by the row-base loads plus the two UB gathers rather than by per-element predicates.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Round 2's own ablation already answered this: masks were free (0.5941 vs 0.5944), so the remaining large-fixture cost is data movement through data-dependent row bases and the two UB gathers, not predicates. Any further work should either (a) make the source-row access fully affine by loading a contiguous input band per program and gathering inside it, or (b) reduce the number of gathers per output element; simply removing more predicates will not help.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Mask and `other`-select elision is not where this kernel's cost lives: the predicates were already cheap relative to the data movement, so a change that looks like an obvious instruction-count win must still be measured rather than assumed. Round 2's ablation had already shown masks are free (k2_center_nomask 0.5944 vs k2_center_masked 0.5941), and this round independently reproduced that null result end to end.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Rounds 1-2 fixed the access pattern (0.0016 -> 0.3033), round 3 fixed the host path (0.3033 -> 0.3450), and round 4 tested the last cheap instruction-level hypothesis and falsified it, so the best candidate remains round 3's.

plan.strategy: Replace per-output-row 256-byte row loads with contiguous multi-KB input blocks and reuse one row pair for two output rows, in a single kernel launch
plan.code_changes: Replaced the fast-path kernel with _blk2x_kernel: one program owns QB consecutive input rows of one image and loads two contiguous multi-KB blocks (rows lb..lb+QB-1 and lb+1..lb+QB) instead of two 256-byte row loads per output row; the same row pair yields the even output row and the odd row one position lower, so two mixed tiles cover 2*QB rows. The two clamped end rows are written by an extra (NB+1)-th program per image inside the same launch. Block size QB*IW is capped at 2048 float32 elements, and the new path requires a fully contiguous NCHW input and the exact 2x geometry; everything else keeps the round-2 kernels. The compiled-launcher fast path is kept and moved to the merged kernel.
plan.hypothesis: The large-geometry deficit is caused by per-row 256-byte loads (65536 transfers, 45 GB/s), not by volume or the store. Switching to contiguous input blocks should cut the 0.629-0.630 ms large-geometry latency to roughly a quarter while leaving the small host-bound cases at parity.

expected_effect.mechanism: Multiplying the transfer size per address computation by 2*QB (256 B row fragments -> multi-KB contiguous block transfers) should remove the measured 316 us of load time on the large geometry while keeping the cheap store, cutting large-geometry latency about 2.3x
