plan.strategy: Establish a native Triton baseline: one flat vector kernel for contiguous storage (copy for real dtypes, alternating-sign conj over the interleaved real/imaginary float stream for complex) plus a rank-generic strided kernel that reads through the input's real strides into a contiguous output.
plan.code_changes: Self-contained tmp/main.py replacing the FlagGems copy_/launch_conj_physical seed (which redispatched to a CPU-only copy and produced wrong values for strided inputs). Turns the lazy conjugate bit into a NEG flag with a metadata-only view, allocates a contiguous output like the reference, and selects UB-safe tile sizes per kernel/dtype after a measured 16384-wide fp32 tile overflowed the unified buffer.
plan.hypothesis: The reference aten::_conj_physical has no NPU kernel and falls back to the CPU with per-call transfer/sync, so a single native Triton pass should already beat it; the remaining gap will be host launch cost on the small inputs.

expected_effect.mechanism: Native device execution replaces a CPU-fallback reference that pays D2H/H2D plus synchronization per call.

conclusion.root_cause: The reference aten::_conj_physical has no NPU kernel and falls back to the CPU (measured warning from aten::conj_physical.out plus per-call 0.13 ms for 1024 elements and 5.8-7.3 ms for 65k-1M elements), so a single native Triton pass already wins on every workload. The candidate's own latency is however nearly constant at 0.106-0.125 ms across 1024, 65536 and 1048576 elements, and its per-call device event span equals its walltime, so the remaining bottleneck is host launch submission (~0.10 ms/call, versus ~7 us for the output allocation), not kernel work or HBM traffic.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline round (no previous measurement). Observed: all 8 correctness workloads pass with abs_err/rel_err 0 and matched_ratio 1, including the lazy conjugate-bit and transposed complex cases, and the two small timing inputs are the limiting ones (1.247x for float32[1024], 1.056x for complex64[1024]) while the four larger inputs reach 49-69x. The size independence of the candidate latency shows the gap to the 0.8x bar is entirely launch-side, which the next round targets.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Add a pre-bound launch fast path for the two contiguous kernels: compile through the ordinary kernel[grid](...) call once per (kernel, dtype, tile, pointer-alignment) specialization, then invoke the generated launcher directly with this call's pointers, element count and current stream, keeping the ordinary JIT path as fallback for the strided kernel and for any binding failure.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Preflight PASSED a candidate whose complex64[1048576] specialization later failed to compile with a unified-buffer overflow (2097408 bits required vs 1572864 available at a 16384-wide fp32 tile); only the debug numeric run over the real timing inputs exposed it. Tile width must be budgeted from buffered bytes per kernel shape, not chosen by taste, and preflight is not a substitute for compiling every frozen timing specialization.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Moved from replicating the FlagGems copy/conj decomposition to a self-contained flat-stream kernel: complex conjugate is applied as an alternating-lane sign flip over the interleaved real/imaginary floats, which keeps load and store contiguous, and the conjugate bit is converted into a constexpr instead of being materialized by a copy.

plan.strategy: Cut host launch cost on the dense contiguous paths with a pre-bound compiled launcher, while keeping the ordinary Triton launch path for non-contiguous layouts and as a fallback.
plan.code_changes: Added _copy_cache/_conj_cache plus _bind_copy/_bind_conj: the first call for a (kernel, dtype, tile, src-alignment, dst-alignment) specialization compiles through the ordinary kernel[grid](...) path, then reuses compiled.run.launch with this call's raw pointers, element count and current stream from _npu_getCurrentRawStreamNoWait. The strided kernel and any binding failure keep the ordinary launch. Complex binding warms up on the interleaved real views because Triton has no complex dtype.
plan.hypothesis: Because candidate latency was nearly constant at 0.106-0.125 ms for 1024 through 1048576 elements, the cost is host launch submission rather than kernel work; bypassing JIT dispatch should cut latency toward the ~0.008 ms launcher plus ~0.007 ms output allocation floor and raise every workload, especially the two small inputs that cap the geometric mean.

expected_effect.mechanism: Replacing Triton's per-call JIT dispatch with a direct launcher call removes roughly 30 us of host submission per invocation, which is the measured bottleneck at every input size.

conclusion.root_cause: Per-call cost is now host-side and size independent: every timing input takes 0.0316-0.0328 ms while its device work ranges from nothing to 16 MB of traffic, so the remaining gap is output allocation plus launcher invocation plus Python glue, not device execution.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected a large gain from bypassing JIT dispatch and observed it: geo_mean 15.30x -> 89.38x, i.e. 5.8x better than round 1, with the same 14/14 pass and abs_err/rel_err 0. Per workload latency collapsed from 0.106-0.125 ms to 0.0316-0.0328 ms and is now flat across 1024, 65536 and 1048576 elements, confirming the hypothesis that host submission, not kernel work, set the cost. The large inputs gained the most (t1 53.8x -> 427x, t2 69.0x -> 399x, t4 49.4x -> 403x, t5 53.2x -> 436x) because their reference pays 12.7-14.1 ms of CPU-fallback transfer. The two small inputs improved least (t0 1.25x -> 3.99x, t3 1.06x -> 4.26x) because their reference is only ~0.13 ms, so they are now pinned by the residual per-call floor: allocation ~0.0075 ms plus launcher ~0.008 ms plus Python glue. min_speedup moved from 1.056 to 3.99 and the bottleneck is unchanged in kind, only smaller.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the remaining ~0.032 ms per-call floor, which is now identical for 1024 and 1048576 elements: split it into output allocation, launcher call and Python glue with a preallocated-output probe, then remove whichever dominates (for example by trimming per-call device/stream lookups or by avoiding a masked tail kernel where the count divides evenly).
conclusion.debug_lesson: The complex specialization never bound because JITFunction.warmup received complex tensors while the kernel's signature is a float stream; the failure was invisible because the bind is wrapped in try/except, and only a probe that printed the cache contents exposed that the fast path was dead (t3 stayed at 0.154 ms). Cache-population state is worth asserting in any host-side fast path.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Kept the round 1 kernels untouched and changed only the launch layer, so the 5.8x aggregate gain is attributable to dispatch cost rather than arithmetic or tiling. The strided kernel and any binding failure still take the ordinary Triton path, and the pre-bound path still keys on pointer alignment, so unaligned views get their own specialization (verified: offset view with ptr%16==4 exact and equally fast).

plan.strategy: Trim the dominant remaining host cost (output allocation) without touching the kernels, by selecting the cheaper allocator entry point on the path where it provably preserves the required contiguous, bit-free output.
plan.code_changes: run() now reads is_conj()/is_contiguous() once and, when the input is contiguous and carries no conjugate bit, allocates with torch.empty_like(input) instead of torch.empty(input.shape, dtype=..., device=...); every other case keeps the contiguous torch.empty allocation so the reference's contiguous output layout is preserved. The two flags are reused by both the complex and real branches instead of re-querying.
plan.hypothesis: The per-call floor is now output allocation (~0.0070 ms) plus launcher (~0.0070 ms) plus stream query (~0.0010 ms); torch.empty_like measured 0.0056 ms against 0.0071 ms for torch.empty(shape, ...), so taking it on the dense bit-free path should cut the floor by roughly 1.3 us, from ~0.0313 to ~0.0280 ms.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing 1.3 us of per-call allocation cost from a floor that is otherwise unchanged raises every workload by the same small factor, with the largest relative gain on the small inputs where the reference is fastest.

conclusion.root_cause: Adopted torch.empty_like on the contiguous bit-free path, the cheapest measured allocation entry point, cutting ~1.3 us from a per-call floor that is otherwise dominated by the ~0.007 ms direct launcher call. Confirmed: every timing workload still runs at 0.028-0.034 ms regardless of whether its device work is zero or 16 MB of traffic.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Candidate-side latency fell as predicted: t0 0.03157 -> 0.02779 ms and t3 0.03205 -> 0.03021 ms, i.e. about 1.3-1.8 us per call, matching the 0.0056 vs 0.0071 ms allocation measurement that motivated the change. The headline geo_mean 89.38 -> 112.15 is larger than that change can explain and must not be attributed to it: the reference side moved as well (t1 reference 13.56 -> 27.16 ms, t4 13.23 -> 19.08 ms), which is the CPU-fallback path's own variance. Reads honestly: all six candidate latencies are within 0.0278-0.0335 ms and still size independent, so the floor remains host-bound; the two small inputs stay lowest (4.69x and 4.73x) because their reference is only ~0.13-0.14 ms, and they are now within ~2x of the level where device time would start to dominate.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Stop trimming host glue: the floor is now ~0.028 ms split between a ~0.0056 ms allocation and a ~0.007 ms launcher call, and the remaining Python glue is only a few microseconds. Any further gain would have to come from the launcher call itself, which is already the cheapest supported path (passing tensors instead of raw pointers measured slower at 0.0152 ms vs 0.0102 ms), so the next experiment should instead revisit whether device work begins to matter at the largest sizes, e.g. by comparing tile sizes at 1048576 elements with the host cost held fixed.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Kept both kernels and the launch mechanism identical to round 2 and changed only the allocation entry point, so the candidate-side delta is attributable to that one host-side choice; the geo_mean movement beyond it is reference variance and is reported as such rather than as an optimization win.

plan.strategy: Make the host fast path fail safe: keep the pre-bound launcher as the default and add an exception-guarded fallback to the ordinary Triton dispatch, verifying the guard neither changes results nor costs measurable time.
plan.code_changes: Both pre-bound launch sites in run() are now wrapped in try/except; on any exception the code falls through to the ordinary kernel[grid](...) dispatch for the same kernel and tile, writing the same output. No kernel, tile, key or allocation logic changed.
plan.hypothesis: The direct launcher passes raw integer pointers, which a profiler-instrumented launch context is documented to reject by calling size() on pointer arguments; a guarded fallback should leave the 0.0278-0.0280 ms floor and all workload results unchanged while removing that failure mode.

expected_effect.mechanism: A passing try/except costs nothing on CPython 3.11, so the measured floor should be unchanged while a launch context that rejects raw integer pointers degrades to the slower JIT path instead of failing.

conclusion.root_cause: Added an exception-guarded fallback around both pre-bound launch sites so a launch context that rejects raw integer pointers degrades to the ordinary JIT dispatch. The guard is free when unused, so the measured per-call floor and every workload result are unchanged; the lower geo_mean of this round comes from faster reference-side measurements, not from the candidate.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Candidate side behaved exactly as predicted: every timing workload stayed within 0.0280-0.0286 ms versus round 3's 0.0278-0.0335 ms, all 14 workloads passed with abs_err/rel_err 0, and the guard was separately proven to produce exact output when the launcher raises, so the added try/except cost nothing measurable. The aggregate metric nevertheless fell from 112.15 to 68.75, which the candidate cannot explain: the reference side was remeasured 2-4x faster on the same workloads (t1 27.16 -> 5.85 ms, t2 13.13 -> 7.30 ms, t4 19.08 -> 6.77 ms, t5 11.62 -> 10.57 ms) while the two small inputs stayed flat (t0 0.1304 -> 0.1308 ms reference, 4.69x -> 4.67x speedup). That is the CPU-fallback reference's own variance, so the round is not a candidate regression; the honest reading is that geo_mean for this operator has moved between 15.3 and 112.1 across rounds largely with the reference, while the candidate's own cost has fallen and then held at ~0.028 ms.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Treat the candidate as settled at a ~0.028 ms per-call host floor and do not spend further rounds on host glue: the allocation, launcher and stream steps have each been measured and the only remaining lever is the ~0.007 ms direct launcher call, whose cheaper alternatives (tensor arguments) measured 50% worse. If more measurement is wanted, remeasure the existing best round instead of changing code, because the spread between rounds 3 and 4 is reference-side.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A failing launcher can be simulated by replacing the cached (launch, function, metadata) tuple with a function that raises; that exercises the guard end to end and proved both the real and complex paths still return exact values, which a plain code review of try/except would not have established.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: This round deliberately optimized for robustness rather than speed, using the round-paired structure as a control: identical candidate latency with a very different aggregate score isolates the reference's variance and shows that further host micro-tuning is below the measurement noise of this contract.

plan.strategy: Establish the authoritative baseline of the supplied seed implementation (contiguous 1-D negation kernel + collapsed-stride gather kernel) in this workspace
plan.code_changes: None: the seed file is evaluated unmodified
plan.hypothesis: The seed already passes all 30 workloads (a prior formal run of this exact file passed 30/30 with geo_mean 0.167); its cost is dominated by a ~55 us Triton launch path for small tensors and a 152 us BLOCK=4096 kernel for 4096x4096 tensors

expected_effect.mechanism: Records the starting point for later launch-overhead and tiling experiments

conclusion.root_cause: Seed cost structure established: 9 of 12 timing workloads are host-launch-bound (55-62 us measured against a 40-55 us Triton launch floor, with per-launch marginal cost measured at ~54 us) and 3 are device-bound (151.6 us for 4096x4096 with BLOCK=4096/grid=4096, i.e. ~0.9 TB/s effective on a 176 MB L2-resident working set where the aten reference reaches 23 us).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline geo_mean 0.1597, min_speedup 0.0830 (timing-3). All 30 workloads pass, confirming the earlier 27/30 flaggems baseline failure was not reproducible for this exact seed. Gap decomposition from paired target measurements: (a) launch path - an empty 1-tensor Triton launch costs 51.3 us while the same kernel through the compiled-kernel raw launcher costs 17.1 us and torch's in-place elementwise op costs 6-10 us, so ~35-45 us per call is pure Triton host overhead that dominates every small workload; (b) device tiling - the seed's BLOCK=4096 grid=4096 config measures 152 us on 4096x4096 fp32/fp16 whereas BLOCK=16384 grid=1024 measures 59.2/59.9 us (already at the then-host-bound floor), a 2.6x device-side gain.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Cut the per-call host cost by launching the precompiled Triton kernel directly (warmup once, then call the compiled runner with the tensor plus constexpr-specialized n), and retile large tensors to BLOCK=16384 so the device work drops under the new launch floor.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Bit-exact re-simulation of the frozen reference inputs showed the 3 reported non-finite mismatches do not reproduce; the only deviation was -0.0 vs +0.0 at index 0, which compare() accepts (|diff|=0 <= atol). A prior formal run of the identical file passed 30/30.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: From prompt-only analysis (suspected strided-gather numerics bug) to paired target evidence: numerics are exact, the real cost is a ~55 us Triton host launch path plus an undersized device tile.

plan.strategy: Remove Triton's per-call host launch overhead by launching the precompiled kernel through Triton's own compiled-kernel entry point, keeping identical device kernels and tiling
plan.code_changes: Split the seed kernel into _neg_exact (no mask) and _neg_tail (masked, other=0.0); keep a per-specialisation CompiledKernel handle (kernel.warmup) and launch it through the compiled-kernel entry point with (gridX,1,1, current stream, function, packed_metadata, t, constexprs), skipping the per-call JITFunction binding/cache lookup. Kernel bodies, tiling (BLOCK=4096 above 4096 elements, next_pow2 single tile below) and the strided gather kernel are unchanged, and the standard kernel[grid](...) call remains the fallback.
plan.hypothesis: If the ~55 us per-call cost of the 9 small workloads is Triton host-side launch overhead rather than device work, then launching the already compiled kernel directly (17.1 us measured for the same launch in probe2 vs 51.3 us through kernel[grid]) should cut those workloads to roughly 25-30 us and raise geo_mean from 0.16 to about 0.30, while the three 4096x4096 workloads stay device-bound at ~152 us because their tiling is unchanged.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removes ~27 us of per-call Python argument binding/cache bookkeeping from the 9 host-bound workloads (n<=1048576), where device work is only a few microseconds

conclusion.root_cause: The 9 host-bound workloads were paying Triton's per-call Python launch overhead (measured 54.5 us marginal per empty launch, 51.3 us for a 1-tensor launch) on top of only a few microseconds of device work; replacing the JITFunction.run binding/cache path with the compiled-kernel entry point removed ~21-27 us per call.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted: 9 host-bound workloads fall from ~55-62 us to ~25-30 us (speedup ~0.30) and geo_mean ~0.30, with the three 4096x4096 workloads unchanged at ~152 us. Observed: geo_mean 0.2831 (+77% vs baseline 0.1597); the nine n<=1048576 workloads measured 31.1-34.5 us (speedup 0.336-0.448, previously 0.170-0.188) and the three 4096x4096 workloads stayed at 151.5/151.8/152.0 us (0.085/0.126/0.150), exactly as predicted. Residual gap versus the prediction: the isolated probe measured 27.4-28.9 us per call (best of 3 trials) whereas the harness records 31.1-34.5 us (median of 3 trials after a 25 ms warmup budget), i.e. ~4-6 us of additional per-call cost in the harness path, and the harness reference timings for the small workloads (11.0-12.9 us) are slower than my probe's (8.8-9.2 us), which raises the reference side and lowers speedup relative to my estimate. min_speedup is unchanged at 0.085 because timing-3 was deliberately left on the old tiling.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Retile the device kernel for large tensors: BLOCK=16384 (exact, mask-free) instead of BLOCK=4096/grid=4096, which probe2 measured at 59 us vs 152 us on 4096x4096, so the three still-device-bound workloads (currently 0.085/0.126/0.150 speedup) drop toward the new host floor.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Per-launch marginal cost measured 54.5 us for an empty Triton launch on this stack; the compiled-kernel entry point costs 17.1 us for the same launch, so on this operator the host path, not the elementwise math, is the primary optimization target for n<=1048576.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Layer 1 (host launch path) is now largely done; the remaining cost splits into ~31 us residual host path for small tensors and ~152 us device time for the three 4096x4096 tensors, which is where the worst speedup now lives.

plan.strategy: Retile the device kernel to one 64 KiB tile per program for large tensors, keeping the direct launch path
plan.code_changes: run() now picks block = 65536 // A.element_size() (16384 elements for fp32, 32768 for fp16/bf16 = one 64 KiB tile) when n > 4096, keeping next_pow2(n) single-tile for n <= 4096, with the same exact/masked kernel split and unchanged host launch path and strided kernel.
plan.hypothesis: If the 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound because a 16 KiB tile per program (BLOCK=4096, grid=4096) under-uses the vector core DMA, then a 64 KiB tile (BLOCK=16384 fp32 / 32768 fp16, grid=1024/512) should cut their latency from 152 us to roughly 34-42 us while the nine host-bound workloads stay at their current ~31-36 us, lifting geo_mean from 0.283 to about 0.42.

expected_effect.mechanism: Larger per-program DMA bursts and 4x fewer programs raise the device-side effective bandwidth of the 4096x4096 workloads from ~0.9 TB/s toward the aten reference's ~5 TB/s, dropping them from 152 us toward the ~33 us host floor

profile.summary: mixed: Nine of twelve timed workloads are dispatch-bound: device task time is 1.5-5.2 us while eval latency is 30.3-31.5 us, 4096x4096 fp32 is device-bound with fully serialized AIV pipes (MTE2+MTE3+VEC+scalar sum equals aiv_time), 64 KiB tiles already sustain ~5.9 TB/s aggregate MTE2 read rate (L2-resident); per-program DMA width is not the residual limit

conclusion.root_cause: The 4096x4096 workloads were device-bound because a BLOCK=4096 tile moves only 16 KiB per program, so 4096 programs per kernel spend most of their time on per-program DMA setup rather than on payload; a 64 KiB tile (16384 fp32 / 32768 fp16 elements) reaches the DMA efficiency needed to fall back under the host launch floor.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted: 4096x4096 workloads drop from 152 us to roughly 34-42 us, the nine host-bound workloads keep ~31-36 us, geo_mean ~0.42. Observed: geo_mean 0.4129 (+46% vs 0.2831); the three 4096x4096 workloads fell from 151.5/151.8/152.0 us to 30.4/34.0/41.4 us (speedup 0.085/0.126/0.150 -> 0.412/0.563/0.548) and the nine others stayed at 29.8-31.5 us, matching the prediction within measurement noise. min_speedup improved from 0.084 to 0.366 and the worst workload is now a small host-bound one (timing-9) rather than a large device-bound one, i.e. the device-tiling bottleneck is gone and the residual gap is the host launch floor plus fp32 4096x4096 device time (41.4 us vs the 30 us floor).
conclusion.next_suggestion: With 11 of 12 workloads now inside a few microseconds of the ~30 us host launch floor, attack the remaining host cost: probe6 showed the same launch costs 12.3 us when the pointer is passed as an integer address and the stream handle is resolved through a pre-resolved torch_npu._C entry point, versus 22.8 us with a tensor argument and the driver registry lookup per call.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On this stack a 64 KiB tile per program is the largest element-wise tile that stays inside the vector core UB: fp32 tiles of 32768 elements and static_range loops of 4-8 tiles did not merely fail to compile, they poisoned the device (vector core exception) while still returning plausible timings, so UB sizing must be validated explicitly rather than inferred from a fast measurement.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Device tiling is now resolved (64 KiB tiles); the binding constraint has moved back to the per-call host cost, which now sets the latency of 11 of 12 workloads, with fp32 4096x4096 still ~10 us above that floor.

plan.strategy: Replace the FlagGems composite with one self-contained Triton pass: flat kernel for contiguous input, constexpr-stride flat kernel for uniformly strided views, up-to-8D index-math kernel otherwise; write back into the caller's storage and return A.
plan.code_changes: New tmp/main.py: _nan_to_num_flat / _nan_to_num_scaled / _nan_to_num_nd kernels, metadata-only layout dispatch, block picker (min 1024, cap 8192, ~8 programs for tiny inputs), fp32 staging with exact round-trip casts.
plan.hypothesis: A single fused pass that replaces NaN and both infinities in place removes the multi-kernel FlagGems chain, so correctness (in-place mutation of strided views) is restored and each workload drops to one device launch.

expected_effect.mechanism: First measured round of this workspace: establishes correctness and per-workload latency for the single-pass Triton design.

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline established: single fused in-place Triton pass fixes the three INCORRECT_NUMERICAL strided cases of the FlagGems seed (30/30 PASSED). Perf is limited by host-side Triton JIT dispatch, not by device work: every tiny case (N=1024) measures 72.0-78.0 us while the 16.7M-element cases measure only 83.5-85.2 us, so ~55 us of per-call Python/JIT dispatch dominates every workload.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: No previous measurement (baseline). Absolute view: correctness is now complete; latency is essentially flat across four orders of magnitude of N (72 us at N=1024 vs 84 us at N=16777216), which localises the cost in the kernel[grid](...) dispatch path rather than in memory traffic. Reference latencies are 10.5-11.8 us on the tiny cases, so the headroom there is pure launch cost.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Resolve the compiled Triton launcher once per (dtype, numel) and invoke it directly with grid + raw stream + device pointer, removing the per-call JIT binder/cache-key work; keep the ordinary kernel[grid](...) launch as the fallback for masked-free/misaligned/debug-profiling cases. Expected effect: tiny cases approach the ~16 us launch floor already demonstrated by the in-place negative_ reference, and the large cases shed the same fixed overhead.

plan.strategy: Cache the resolved compiled Triton launcher per (dtype, numel) and drive it directly instead of re-entering JITFunction.run on every call.
plan.code_changes: Added _build_entry: one warmup per (dtype, numel) resolves launcher.launch/function/packed_metadata/grid/block plus a per-device current-stream getter, cached in _ENTRIES; run() then calls the compiled launcher directly and keeps kernel[grid](...) only as fallback (build failure, debug/msprof launches, non-contiguous layouts). Also cached torch.finfo per dtype.
plan.hypothesis: Round 1 latency was flat at ~72 us for N=1024 and ~84 us for N=16.7M, i.e. dominated by the Python-side JIT dispatch path rather than device work; bypassing the binder and invoking the already-compiled launcher with grid + raw stream + device pointer should cut the tiny-case cost toward the ~16 us launch floor while nan/posinf/neginf remain ordinary runtime args (no recompile, values still honoured).

expected_effect.mechanism: Removes the per-call Triton JIT binder/cache-key/dispatch work (~55 us of the measured ~72 us on tiny inputs), so all workloads converge on max(host launch rate, device time).

conclusion.root_cause: Per-call Triton JIT dispatch was the dominant cost for small tensors and removing it delivered a 3.6x geo_mean gain; the remaining 4096x4096 cases are limited on the device by per-program/tile granularity (2048 programs of 16 KiB staging tiles) rather than by the launch path.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: bypassing the JIT binder cuts ~55 us of per-call host cost so every workload converges on max(host launch rate, device time), raising geo_mean. Observed: tiny cases fell from 72.0-78.0 us to 19.0-20.0 us (-73%) and geo_mean rose from 0.208 to 0.748, so the host-overhead mechanism is confirmed. Gap: the same fixed cost was not the whole story for the large workloads - their latency did not move at all (timing-3 83.51 -> 83.44 us, timing-7 85.22 -> 85.12 us) and timing-11 regressed 84.21 -> 88.72 us, which proves those three cases are device-bound, not dispatch-bound. A bounded debug job (MEASURED on target, staging kernel = 84.4 us at 4096x4096 float16) confirmed that the device time is real and that the tile size, not the host path, is what limits it (native-dtype clamp with a 16384-element tile measured 58.5 us). My round-1 inference that the large cases were mostly host overhead was wrong because it came from subtracting two independent measurements.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the device side for the three 4096x4096 workloads: keep the validated fp32-staged compare/select kernel for float32 and general (non-saturating) values, but for 2-byte float dtypes in the saturating case lower the infinity handling to max(min(x,pos),neg) in the input dtype and raise the tile to 16384 elements (32 KiB staging cap).

plan.strategy: Slim the host launch path for the saturating-default request: bake posinf/neginf/nan defaults into constexpr kernel bounds (2 runtime arguments instead of 5) and collapse run() to two dict lookups plus a prebuilt closure, keeping every device kernel's math bit-identical.
plan.code_changes: Added _ntn_default/_ntn_default_masked (native clamp with POS/NEG baked as constexpr) and _ntn_stage_default/_ntn_stage_default_masked (same fp32-staged compare/select math, constants baked). run() now does one dict get by dtype, one by numel, pointer-alignment and contiguity tests, then fires a prebuilt closure whose argument list is 2 runtime scalars (ptr, nan) instead of 5. Below 4 MiB of traffic the smaller-tile slim kernel is preferred (device time hidden under the host floor); above it the measured-fastest tile per dtype is kept (fp16 native clamp 16384, bf16/fp32 staged 8192). Generic/strided/explicit-arg paths untouched.
plan.hypothesis: Round 1's nine small/medium timing cases are launch-cost bound (16.32 us flat from 4 KiB to 8.4 MB), and the prebuilt Triton launch is the dominant term: measured 11.24 us with the seed's 5 runtime arguments versus 9.86 us with 2 (probe, same kernel math, repeated twice). Slimming the argument list plus the Python hot path should cut those cases by ~2 us without touching device behavior.

expected_effect.mechanism: Launch argument marshalling and Python dispatch shrink per call while every device kernel keeps bit-identical math, so the nine host-bound timing cases (flat at 16.3 us) drop toward the 9.9 us prebuilt-launch floor; the three device-bound 4096x4096 cases should not move.

conclusion.root_cause: Launch-argument marshalling was indeed the dominant term for the nine host-bound cases: reducing the default-request launch from five runtime arguments to two (with a prebuilt closure instead of per-call entry unpacking) cut those cases by 2.3 us on average and brought them to reference parity. The regression on the two large non-fp16 cases comes from the same edit: compile-time bounds (POS/NEG as constexpr) changed the generated code for the large-input kernels, and the fp16 4096x4096 case now runs the fp32-staged 8192 tile (82.02 us, matching the measured 82.75 us staged time) instead of the mask-free native clamp at 16384 (measured 58.30 us), a 1.4x device slowdown that no host-side gain can offset.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Observed vs frozen plan: the host-side half of the prediction held and slightly exceeded it - the nine host-bound cases moved from 15.86-16.91 us (mean 16.32) to 13.64-14.91 us (mean 14.02), -2.3 us or -14%, and timing-0 now beats the reference (1.025x) while timing-1/2/4/5/6/10 sit at 0.960-0.982. Aggregate geo_mean rose 0.7142 -> 0.8443 (+18.2%) and all 30 workloads pass with abs_err 0 and rel_err 0. The predicted 'no change' for the three device-bound cases did NOT hold: timing-3 regressed 57.59 -> 82.02 us (speedup 0.531 -> 0.373) and timing-11 83.60 -> 93.37 us (0.699 -> 0.697), while timing-7 stayed 84.04 -> 83.65. Diagnosis from the frozen probe evidence: for 4096x4096 fp16 the plan should have been the mask-free native clamp at BLOCK 16384 (measured 58.30 us device), yet 82.02 us matches the fp32-staged BLOCK 8192 kernel (82.75 us). So baking posinf/neginf as constexpr bounds changed the large-input codegen path (staged fallback or worse lowering) even though the arithmetic is identical; the same mechanism plausibly explains the fp32 case (93.37 vs 84.80 staged). Net: the +18.2% is real and kept, and ~2.8 geo_mean points are recoverable by restoring the round-1 device kernels for the >4 MiB regime.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep the slim kernel for inputs whose traffic is under the host floor, but route large inputs (traffic > 4 MiB) through the exact round-1 device kernels (mask-free native clamp at BLOCK 16384 for 2-byte fp16, mask-always fp32-staged at BLOCK 8192 for bfloat16/float32), whose device times were measured at 58.3/85.2/84.8 us. Host cost is irrelevant there because device time dominates.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A host-side launch-cost change can silently perturb device codegen: timing-3 landed at 82.02 us, which matches the staged-8192 device time (82.75 us) rather than the native clamp-16384 time (58.30 us) for identical math. Any host experiment must therefore be validated case-by-case on the device-bound cases too, not only on the cases it targets.

plan.strategy: Split the default-request launch plan by traffic regime: device-optimal round-1 kernels above 4 MiB, slim 2-argument kernels below it.
plan.code_changes: _build_default now has two regimes: traffic <= 4 MiB keeps the slim 2-runtime-argument constexpr kernels; traffic > 4 MiB uses the exact round-1 kernels and 5-runtime-argument launch (_nan_to_num_clamp/_nan_to_num_clamp_masked at BLOCK 16384 for 2-byte dtypes with fallback to _nan_to_num_stage at BLOCK 8192, and the mask-always _nan_to_num_stage at BLOCK 8192 for float32). The small-input path, the generic dispatch, strided kernels and public signature are unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The >4 MiB cases are device bound, so routing them through the round-1 kernels restores timing-3 to ~57.6 us (speedup 0.373 -> ~0.53) and timing-11 to ~84 us, while the round-2 host gains are retained because the launch argument count is irrelevant when device time dominates.

expected_effect.mechanism: Large inputs return to the device kernels whose device times were measured at 58.30/85.19/84.80 us (clamp16384 for fp16, staged8192 for bfloat16/float32) instead of the 82.02 us staged path the constexpr variants produced, while the nine host-bound cases keep their round-2 13.6-14.9 us latencies.

conclusion.root_cause: The remaining cost is device-bound: the large cases are limited by the per-program load/compute/store structure of the clamp (fp16) and fp32-staged (bfloat16/float32) kernels, which reach 1.15-1.6 TB/s versus 2.1-2.3 TB/s for the reference and 3.5 TB/s for a native copy of the same bytes. Tile size is the strongest measured driver (fp16 BLOCK 16384 = 58.30 us vs 8192 = 81.39 us), and bfloat16/float32 cannot grow past 8192 because bfloat16's native clamp needs 18.1 bytes/element of UB and fp32's staged form 22, against a 192 KiB budget.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: routing >4 MiB traffic through the round-1 kernels restores the large cases without losing the round-2 host gains. Both halves held. timing-3 went 82.02 -> 57.59 us (speedup 0.373 -> 0.531, exactly the round-1 value) and timing-11 93.37 -> 83.60 us (0.697 -> 0.700), while the nine host-bound cases stayed at 12.49-13.93 us (timing-0 1.013x, timing-2 1.033x, timing-6 1.070x now faster than the reference; timing-1/4/5/9 at 0.976-0.989). Aggregate geo_mean 0.8443 -> 0.8879 (+5.2%). Remaining deficits, all device bound: timing-3 57.59 vs 30.57 (0.531), timing-7 84.02 vs 62.13 (0.739), timing-11 83.60 vs 58.55 (0.700). Against the probe's native copy_ calibration (19.2 us for the same 67 MB of 2-byte traffic, 3.5 TB/s) our clamp16384 reaches only 1.15 TB/s, so the gap is kernel structure rather than unavoidable bandwidth; the two smaller residual host gaps are fp32 1024/1048576 (0.903/0.918, 13.91-13.93 us vs 12.58-12.78).
conclusion.next_suggestion: The three 4096x4096 cases now dominate the remaining gap (0.531/0.739/0.700) and are device bound. Sweep device-side launch/compile parameters that leave semantics untouched (num_warps, num_stages) for the winning kernels per dtype, and test a pipelined in-program loop for bfloat16/float32 whose tiles cannot grow past the 192 KiB UB budget; the native copy_ of the same bytes measured 19.2 us for 2-byte, so ~3x of device headroom exists.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The two regimes must be routed by measured mechanism, not by one rule: below the launch floor the argument count matters and the device tile does not, above it the device tile matters and the argument count does not. Round 2 and round 3 together pin that crossover at ~4 MiB of traffic for this operator.

plan.strategy: Use sequential-loop device kernels (2-4 tiles per program, num_stages=1) for the device-bound >4 MiB regime, chosen from the measured per-dtype winners.
plan.code_changes: Added _ntn_clamp_loop and _ntn_stage_loop: masked sequential-loop bodies taking runtime bounds with ITERS/BLOCK constexpr, compiled with num_stages=1. The >4 MiB branch of _build_default now selects (clamp loop, tile 16384, ITERS=2) for 2-byte dtypes, falling back to (staged loop, tile 8192, ITERS=4) if that build fails, and float32 uses (staged loop, tile 8192, ITERS=4). The <=4 MiB slim path, the generic/strided dispatch and the public signature are unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: All three 4096x4096 cases are limited by per-task load/compute/store serialisation rather than by UB-limited tile size alone, so processing 2 (fp16) or 4 (bf16/fp32) sequential tiles per program with num_stages=1 improves them by 8-12% and lifts geo_mean from 0.888 to ~0.905.

expected_effect.mechanism: Halving-to-quartering the task count while keeping the fastest measured tile amortises per-task setup: timing-3 58.4 -> 51.5 us, timing-7 84.8 -> 78.2 us, timing-11 84.4 -> 77.0 us of device time.

conclusion.root_cause: The 4096x4096 cases were limited by per-task load/compute/store serialisation as well as tile size: each task paid its own MTE setup, and with ~1024-2048 tasks over 20 vector cores that overhead was paid 25-50 times per core. Processing 2 sequential tiles per program for float16 (BLOCK 16384) and 4 for bfloat16/float32 (BLOCK 8192) with num_stages=1 amortises it without exceeding the 192 KiB UB budget, which the double-buffered default (num_stages=2) cannot do at these tiles.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: timing-3 58.4 -> 51.5 us, timing-7 84.8 -> 78.2 us, timing-11 84.4 -> 77.0 us, geo_mean 0.888 -> ~0.905. Observed: timing-3 50.86 us (speedup 0.600, prediction 0.59-0.60), timing-7 77.48 us (0.802, predicted 0.79), timing-11 76.41 us (0.764, predicted 0.76) - all met within noise, and the nine host-bound cases held at 11.92-12.77 us, seven of them now faster than the reference. Aggregate geo_mean 0.8879 -> 0.9552 (+7.6%), all 30 PASSED with abs_err 0 and rel_err 0. Residual gap is now only the three 4096x4096 cases: timing-3 50.86 vs 30.53 (0.600), timing-7 77.48 vs 62.13 (0.802), timing-11 76.41 vs 58.41 (0.764). Against the probe calibration (copy_ 19.2 us, torch 32.1 us for the same 67 MB) fp16 still runs at 1.30 TB/s versus 2.1-3.5 TB/s attainable, so device headroom remains but the host-side opportunity is exhausted (those cases are at 0.997-1.125).
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep pushing the device-bound regime: sweep more sequential tiles per program (8/16) for bfloat16/float32, and test two-stage software pipelining (num_stages=2 with the tile halved so the doubled buffer still fits UB) for all three dtypes, since tile and task count now dominate and both are UB-limited.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The winning device structure was invisible to per-kernel micro-benchmarks until the kernel body was compiled with num_stages=1: the same 2-iteration loop overflowed UB at the default num_stages=2 (double buffering), which is why probe 7's first attempt failed and probe 6 only succeeded on the variant that passed num_stages=1 explicitly.

plan.strategy: Try a native-dtype compare/select loop on the large bfloat16 tile, falling back to the measured staged loop when the tile does not fit UB.
plan.code_changes: Added _ntn_cs_loop: a masked sequential-loop compare/select body kept entirely in the input dtype (no fp32 staging), same signature and num_stages=1 convention as the other loop kernels. In the >4 MiB branch, bfloat16 now tries (_ntn_clamp_loop tile 16384 ITERS 2) then (_ntn_cs_loop tile 16384 ITERS 2) then the existing (_ntn_stage_loop tile 8192 ITERS 4); float16 and float32 candidate lists are unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: bfloat16's 4096x4096 deficit (77.48 us vs the 62.13 us reference) comes from its staged kernel upconverting to fp32, which doubles UB per element and forces an 8192 tile where float16 uses 16384. A native-dtype compare/select on the 16384 tile should recover most of the tile-size advantage if the build fits; if it does not compile, the existing staged loop (measured 78.2 us) is retained unchanged, so the downside is bounded.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing the fp32 staging for bfloat16 should cut its UB per element from 18-22 B toward the ~10-12 B of the fp16 native path, letting the 16384 tile compile so timing-7 can approach float16's 50.9 us instead of 77.5 us.

conclusion.root_cause: Replacing the fp32-staged bfloat16 body with a compare/select kept in the input dtype did not free the UB budget: at tile 16384 the build still overflowed, so bfloat16 stays capped at tile 8192 (its per-element UB cost is inherent to the bf16 compare/select lowering, not only to the explicit upconvert) and timing-7 kept its staged-loop time of 77.5 us. The round is therefore a no-op on device behaviour, and the small geo_mean movement is reference-side noise on unchanged paths.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: bfloat16's timing-7 would drop from 77.5 us toward float16's 50.9 us if the native compare/select freed enough UB for a 16384 tile; if it did not compile the staged loop (78.2 us) would be retained with bounded downside. Observed: timing-7 = 77.52 us (speedup 0.802), identical to round 4, so the native-dtype body at tile 16384 did not fit and the fallback ran - the hypothesis is falsified but the downside materialised only as the expected no-change on that case. Aggregate geo_mean moved 0.9552 -> 0.9484 (-0.7%), which is entirely measurement variation on cases whose code path did not change: the nine host-bound cases re-timed at 12.47-13.89 us and their references were re-measured at 13.34-14.25 us (round 4 references were 12.55-13.87 us), and timing-3/timing-11 reproduced to within 0.01 us (50.86 vs 50.86, 76.41 vs 76.41).
conclusion.next_suggestion: Try the native compare/select at the size bfloat16 can actually fit (tile 8192, ITERS 2 and 4) to see whether dropping the fp32 conversions alone beats the staged loop's 77.5 us, and check whether float16 benefits from the same body at 16384. If neither wins, the three large cases are at the practical ceiling of this backend's elementwise codegen and the remaining work is host-side only.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The bfloat16 tile cap cannot be escaped by removing the fp32 staging: the native compare/select body still exceeded the UB budget at tile 16384 (timing-7 stayed at the staged fallback, 77.52 us), so bfloat16's per-element UB cost comes from the bf16 compare/select lowering itself, not only from the explicit upconvert.

plan.strategy: Replace the inherited FlagGems cross wrapper with two purpose-built Triton kernels: a flat contiguous kernel for the dominant last-axis layout (eight shifted contiguous block loads + four selects reproduce aten's cross arithmetic with no gather) and a generic (outer,3,inner) kernel for arbitrary cross axis / strides / broadcasting.
plan.code_changes: New self-contained tmp/main.py: _cross_flat_kernel over the flat 3*N index space using only +1/+2/-1/-2 shifted contiguous loads and per-lane column selection; _cross_general_kernel with six slice loads and three slice stores; wrapper resolves dim (incl. dim=None first-size-3 rule), validates dtype/shape/device and resizes out like the aten out-variant.
plan.hypothesis: The inherited FlagGems path is far off the roofline (geo_mean 0.136, i.e. ~7x slower than the aten reference) because it pays host-side validation plus a general strided kernel. A dedicated flat kernel with fully contiguous accesses should move all nine timing workloads toward the memory roofline.

expected_effect.mechanism: First measured round of a dedicated flat Triton cross kernel; establishes the reference point for later tuning.

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline round. The inherited FlagGems path measured geo_mean 0.136 (every timing case below 1.0). The new dedicated flat kernel lifted geo_mean to 0.4975 with all 21 workloads numerically correct, but bounded diagnostics showed the flat kernel itself is bound neither by bytes nor by loads: 1M rows of fp16 and fp32 both take ~1.70 ms, i.e. ~20 core-cycles per element, while an aligned copy of the same element count takes 0.065-0.074 ms. Diagnostics also showed that eight shifted (+1/+2/-1/-2) contiguous loads with one affine mask reach 0.078 ms, so the per-lane `off % 3` phase computation plus the four distinct per-load boolean masks are what force the backend onto a scalar path.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline, so no prior measurement to compare against. Workload-level picture versus the 0.1357 starting KPI: all 9 timing cases passed but only the two 65536-row cases and the three 1048576-row cases exceeded 0.66x, while the three 1024x3 cases reached only 0.248-0.259x. Two independent limits were quantified by bounded diagnostics: (a) device kernel - the flat kernel needs ~1.70 ms for 1M rows where the aligned-copy ceiling is 0.073 ms, a ~23x gap caused by the runtime modulo phase; (b) host dispatch - an empty Triton launch costs ~60.5 us walltime while the plain Python wrapper arithmetic costs only 6.1 us, and the aten reference performs the whole 1024x3 cross in ~19 us, so the three smallest cases are almost entirely host-overhead bound and cap the geo_mean regardless of device speed.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Replace the runtime `off % 3` phase with a compile-time constant pattern by making every program's flat base a multiple of 3 (STEP = BLOCK - BLOCK % 3, phase = arange % 3), keeping the same eight plain-affine shifted loads, then separately attack the ~60 us Triton host dispatch overhead that dominates the three 1024x3 cases.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On this Ascend backend only plain-affine block indices lower to block DMA: `tl.minimum`/`tl.maximum` index clamps cost 70x (5.5-7.3 ms vs 0.078 ms) and 2-D strided tiles cost 130x (10.1 ms). Load count is nearly free (4/6/8 shifted loads all ~0.078 ms), so tiling decisions should target index-expression simplicity, not byte volume.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Started from the FlagGems seed (0.136). Moved to a self-contained pair of Triton kernels (flat last-axis kernel + generic (outer,3,inner) kernel) for a 0.4975 geo_mean baseline. Bounded microbenchmarks then redirected the effort from bandwidth/tiling toward (i) index-expression lowering and (ii) host dispatch overhead, which the device-side roofline alone would not have revealed.

plan.strategy: Establish the measured baseline with the seed implementation (flat gather kernel + cached direct launcher for the last-dim contiguous case, generic stride kernel otherwise), with alias protection re-expressed as a metadata byte-range overlap test because torch._C._is_alias_of is rejected by candidate admission.
plan.code_changes: Seed code copied verbatim except the two torch._C._is_alias_of alias checks, which are replaced by a data_ptr/element byte-range overlap test plus clone() for the aliased input.
plan.hypothesis: The unmodified seed reproduces roughly 0.76 geo-mean speedup: small cases are launch-overhead bound (~0.87x) while the large 1M-vector cases are ~0.68x because the four tl.gather permutations on the interleaved last-dim layout dominate the kernel.

expected_effect.mechanism: Reference measurement of the current best-known candidate on the authoritative suite.

profile.summary: failed: msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker (5/5 attempts: batch of 4 workloads at metrics level, one workload at metrics level, one workload at instruction level). capabilities=[], artifacts=[], metrics={} on every attempt; only request/result manifests were written, which the recorder does not accept as evidence artifacts.

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline of the seed candidate. The flat last-dim path costs ~0.69x on all large/mid cases (timing-2 fp16 1.6996ms vs 1.1738ms reference; timing-8 fp32 1.7125ms vs 1.1402ms) while the 1024x3 cases are launch-overhead bound at 0.79-0.93x. Reference latency is essentially dtype-independent per element (1.174ms fp16 vs 1.140ms fp32 for the same 3.1M elements), so the kernel is per-element bound, not byte bound.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Bounded target-side diagnostics isolated the mechanism: a pure copy of the same footprint is 0.0682ms, four misaligned shifted loads are 0.0672ms, but adding only `lane % 3` raises it to 2.171ms and the seed's four tl.gather shuffles cost ~0.41ms each. Replace the integer modulo with an fp32-reciprocal phase and the four gathers with eight shifted contiguous loads: the correct formula then runs at 0.0752ms for 1M vectors.

Capping the grid at the reported 40 vector cores and streaming unmasked contiguous tiles cut 4096x4096 fp16 from 87.3 us to 48.8 us (96 MB of traffic, ~2.0 TB/s) and bf16 on the same shape from 88.5 us to 48.9 us, while the nine host-dispatch-bound workloads were unaffected as predicted.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected a large-workload gain from replacing 2048 single-tile programs with one program per vector core; observed far more than the microbenchmark predicted. geo_mean 0.8546 -> 0.9319 (+9.0%). timing-3 87.34 -> 48.80 us (speedup 0.5266 -> 0.9605, better than the 67.6 us the isolated sweep predicted and close to aten's 51.9 us), timing-7 88.54 -> 48.92 us (0.9956 -> 1.8139), timing-11 180.25 -> 166.55 us (0.9833 -> 1.0612). The nine host-bound workloads were predicted flat and stayed flat: timing-0 29.11 -> 30.14, timing-1 29.00 -> 29.50, timing-2 31.45 -> 29.99, timing-4 29.08 -> 29.04, timing-5 29.76 -> 29.27, timing-6 29.02 -> 29.43, timing-8 29.03 -> 29.27, timing-9 30.28 -> 29.24, timing-10 31.18 -> 29.98 us. Their small net change (-0.35 us mean) is consistent with the streaming loop's scalar prologue replacing straight-line tile code, so the 2048-program setup overhead hypothesis is confirmed for large n while the streaming loop is not optimal for a single tile. All 18 correctness workloads still pass and every streaming/tail variant was verified bit-identical to the flat reference before submission.
conclusion.next_suggestion: The nine remaining workloads share one flat per-call cost (29.0-30.1 us against 24.5-27.0 us references) with negligible device work, decomposed on the target as torch.empty(shape,device,dtype) 7.85 us + wrapper validation/dispatch ~7.7 us + an 11.6 us launcher closure of which ~1.1 us is data_ptr and ~0.4 us the raw stream. Next: flatten the host path to a single frame with a module-level identity-compared plan slot (no tuple/dict lookup, no helper-call layer, torch.empty_like instead of torch.empty(tuple(shape),...)) and specialize the exact single-tile case to a straight-line kernel with no loop prologue, since the streaming form cost ~1 us on those loads (timing-0 29.11 -> 30.14 us).
conclusion.debug_lesson: Two cheap target microbenchmarks (host-component breakdown plus a kernel-variant sweep) resolved two independent hypotheses without consuming evaluation rounds; the microbenchmark's own 67.6 us device figure for 4096x4096 fp16 was pessimistic versus the 48.8 us observed under the evaluation harness, so microbenchmark absolutes were treated only as relative guidance.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: R1 baseline isolated two independent limiters (host floor on 9/12 workloads, device program count on the 3 large ones). R2 took the device limiter only, deliberately leaving the host path byte-identical so the effect was attributable; that succeeded, so R3 can take the host limiter on top of a proven device kernel.

plan.strategy: Collapse the per-call host path into a single frame with an identity-compared module-level plan slot and torch.empty_like, and specialize the exact single-tile geometry to a straight-line kernel.
plan.code_changes: Hot path is now one frame: four identity/integer comparisons against the module-level _FAST plan slot (dtype is, n ==, get_device ==, plus self_t dtype/shape and two is_contiguous checks), one torch.empty_like bound as a module global (replacing torch.empty(tuple(shape),device=,dtype=)), then an int-address launch with the launch/grid/block/fn/packed/stream fields taken straight from the slot - no _dispatch helper call, no tuple key, no dict lookup. Also added _hsb_tile, a straight-line exact-single-tile kernel used when grid == 1 and no tail exists (n=1024-class loads), which removes the streaming loop prologue measured at ~1 us on those loads. All validation, errors, strided layout handling and the cold-path plan construction moved unchanged into _slow; the stream is still re-read per call.
plan.hypothesis: The nine remaining workloads are pure per-call fixed cost: 29.0-30.1 us against 24.5-27.0 us references with negligible device work. Target decomposition of the current 28.4 us path was torch.empty(tuple,device,dtype) 7.85 us, wrapper validation/dispatch ~7.7 us, and an 11.6 us launcher closure, versus torch.empty_like 6.0 us and a 20.7 us lean_run floor, so flattening the frame and switching the allocation should recover roughly 6-8 us on each of them.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing ~3 Python call frames, the tuple/dict plan lookup and the tuple(shape) allocation path from every call cuts the fixed per-call host cost that dominates these loads, while the straight-line single-tile kernel removes the streaming loop prologue.

conclusion.root_cause: Confirmed host-side fixed cost: the previous path paid a helper-call layer, a tuple key into a dict plan cache, and torch.empty(tuple(shape),device=,dtype=) on every call. Collapsing to a single frame with an identity-compared plan slot plus torch.empty_like, and giving the grid==1 exact case a straight-line kernel with no loop prologue, cut 3.4-4.5 us from every host-bound call and raised geo_mean from 0.9319 to 1.0278.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted 6-8 us recovered per call on the nine host-bound workloads; observed 3.4-4.5 us, i.e. the mechanism acted but at roughly 60% of the predicted magnitude. Own latencies: timing-0 30.14 -> 25.64, timing-1 29.50 -> 25.75, timing-2 29.99 -> 28.05, timing-4 29.04 -> 27.56, timing-5 29.27 -> 28.43, timing-6 29.43 -> 29.18, timing-8 29.27 -> 25.78, timing-9 29.24 -> 26.10, timing-10 29.98 -> 27.36 us, with speedups 0.897/0.862/0.850/0.849/0.847/0.837/0.839/0.842/0.832 -> 0.972/1.066/0.945/0.996/0.973/0.943/0.957/0.956/0.918. geo_mean 0.9319 -> 1.0278 (+10.3%), which matches the 9/12-weighted ~13% per-case gain on the host-bound set. The residual 25.6 us versus the 20.7 us measured lean_run floor is the per-call contract work the probe skipped (shape equality, device query, dtype identity, alignment guard, float coercion), and the earlier 7.85 us allocation was replaced by the 6.0 us empty_like path. The three large workloads were unchanged by design and moved only by noise: timing-3 48.80 -> 50.13, timing-7 48.92 -> 49.94, timing-11 166.55 -> 166.72 us. All 18 correctness workloads still pass, including the strided ones that route through _slow and the strict Triton copy path.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Further host trimming is below the measurement noise: the references themselves move 24.7-27.7 us (up to 10%) between rounds, and removing the two remaining contract checks (device query 0.31 us, shape equality 0.78 us) would trade observable error semantics for under 1 us. If another round is spent, target the device side only: for 4096x4096 fp32 the 192 MB working set exceeds the 168 MB L2, so 166.7 us at 1.15 TB/s is HBM-bound; the same applies to the 2.0 TB/s of the 2-byte 4096x4096 case, where the frozen reference reaches the same 2.0 TB/s, leaving timing-3 essentially capped near parity.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The measured component costs (empty tuple+kwargs 7.85 vs empty_like 6.0 us; lean_run floor 20.7 us for the whole allocate+launch path) correctly ranked the host levers, but they over-predicted the total: the reachable floor still has to pay the checks the lean probe omitted, so a measured floor should be treated as a lower bound, not an attainable target.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: R2 removed the device limiter (many tiny programs -> one program per vector core) and left the host path byte-identical. R3 removed the host limiter on top of that proven device kernel using the target-measured component breakdown. Both limiters identified at baseline are now addressed, and the remaining gap is dominated by reference noise and by hardware rooflines that the frozen reference also sits on.

plan.strategy: Guard the predicated tail tile with a scalar range check so only programs that actually own tail elements execute it.
plan.code_changes: In _hsb_stream_tail, the single predicated tail tile is now wrapped in a scalar guard `if base < N` where base = full + pid*BLOCK, so programs whose tail start already lies past the end issue no masked vector work at all. The hot loop, masks, geometry, host path and all other kernels are unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: For 1048576-element loads with grid=40 and BLOCK=8192 the tail region is only 8 tiles, so 32 of 40 programs run a completely masked tile whose vector ALU work and sync are pure overhead on a kernel of roughly 3 us; guarding it should trim the three mid-size workloads (timing-2/6/10, now 0.945/0.943/0.918) by a fraction of a microsecond each, and slightly reduce the 4096x4096 tail overhead.

expected_effect.mechanism: Programs that own no tail element skip a fully-masked tile (and its pipeline sync), removing provably empty per-program work from the mid-size and large launches.

A future session should first re-establish a same-round baseline before chasing sub-microsecond host deltas, since reference-side drift of 10-15% exceeds every remaining candidate-side lever.

Every candidate latency rose (host-bound cases 25.6-29.2 -> 28.2-30.8 us) while the reference side rose more (24.9-27.7 -> 29.1-29.7 us), so the frozen ratio metric rose even though my absolute candidate times regressed. Absolute latency comparisons across rounds are therefore unreliable on this shared device; only the same-round candidate/reference ratio, and single-round microbenchmarks, can be used to attribute a mechanism.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: R1 baseline separated host and device limiters. R2 fixed the device limiter (many tiny programs -> one program per vector core), R3 fixed the host limiter (single-frame hot path + straight-line single-tile kernel), reaching 1.0278. plan.strategy: Replace the FlagGems seed with a self-contained Triton in-place subtract kernel: flat unit-stride kernel for contiguous operands plus a constexpr (shape, strideA, strideB) index kernel for strided views and broadcasting.
plan.code_changes: New tmp/main.py: _sub_flat (fp32 compute, mask on n), _sub_flat_native for integral dtypes, _sub_strided with collapsed constexpr dim/stride tuples; run(A, B, *, alpha=1) mutates A in place and returns A; plain kernel[grid](...) launches with BLOCK=4096 (512 for the strided path).
plan.hypothesis: Correct IEEE arithmetic in the kernel preserves +-inf/NaN from the special-value inputs (fixing the three non-finite mismatches of the FlagGems seed) and gives a fully passing baseline whose large-case speeds are set by HBM traffic.

expected_effect.mechanism: First measured round: establishes a correct Triton baseline with plain JIT launches so the host-dispatch overhead and the device throughput can be separated in later rounds.

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline established: the self-contained Triton in-place kernel reproduces A.sub_(B, alpha=0.5) semantics bit-exactly enough for all 30 frozen workloads (18/18 correctness incl. the three 2D-strided special-value cases that the FlagGems seed failed). Performance is bimodal: the three 4096x4096 workloads run at device bandwidth (2.50x and 2.45x versus the fp16/bf16 reference, 0.86x versus the fp32 reference at 172.6 us), while all nine remaining timing workloads sit at a fixed ~62 us regardless of element count (1024 or 1048576 elements), i.e. they are pure Triton JIT host-dispatch cost, not device time.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: No prior measured round, so this is the reference point for later rounds. Absolute evidence: 9 workloads at 61.5-64.1 us candidate versus 12.4-16.8 us reference (speedup 0.20-0.27) with latency independent of numel -> per-call host overhead; a bounded debug probe measured plain JIT kernel[grid](...) dispatch at 59.2 us and the flag/torch reference at 14.7 us for the same 1024-element call, confirming the gap is host-side. Large cases: fp16 4096^2 152.1 us (2.50x), bf16 4096^2 152.0 us (2.45x), fp32 4096^2 172.6 us (0.86x, 1.17 TB/s logical) so the fp32 tile/grid organisation still leaves device-side headroom versus the 148.4 us reference. geo_mean 0.395 is therefore dominated by the nine host-bound workloads.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep the device kernel; replace the per-call JIT dispatch with the backend's low-level compiled launcher (CompiledKernel.run.launch with int grid, cached function/packed_metadata, freshly read stream and pointers) for the contiguous path, which is expected to cut the ~62 us host cost toward the reference's ~14 us on the nine small/medium workloads.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 establishes a correct Triton baseline that already fixes the seed's three non-finite correctness failures; the measured evidence splits the remaining problem into host dispatch (9 workloads) and fp32/bf16 device tiling (3 workloads).

plan.strategy: Keep the round-1 device kernel and replace only the host dispatch: launch the pre-compiled kernel through the backend's low-level launcher instead of the Triton JIT entry, after verifying on the target that the direct path is numerically identical and re-reads pointers/alpha/stream per call.
plan.code_changes: Added _ENTRIES cache keyed by (dtype, numel, device) holding the compiled artifact resolved through _sub_flat.warmup(); run() now launches that entry via compiled.run.launch(gridX, 1, 1, stream, function, packed_metadata, None, None, None, a_ptr, b_ptr, alpha, n, BLOCK) guarded by 16B pointer alignment and the launcher debug flags, with a plain kernel[grid](...) fallback for unaligned pointers, non-contiguous views and integral dtypes. Kernel bodies, block size and grid shape are unchanged from round 1; pointers, alpha and the current stream are read on every call. The low-level launch entry was chosen from the batch's injected historical note that compiled.run.launch is this backend's low-level launch path; the method was verified on the target (numerics identical for fresh pointers/alpha and for a larger grid) before adoption.
plan.hypothesis: The nine small/medium timing workloads are dominated by Triton JIT dispatch, not device work, so launching the already-compiled artifact through the backend launcher with only fresh pointers/scalars/stream will cut their per-call cost to roughly the reference's 12-17 us and raise geo_mean well above 0.395 without changing the large-case results.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removes Triton's per-call argument binding / cache-key / dispatch work (~59 us measured for the same 1024-element launch) on the nine host-bound timing workloads; they were 61.5-64.1 us and should approach the ~9-12 us launch cost, while the three bandwidth-bound 4096x4096 workloads stay at their round-1 device time.

conclusion.root_cause: Confirmed: the nine small/medium workloads were bound by Triton's JIT dispatch (59.4 us measured, versus 8.5 us for the backend launcher and 13.7 us for the reference), not by device work. Replacing only the host dispatch cut them to 15.5-17.4 us and left the three large workloads unchanged, so the device kernels were already correct and unchanged.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted: the nine host-bound workloads drop from ~62 us toward the reference's 12-17 us; observed: all nine fell to 15.5-17.4 us (fp16/bf16 0.80-1.08x, fp32 0.80-0.82x), i.e. slightly above the 8.5 us bare-launch/host floor measured on the target because our call also pays ~2.8 us of wrapper prelude (numel, contiguity, shape compare, data_ptr, dict key, stream query). The three bandwidth-bound workloads were untouched as planned: fp16 4096^2 151.9 us, bf16 151.9 us, fp32 177.7 us, so the aggregate geo_mean rose from 0.395 to 1.130 (2.86x) with the per-workload ordering preserved. Remaining gap: nine workloads still ~0.8-1.08x because their latency is host dominated, and the fp32 4096^2 tile (4096 elements = 16 KiB per operand) is below the 32 KiB per-operand tile that target probes showed to be ~2.4x faster (653 -> 1558 GB/s) for 2-byte dtypes.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Next bottleneck: the three 4096x4096 workloads are now device-bound and the fp16/bf16 tiles are too small (BLOCK=4096 gives 653 GB/s while 16384 gives ~1560-1660 GB/s in target probes, and 32768 overflows the 192 KiB unified buffer); size the flat tile to ~32 KiB per operand and use the unmasked kernel when numel is a multiple of it, keeping the nine host-bound workloads on their current path.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 isolated the problem into host dispatch (9 workloads) and device tiling (3 workloads). Round 2 fixed the host side; the device side is now the next target, with the tile policy already screened on the target.

conclusion.next_suggestion: Pin ck.run.launch and cache the stream handle per specialization, which the diagnostic measured as 3.8us plus 9.8us per call, then attack the remaining wrapper overhead (two new_empty allocations plus one unbind, which accounted for the 27.9us gap between the bare launch and the full wrapper).
conclusion.debug_lesson: The per-specialization tuner was harmful because 16-iteration min comparisons cannot separate entries that differ by ~15%, and a runtime query that looks negligible standalone can be serialized against the launch queue; both must be measured inside the real per-call path.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Launch-entry selection must be deterministic rather than timing-selected, and the stream handle must be captured once per specialization; allocation/view dispatch is now the largest removable wrapper term.

plan.strategy: Replace the FlagGems pointwise_dynamic wrapper with a self-contained in-place Triton kernel driven through its own compiled launcher (pattern taken from the prompt-injected expm1_/nan_to_num_ host examples), and add explicit stride-aware kernels for non-contiguous views.
plan.code_changes: New tmp/main.py: (1) flat unmasked kernel (ptr + BLOCK constexpr) for exact-multiple sizes, masked flat kernel otherwise, uniform-stride SCALE kernel and up-to-8D index kernel for non-contiguous input, all staging the transcendental in float32 and storing back in the input dtype; (2) wrapper resolves the compiled launcher once per (dtype, numel, device) and calls launcher.launch(gridx,1,1,raw_stream,function,packed_metadata,None,None,None,ptr,*params) with the raw stream handle re-queried every call; (3) per-dtype tile caps 16384 (2-byte) / 8192 (4-byte) because BLOCK=32768 was measured to overflow the 192 KiB UB on this target; (4) stride coalescing + scaled/ND kernels for non-contiguous views, adapted from the prompt-injected expm1_/nan_to_num_ examples.

plan.strategy: Measure the provided seed implementation unchanged to establish the baseline latency and correctness for torch.fix truncation
plan.code_changes: None; seed written verbatim to tmp/main.py
plan.hypothesis: The seed's floor/ceil + sign-bit restoration kernel preserves -0/NaN/Inf semantics and passes all 18 correctness cases; baseline geo_mean establishes the reference ratio

expected_effect.mechanism: Unmodified seed measurement

conclusion.root_cause: Seed baseline passes all 18 correctness cases bit-exactly (abs_err=0, matched_ratio=1) but is slow: geo_mean 0.518. Two independent gaps, both measured: (1) per-call host cost is ~26 us versus ~14 us for the reference torch.fix on every workload with n<=1M (9 of 12 timing cases sit at a flat 0.67-0.74x regardless of size, so the difference is host submit, not device work); (2) at n=16.7M the device kernel costs ~127 us of the ~152 us latency while the reference executes the same case inside its ~19.8 us host floor, and fp16 (0.13x) and fp32 (0.13x/0.59x) cost nearly the same despite 2x different byte counts, which points to vector-instruction count and per-block overhead rather than DMA bandwidth. The seed's kernel also masks every load/store even when BLOCK divides n exactly, and spends 9 vector ops per element (cvt, cmp, floor, ceil, select, 2x and, or, cvt).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: No previous measurement to compare against (first round). Workload-level facts recorded for the next round: flat ~0.69x for n in {1024, 65536, 1048576} across fp16/bf16/fp32, 0.1298x for fp16 4096x4096, 0.1287x for bf16 4096x4096, 0.5876x for fp32 4096x4096; min_speedup 0.1287 at fix-timing-7.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Remove the per-element mask on the contiguous path when BLOCK divides n, raise the tile to 8192 elements, replace floor+ceil+select (9 vector ops) with an abs/floor/sign-restore form (6 vector ops), and slim the host path (drop memory_format on the fast path, cache the raw-stream getter and device index) to attack both the flat host-bound cases and the op-count-bound 16.7M cases.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Target-side probing showed torch.empty_like ~5.6 us and the raw Triton launcher dominating the remaining host cost; because eval timing is submit-limited for all n<=1M, device-side tuning cannot move those cases.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Baseline measured; next round attacks mask removal, tile size, vector-op count and host glue together, then a final round tunes based on per-case evidence.

plan.strategy: Shrink both terms of the kernel cost model: unmasked loads/stores when BLOCK divides n, larger tiles to halve the block count, and a lower vector-op count per element
plan.code_changes: Added an unmasked contiguous kernel (_fix_nomask) selected whenever n is divisible by a power-of-two BLOCK >= 512, raised the tile cap from 4096 to 8192, replaced the 9-op floor+ceil+select+bitops truncation with a 6-op abs/floor/sign-restore form, and slimmed the host path (no memory_format on the fast path, module-level raw-stream getter, single cached entry list keyed by (dtype, n))
plan.hypothesis: The 16.7M cases are vector-instruction and per-block-overhead bound rather than DMA bound, so dropping the load/store masks, doubling the tile to 8192 elements, and cutting the truncation from 9 to 6 vector ops per element should sharply reduce device time for fix-timing-3/7/11 while leaving the 9 submit-limited cases near their host floor

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing per-element mask computation and halving the block count cuts per-block and per-element vector work at n=16.7M, where fp16 and fp32 currently cost the same ~127 us despite 2x different byte counts; the slimmer host path removes a few microseconds from the submit-limited cases
