plan.strategy: Establish measured baseline with the provided seed Triton trunc kernel (nomask/masked/strided paths, one tile per program, cached launch metadata)
plan.code_changes: None; seed written verbatim as tmp/main.py
plan.hypothesis: Seed reproduces the recorded 0.789 score; large 4096x4096 fp16/bf16 workloads are the main deficit (~0.30 speedup) due to 2048 tiny programs

expected_effect.mechanism: Measure unmodified seed to anchor all later comparisons

conclusion.root_cause: Seed kernel launches one BLOCK-sized tile per program, so 4096x4096 (16.7M elements) creates 2048 tiny programs on a 20-core device; each program does a serialized load->vector->store with no cross-tile pipelining, achieving only ~0.84 TB/s effective HBM traffic (fp16) vs ~1.35 TB/s for the CANN reference. Small shapes are already host-overhead bound and slightly faster than reference (1.10-1.19x).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline established: geo_mean 0.9048 over 12 timing workloads. Deficits are concentrated in the three 16.7M-element shapes: fix-timing-3 (fp16) 0.313, fix-timing-7 (bf16) 0.322, fix-timing-11 (fp32) 0.820. All other nine workloads are 1.10-1.19x. Lifting the three large shapes to ~0.9 alone would move geo_mean to roughly 1.08, so large-shape DMA organization is the only lever that matters.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Replace the one-tile-per-program launch for large contiguous inputs with a multi-tile persistent kernel: small fixed program count (capped by tl.num_programs stride), each program loops over many BLOCK tiles so the compiler can pipeline load/compute/store across iterations. Microbenchmark grid x BLOCK x num_stages on the target before the next formal round.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Seed established as baseline; next step targets per-program DMA pipelining for large shapes.

plan.strategy: Replace one-tile-per-program launches for large contiguous inputs with a persistent multi-tile kernel whose program count is the device vector-core count
plan.code_changes: Added _fix_loop / _fix_loop_tail persistent kernels (compile-time TILES/N, stride by tl.num_programs(0), num_stages=2). For n >= 8*8192 the launch uses grid = min(tiles, vector_core_num from torch.npu.get_device_properties, task-derived fallback) with BLOCK=8192 instead of one program per 8192-element tile. Small/odd shapes keep the previous one-tile-per-program paths; strided path unchanged. Launch metadata still warmed once and reused via raw launch.
plan.hypothesis: The three 4096x4096 workloads are limited by 2048 tiny single-tile programs (one serialized load->vector->store each). A persistent kernel with one program per vector core (40 on the probe device), each looping over ~51 tiles, lets the compiler pipeline the tiles and raises effective bandwidth, so fp16/bf16 speedups should roughly double and fp32 should improve slightly.

expected_effect.mechanism: Each program streams many tiles so load/compute/store pipeline across iterations instead of paying per-program dispatch and an unoverlapped single-tile DMA; measured device time for the 4096x4096 fp16 case drops from ~80us to ~34us

conclusion.root_cause: The persistent entries were built with kern.warmup(..., num_stages=2), which did not yield a usable compiled launch, so entry.launch stayed None and every call used the slow JIT dispatch path (~100us of Python per call, size independent). Additionally the threshold n>=65536 routed medium shapes (65536..1M elements, device time only a few microseconds) onto the loop path, where that fixed host cost dominated.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected a large gain on the three 4096x4096 shapes; observed a global regression from geo_mean 0.9048 to 0.4456. Nine of twelve timing workloads moved to ~80-88us regardless of size (e.g. fix-timing-6, 1M bf16: 21.9->87.7us; fix-timing-1: 23.3->81.8us), while fix-timing-3 (fp16 16.7M) stayed flat at 80.6us and fix-timing-11 (fp32 16.7M) improved 116.6->88.7us. A size-independent ~80us floor indicates per-call host cost, not device time: the loop entry never obtained the cached raw launch (warmup with a launch-level num_stages argument failed), so every call fell through to full Triton JIT dispatch. Probe measurement of the same kernel shape put its real device time at only ~33.5us (fp16) and ~97us (fp32), confirming the device side did improve while the host path regressed.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Re-submit the persistent kernel but move loop pipelining from the launch option into tl.range(num_stages=2) inside the kernel body, warm up with the proven plain call (no num_stages kwarg) so the cached raw launch is built, and only take the persistent path when that raw launch is actually available (otherwise fall back to the seed one-tile kernel). That keeps the 33.5us device win without risking the JIT-dispatch regression.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Three probes and one eval established the mechanism: (1) the persistent loop kernel's *device* time is genuinely better (reps-slope K=33.5us fp16 16.7M vs ~80us for one-tile-per-program; probe5: constexpr vs runtime TILES identical, 33.5 vs 31.3); (2) the eval regression came from launch metadata: probe6 showed raw_launch=False for loop-path entries, so every call paid full Triton JIT dispatch (cand.run 175us vs torch.fix 80us per call in the debug harness); (3) a constexpr-vs-runtime TILES change is not a factor, so the failed warmup(..., num_stages=2) call is the suspect. Lesson: verify that the cached raw launch actually exists before assuming a kernel-structure win translates to end-to-end time.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Architecture is right but the host launch path must be preserved: keep the persistent multi-tile kernel, move pipelining into the kernel body, and make the persistent path conditional on a successful cached raw launch with the seed kernel as fallback.

plan.strategy: Keep the persistent multi-tile kernel but guarantee its host launch path: pipelining inside the kernel body, plain warmup, and fall back to the seed kernel if no cached raw launch is obtained
plan.code_changes: Moved loop pipelining from the launch option into the kernel body (tl.range(..., num_stages=2)) and warm up the persistent kernel with the plain, already-proven call (no num_stages kwarg) so the cached raw launch is actually built. Added a plain-range kernel variant as a build-time fallback. The persistent entry is now only used when compiled.run.launch is available; otherwise the one-tile-per-program kernel is used for that shape.
plan.hypothesis: Round 2's regression was caused purely by the lost raw launch (JIT dispatch per call), not by the kernel. With pipelining baked into tl.range and a plain warmup, the persistent kernel should keep its ~33.5us device time (fp16 16.7M) end to end, lifting fix-timing-3/-7 from 0.31 to about 0.7, while medium and small shapes stay on their previous (~22us host-bound) behaviour thanks to the fallback.

expected_effect.mechanism: Same persistent kernel now runs through the cached low-level launch (~20us host) instead of Triton JIT dispatch (~100us host), so the measured 33.5us device time for fp16 16.7M is no longer masked

key_params.fallback: one-tile kernel when no raw launch

conclusion.root_cause: The cached low-level launcher call copied from the seed kernel passes 9 fixed slots plus 3 values (X, Y, BLOCK) for a 3-formal kernel. The persistent kernel has 4 formals (X, Y, TILES, BLOCK), so the launcher needs 13 arguments; the 12-argument call raised TypeError, which the fallback silently converted into permanent JIT dispatch for that shape.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected the persistent kernel to reach about 0.7 on the fp16/bf16 4096x4096 shapes; observed all nine loop-path workloads pinned at 85-88us with geo_mean 0.4268. The measured pattern matches max(host, device) with a constant ~85us host cost: fix-timing-11 (fp32 16.7M, device ~97-106us) is unaffected at 106.3us (speedup 1.008, better than round 1's 116.6us), while fp16 16.7M (device ~33.5us) still costs 85.2us. So the device improvement is real but the host path is still Triton JIT dispatch: the cached raw launch was obtained at build time and then rejected on first use because the call supplied 12 arguments while this kernel's launcher requires 13 (one slot per formal parameter, constexpr included).
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep the persistent kernel and pass the full launcher argument list by appending each kernel formal's value after the two pointer arguments (TILES, BLOCK, and N for the tail variant), keeping the fallback to the one-tile kernel when no raw launch is available.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The NPU launcher signature is fixed-count: probe9 captured the exact call Triton makes for the persistent kernel, [gridX, gridY, gridZ, stream, func, metadata, launch_metadata, enter_hook, exit_hook, X, Y, TILES, BLOCK] = 13 arguments. Every kernel formal parameter (including tl.constexpr ones) consumes one launcher slot, so the seed's 12-argument form is only valid for its 3-formal kernel. probe8 confirmed the TypeError 'function takes exactly 13 arguments (12 given)', and replaying the 13-argument form was exact and ~51us per call with a 33.5us device time. Lesson: when reusing a cached low-level launcher, derive the argument count from the kernel signature instead of copying a call from a different kernel.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Architecture unchanged; the remaining gap is purely the host launch path, now diagnosed exactly and fixable by matching the launcher argument count to the kernel signature.

plan.strategy: Correct the cached raw launch arity so the persistent multi-tile kernel actually uses the low-overhead launch path
plan.code_changes: The cached raw launch now receives the full launcher argument list: 9 fixed slots plus one value per kernel formal, so the persistent kernels get (gridx,1,1,stream,func,meta,None,None,None,X,Y,TILES,BLOCK) and the tail variant additionally N. One-tile kernels pass (X,Y,BLOCK) or (X,Y,N,BLOCK). Entry cache key returned to (dtype, n) to keep the host path as lean as round 1.
plan.hypothesis: Round 3's residual ~85us floor was a TypeError caused by a 12-argument launch call for a 4-formal kernel (probe9 captured the real 13-argument call). With the arity corrected, all loop-path shapes should drop to max(host~20us, device) - roughly 35us for the fp16/bf16 4096x4096 shapes - pushing their speedups from about 0.31 to about 0.7 and keeping medium shapes at their ~22us floor.

expected_effect.mechanism: The persistent kernel finally dispatches through the ~18us cached raw launch instead of ~60-85us Triton JIT dispatch, exposing its 33.5us device time

profile.summary: failed: msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker. 5/5 attempts failed: fix-timing-3 (metrics and instruction), fix-timing-7, fix-timing-11, fix-timing-0. Every manifest records stage_count=1, status=failed, capabilities=[], artifacts=[]; only manifest.json files exist under .kernelgen/profiles/round-0004 and a workspace-wide glob found no msprof CSV, so zero measurements were produced.

conclusion.root_cause: With the launcher arity corrected, the persistent multi-tile kernel finally dispatches through the ~18us cached raw launch, exposing its measured 33.5us device time (fp16 16.7M) instead of paying ~85us of Triton JIT dispatch per call. All loop-path shapes now reduce to max(host~20us, device), which is why medium shapes sit at their host floor and the two 16-bit large shapes are limited by the kernel's fp32-lane vector work.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected the persistent path to reach ~0.7 speedup on the fp16/bf16 4096x4096 shapes and to leave the rest unchanged; observed exactly that: fix-timing-3 0.313->0.7095 (80.3->42.8us), fix-timing-7 0.322->0.7164 (81.6->43.8us), fix-timing-11 0.820->1.0094 (116.6->101.5us vs reference 102.4us), and the eight medium/small workloads 1.05-1.13 at 22.5-24.1us. geo_mean rose 0.9048->1.0143 and min_speedup 0.313->0.709. Residual gap: for 16-bit dtypes the device time is ~33.5us (2.0 TB/s) against CANN's ~19us, whereas for fp32 we now match CANN exactly, so the remaining deficit is 16-bit vector throughput, not DMA organization.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the remaining fp16/bf16 device-time gap (33.5us vs CANN ~19us for 67MB). fp32 already matches CANN (101.5 vs 102.4us), which points at vector-lane width: our bit-twiddle runs in fp32 lanes (cvt, and, floor, and, or, cvt) while CANN appears to operate on 16-bit lanes. Probe an fp16-lane formulation (uint16 bitcast, 15-bit magnitude mask, native fp16 floor, sign bit OR) and larger fp16 tiles against the reps-slope measurement before committing a round.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The launcher's argument count is derived from every kernel formal, so the persistent kernel needs 13 slots ([gridX,gridY,gridZ,stream,func,metadata,launch_metadata,enter_hook,exit_hook,X,Y,TILES,BLOCK]) - probe9 captured this exactly. Correcting the arity turned an 85us floor into 42.8us and a new best. Lesson: any custom low-level launch must be validated by capturing the real call Triton makes (spy on runner.launch), not by copying the form from a kernel with a different signature.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Persistent multi-tile architecture is now confirmed end to end (device 80->33.5us for fp16, +0.11 geo); the next lever moves from launch/host plumbing to 16-bit vector-lane throughput. Profile collection intentionally skipped: the campaign notes that the standard KGS msprof collection fails in this environment (missing completion marker), and the existing independent msprof op evidence plus target-side probes already separate vector work from DMA.

plan.hypothesis: Seed passes all 30 workloads but is far below the torch reference on the 4096x4096 cases because _round_value emits ~24 vector ops per element (floor/fraction/int32 parity selects); baseline measurement is needed to quantify the per-workload gap before changing the rounding formula

profile.summary: failed: msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker (5/5 collection attempts across 5 workloads and both levels; 0 artifacts, 0 metrics, capabilities [] returned for every profile)

conclusion.root_cause: Two regimes. (a) 4096x4096 cases (t3/t7/t11): measured 0.26895 / 0.27153 / 0.27835 ms with only a 4.7% spread across fp16/bf16/fp32 even though fp32 moves 2x the bytes in each direction, so the time is not MTE-bound but is governed by the dtype-independent FP32 per-element vector-op count of _round_value (abs/floor/sub/tl.minimum/int32 cast/parity and/eq/ne/or/3x tl.where/2x bitcast/2x guard where, ~20-24 vector ops after the up-convert). (b) N<=1048576 cases (9 workloads): 16.5-19.4 us against a 12.4-14.5 us reference, flat across a 1024x range in N, so the 2.6-4.7 us gap is a constant host-dispatch/launch cost, not workload work. Profiler (msprof) produced zero artifacts on 5 attempts (base collection never signaled completion), so no counter-level pipeline split is available; the dtype-flatness argument above is eval-latency evidence only.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: geo_mean 0.4911 with all 30/30 workloads passing and matched_ratio 1.0. The three large workloads carry the whole deficit: t3 0.1169, t7 0.0705, t11 0.3552 versus 0.643-0.846 for the nine small ones. Reference latency itself scales with bytes on the large cases (0.0314 fp16 / 0.0191 bf16 / 0.0988 fp32), i.e. the reference sits near cache-bandwidth rates, while the candidate is pinned at ~0.27 ms regardless of dtype: eliminating the arithmetic redundancy is the only lever with enough range to move the geometric mean, and the small-case ceiling (<=4.7 us of host overhead) is worth at most a few percent.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Replace the floor/fraction/int32-parity/3x-select RNE core of _round_value with the magic-constant form: r = (|v| + 2^23) - 2^23 (the add is exact RNE at ulp=1 for all |v| < 2^23, and the existing passthrough select at |v| >= 2^23 covers the already-integral range), drop the redundant NaN/Inf guard because NaN falls through the compare and Inf takes the passthrough branch, and keep abs() plus the sign-bit re-application (the magic path yields +0.0 for small negative inputs while round(-0.4) must be -0.0). Keep the DECIMALS!=0 scale/div_rn tail. This cuts ~24 ops/element to ~9 and removes several live FP32 temporaries; if the large cases do not drop by at least ~40%, the ALU-op hypothesis is falsified and the next attack must be block/UB geometry or a single-instruction RNE intrinsic (tl.math.rint / round-to-nearest-even convert) instead.
conclusion.debug_lesson: For this operator the dtype-flatness of the candidate latency across fp16/bf16/fp32 is by itself a discriminating signal: an MTE-bound kernel cannot be flat against a byte-scaling reference. msprof collection currently fails at the base stage on this server, so plan to discriminate hypotheses with eval-latency structure plus bounded debug microbenchmarks rather than pipeline counters.

plan.strategy: Establish the measured baseline of the provided seed implementation (per-program flat kernel, BLOCK<=4096, FP32 magic-constant rounding with abs/sign restore).
plan.code_changes: None: the seed source is submitted verbatim as tmp/main.py.
plan.hypothesis: The seed's 4096-element per-program grid leaves large 4096x4096 workloads far behind the CANN reference; baseline will quantify per-workload gaps.

expected_effect.mechanism: No change; establishes reference point for later rounds.

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline of the provided seed: one 4096-element program per tile (4096 programs on the 4096x4096 cases), FP32 magic-constant rounding with abs/sign-restore plus NaN/Inf select. Small workloads sit at 0.83-0.89 (host launch overhead dominated, ~16-17us vs ~14us reference). Large workloads collapse: timing-3 0.192 (163us vs 31.5us), timing-7 0.116 (165us vs 19.1us), timing-11 0.531 (177us vs 94us).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected an established baseline only. Observed geo_mean 0.6220 with min_speedup 0.1158 on round_out-timing-7. The gap is concentrated in the three 4096x4096 workloads, where the per-block fan-out (4096 programs) plus a ~12-vector-instruction rounding sequence per element leaves the kernel far from the reference's 40-program streaming kernel (independent paired msprof: reference aiv_mte2_ratio 0.85 vs candidate 0.175, GM_to_UB bandwidth 32.5 GB/s per block vs 4.4 GB/s per block, same total GM_to_UB bytes). Small workloads lose 2-3us of wall time to wrapper/launch overhead, which matters because 10 of 12 timing workloads are small.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Replace the per-tile program model with a vector-core persistent streaming loop (grid = reported num_vectorcore) over unmasked full blocks plus a masked tail, and cut the rounding sequence from ~12 vector ops to ~4: use the (x + 1.5*2^23) - 1.5*2^23 magic constant, which is round-half-to-even for negative and positive operands alike and propagates NaN/Inf naturally, dropping abs/sign-restore and the NaN/Inf select.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Baseline recorded; next round changes both the program geometry (streaming persistent kernel) and the per-element arithmetic (2-op magic constant).

plan.strategy: Replace the 4096-element fan-out with a vector-core persistent streaming loop and cut the rounding sequence to two FP32 adds using the (x + 1.5*2^23) - 1.5*2^23 half-to-even identity.
plan.code_changes: tmp/main.py rewritten: (1) _round_stream persistent kernel, grid = min(num_vectorcore=40, cdiv(n,BLOCK)), unmasked full-tile loop with step = num_programs*BLOCK plus one masked tail tile, BLOCK=8192 for n>8192 and next_pow2(n) below that; (2) _value replaced by the 2-op FP32 magic constant (x+12582912.0)-12582912.0 (decimals!=0 keeps mul/round/div_rn), dropping abs, sign bit restore, the >=2^23 select and the NaN/Inf select; (3) host side uses the raw NPULauncher with three int grid args (verified signature and numeric match in a bounded debug job) behind a single-slot identity-checked fast path; (4) non-contiguous path unchanged in spirit (_round_strided with real strides).
plan.hypothesis: The 4096x4096 workloads are limited by per-block launch/MTE organization plus a ~12-instruction rounding sequence; a 40-program persistent streaming kernel with a 2-op magic-constant rounding removes both, while the raw launcher trims small-input host overhead.

expected_effect.mechanism: Per-element vector work drops from ~12 FP32 ops to 2 (debug: full fp16/bf16 domain bit-exact vs torch.round, fp32 adversarial 0 mismatches), and 4096 programs collapse to 40 persistent programs, so the memory-bound 4096x4096 cases should move from 163/165/177us to about 59/60/94us per the debug microbenchmark.

profile.summary: failed: msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker (round_out-timing-7 profile_id 0b94062d16c8487abbf1affd8b89339c and round_out-timing-3 profile_id bf3c6ee6b3c14b0b8afe6b038d2d9c95 both status=failed, artifacts=[], metrics={}, empty per-result capabilities). Zero round-2 device counters were produced, so no counter-backed finding can be registered; the analysis below rests on the frozen round-1 paired msprof counters, the round-1/round-2 eval snapshots and targ

conclusion.root_cause: The remaining bottleneck is 16-bit streaming organization, not arithmetic: with 40 persistent programs and unmasked 16KB full tiles the per-core GM->UB rate reaches ~34.9GB/s on bf16 versus ~43.0GB/s for the reference, and the single-stage loop gives no load/compute overlap. Small workloads are already at or above the reference and sit on a fixed ~13.5us host floor.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted 59/60/94us for the three 4096x4096 cases from the debug microbenchmark; observed 21.2/23.5/105.7us and geo_mean 1.0226 vs the 0.622 baseline. The prediction was wrong in the favorable direction because the debug microbenchmark used the JIT kernel[grid] path, which a later probe measured at ~59.8us of pure host cost per call, so those numbers were host-bound and not device evidence. The observed per-workload direction matched the hypothesis: timing-3 went 163.4->21.2us (0.19->1.48), timing-7 165.3->23.5us (0.116->0.811), timing-11 177.5->105.7us (0.531->1.012), and every small workload moved from 0.83-0.89 to 0.97-1.03 through the raw launcher. The residual gap is timing-7 only: bf16 4096x4096 is 4.4us behind the reference and is streaming-bound rather than vector-bound (fp16 vs bf16 at identical bytes, grid and BLOCK differ by only ~2.3us, so the whole convert+2-add charge is <=10% of the block time; the round-1 paired profile shows the reference is MTE2-dominated at ~22.8KB per MTE2 burst and ~37.7GB/s active).
conclusion.next_suggestion: Pipeline only the 16-bit streaming path: tl.range(pid*BLOCK, full, step, num_stages=2) with BLOCK=8192 and grid=40 unchanged, leaving fp32 at one stage (a 2-stage fp32 path would need ~192KB UB). Verify in the compiled artifact that a second load buffer actually materialized and confirm timing-11 does not regress.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Microbenchmarks that launch through JIT kernel[grid] measure host cost (~60us/call here), not device time; only the raw launcher plus a long loop reproduces eval-representative latency. Also: native fp16/bf16 magic arithmetic is numerically invalid (fp16 overflows to Inf near 65504, bf16 sub-rounds small values), confirmed by a full-domain sweep.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Architecture is now a persistent 40-program streaming kernel with a 2-op rounding identity; remaining work is pipeline depth (and only for the 16-bit path), not op count or partition style.

plan.strategy: Pipeline only the 16-bit streaming loop with two stages to overlap DMA and vector work, leaving the fp32 path single-stage.
plan.code_changes: Added _round_pipe, an otherwise identical copy of _round_stream whose full-tile loop uses tl.range(..., num_stages=2) so the next GM->UB load overlaps the current tile's convert+2-add+store. _build selects _round_pipe for float16/bfloat16 and keeps the single-stage _round_stream for float32 (a 2-stage fp32 path would need about 192KB UB). BLOCK=8192, grid=min(40, cdiv(n,BLOCK)), raw-launcher argument layout unchanged (xp, yp, n, decimals, block).
plan.hypothesis: The 16-bit streaming path is limited by a single-stage loop with no load/compute overlap (bf16 at ~34.9GB/s vs reference ~43.0GB/s per core); pipelining two stages should recover most of that gap without touching arithmetic or partition style.

expected_effect.mechanism: Overlapping the 16KB next-tile DMA with vector work raises effective GM->UB rate toward the reference's ~43GB/s per core; timing-7 bf16 4096x4096 should fall from 23.5us toward ~20.5us and timing-3 fp16 from 21.2us toward ~19us.

conclusion.root_cause: The 16-bit streaming loop is not limited by load/compute overlap: adding a second pipeline stage materialized no gain, and the residual bf16 4096x4096 gap (23.5us vs reference 19.3us) must come from DMA burst organization, per-core concurrency, or the dtype conversion path rather than from pipeline depth.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Two-stage pipelining produced no measurable change on the workloads it targeted: timing-3 fp16 4096x4096 21.258us vs 21.240us in round 2, timing-7 bf16 4096x4096 23.566us vs 23.492us, timing-11 fp32 105.7us vs 106.3us (fp32 was deliberately left single-stage). All 18 correctness workloads still passed, so the change was neutral-to-slightly-negative rather than harmful. The aggregate fell from 1.0226 to 0.9868 mainly because the reference itself measured faster in this run (small-workload references 13.23-13.53us here vs 13.67-14.05us in round 2) while candidate small latencies stayed at 13.20-14.88us; the reference shift is run-to-run drift, not a candidate regression. Conclusion: the single-stage loop was already at the streaming limit for the 16-bit path, so pipeline depth is not the residual bottleneck; the predicted 3us bf16 gain did not exist.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Revert to the single-stage kernel (round 2). Before spending another round, measure with the raw launcher (device-dominated, unlike the JIT path) the pure load/store copy floor for bf16 4096x4096 plus BLOCK in {4096, 8192, 16384}, grid in {20, 40, 80}, and a max_contiguous/multiple_of alignment hint variant, to separate a conversion cost from a DMA-organization limit.
conclusion.debug_lesson: num_stages on tl.range neither helped nor hurt on this backend for this kernel; the JIT-vs-raw-launcher distinction (60us vs 13.4us host cost) must be respected when designing any device-time microbenchmark.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Pipelining is a dead end; the next probe isolates the streaming floor (pure copy) and DMA-organization parameters (tile size, grid, alignment hints) before another round.

plan.strategy: Raise the streaming tile to 16384 elements on the 16-bit path only, which the device-level probe showed to be ~5% faster than 8192 at grid=40.
plan.code_changes: In _geometry, the streaming tile cap is now dtype dependent: 16-bit (float16/bfloat16) inputs use BLOCK=16384, float32 keeps BLOCK=8192 (a 16384 fp32 tile would need ~192KB UB). Everything else (grid=min(40, cdiv(n,BLOCK)), single-stage loop, tail tile, 2-op magic rounding, raw launcher) is unchanged from the round-2 best.
plan.hypothesis: The residual 16-bit streaming gap is per-tile transfer/handshake overhead rather than pipeline depth; a 32KB tile should lift timing-7 from 23.5us toward 22.3us and timing-3 from 21.2us toward 20.3us.

expected_effect.mechanism: Doubling the 16-bit tile to 32KB per GM<->UB burst and per program iteration reduces per-tile instruction and handshake overhead; device-side probe measured bf16 4096x4096 at 23.09us with BLOCK=16384 versus 24.32us with BLOCK=8192 (same protocol, host floor 11.35us).

conclusion.root_cause: The 16-bit tile change works as intended (about 1us on each large 16-bit case) but is smaller than the run-to-run measurement drift of the shared device, and 9 of 12 timing workloads are pinned at a ~13.5us host/launch floor where the candidate already sits within 0.3-0.6us of the reference.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Both targeted predictions held at the workload level: timing-7 bf16 4096x4096 fell from 23.492us to 22.494us (speedup 0.8113 -> 0.8549) and timing-3 fp16 from 21.240us to 20.334us (1.4794 -> 1.5512); timing-6 bf16 1M also improved 14.624 -> 13.372us. The aggregate nevertheless fell (1.0226 -> 0.9847) because the untargeted, floor-bound cases compared against a faster reference this run: reference small-case latencies were 12.96-13.90us here versus 13.67-14.16us in round 2, and timing-11 (an unchanged fp32 code path) moved 105.7 -> 96.3us alongside its reference 107.0 -> 92.7us. That reference-side drift of 4-9% exceeded the ~4% aggregate effect of the tile change.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Re-apply the 16-bit BLOCK=16384 tile (device-verified win on the three 16-bit timing cases) together with a slimmer host launch path, and stop chasing sub-microsecond host-floor effects afterwards.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Device-level microbenchmarks must use the raw launcher; with it, the bf16 4096x4096 streaming floor is a pure copy at 15.3us versus 23.8us with the 2-add rounding, and each extra FP32 vector pass costs about 4us, which is why op count matters more than tile size on the 16-bit path.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Tile tuning is now understood: BLOCK=16384 for 16-bit is the best streaming tile, grid=40 is optimal, and the remaining work is host-path slimming plus combining both verified wins in one candidate.

conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected a first measured map, observed it. conclusion.strategy_evolution: Host path is now near its floor; remaining loss is entirely in the three 4096x4096 workloads, which are vector-compute bound rather than memory bound.

plan.strategy: Minimal exact FP32 magic-number rounding core
plan.code_changes: _value() now: converts to fp32, applies decimals scaling only when DECIMALS!=0, computes magnitude, applies the 2^23 magic round with the large-magnitude clamp, and restores the sign by OR-ing the input sign bit into the (always non-negative) rounded value. Removed the explicit isnan/isinf select (NaN/Inf propagate through the magic unchanged) and the redundant AND-mask before the sign OR. Kernels and host fast path unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The three 4096x4096 workloads are bound by the number of FP32 vector ops in the rounding core, so removing the redundant NaN/Inf select and the sign mask lowers their latency by roughly 30% while staying bitwise-exact for ties, negative zero, NaN and Inf.

expected_effect.mechanism: Vector op count over 16.7M elements drops from ~14 fp32 ops to 9 for bf16/fp16 and to 7 for fp32; at the measured ~7.1us per fp32 vector op this removes roughly 30-35us from the 16-bit workloads and pushes the fp32 workload from 136us toward the 89us memory floor.

conclusion.root_cause: The rounding core was still issuing reducible FP32 vector work (NaN/Inf select, sign mask) and was compute-bound; on Ascend an FP32 vector op over 16.7M elements costs ~7us, so op count directly sets the large-shape latency.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: ~30% lower latency on the three 4096x4096 workloads by cutting the core from ~14 to 9/7 FP32 vector ops. Observed: timing-3 109.8->66.8us (0.287->0.471), timing-7 111.7->68.0us (0.172->0.320), timing-11 136.6->103.6us (0.777->0.915) - a 1.64x, 1.64x and 1.32x latency reduction, matching the op-count model (each removed FP32 vector op is worth ~7us over 16.7M elements). All 30 workloads stayed numerically exact, confirming the removed NaN/Inf select and sign mask were redundant. The nine launch-bound workloads were unchanged in absolute terms (12.6-13.3us -> 13.0-14.7us, within noise) but their reference latencies fell 13%, so their speedup ratios dropped from 1.18-1.23 to 0.94-1.04 and the aggregate geo mean moved 0.873->0.853 despite a genuinely 1.6x faster kernel on the shapes that dominate absolutely.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Re-apply the minimal core and add a native 16-bit path for bf16/fp16 that avoids the constructs that made the earlier native attempt numerically wrong (no 16-bit bitcast for sign restore and no tl.abs on 16-bit; use where-based magnitude and sign), since 16-bit vector ops cost about half an FP32 op and the two 16-bit shapes are still 3-5x above the 12.5us copy floor. Also push the FP32 shape from 103.6us toward its measured 89.3us memory floor.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Reference-side latency on launch-bound workloads moved 15.5->13.5us between rounds 2 and 3 and a retest verified the new value as stable, so cross-round geo_mean comparisons are confounded at the ~9% level on nine of twelve workloads; absolute candidate latency is the reliable signal for the large shapes.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Large shapes now scale with vector op count, not memory; the next lever is switching bf16/fp16 to native 16-bit arithmetic while keeping exactness for ties, negative zero, NaN and Inf.

plan.strategy: Native 16-bit magic-number rounding core for bf16/fp16
plan.code_changes: Re-applied the minimal FP32 core (round 3) and added a native 16-bit path used whenever decimals==0 and dtype is bf16/fp16: neg = x<0, magnitude = where(neg,-x,x), rounded = (magnitude+M)-M with M=1024.0 (fp16) or 128.0 (bf16), clamp at M, result = where(neg,-rounded,rounded). No 16-bit bitcast and no tl.abs on 16-bit, so it cannot fail through the two constructs that broke the earlier native attempt. decimals!=0 keeps the exact FP32 scale/div_rn path.
plan.hypothesis: The bf16 and fp16 4096x4096 workloads are bound by FP32 vector throughput at ~7us per op; expressing the identical exact rounding in native 16-bit arithmetic nearly halves that cost, while remaining bit-exact for ties, negative zero, NaN, Inf and large magnitudes.

expected_effect.mechanism: 16-bit vector ops cost roughly half an FP32 op on the AIV unit; replacing 9 FP32-equivalent op slots (7 ops plus 2 conversions) with 9 native 16-bit slots cuts the two 16-bit large-shape latencies from ~68us toward ~40us.

conclusion.root_cause: The Ascend Triton backend promotes bf16/fp16 arithmetic to FP32, so a 16-bit magic constant cannot round and the native path adds promotion cost on top; native 16-bit vector throughput is not available through this compiler.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: native 16-bit arithmetic roughly halves the two 16-bit large-shape latencies. Observed the opposite and a correctness break: timing-3 66.8->77.3us, timing-7 68.0->126.8us (1.16x and 1.86x slower than the FP32 core), with correctness-6, correctness-8 and correctness-10 failing at matched_ratio 0.0/0.048/0.048. The failure signature (abs_err 0.36-0.5, ~5% matched, i.e. values that were already integral) is the identity, showing the add/sub pair was executed in FP32 with a 1024/128 magic that cannot round there. The FP32 core from round 3 remains the best formulation and timing-11 stayed at 103.6us across both rounds, confirming the fp32 path is unchanged.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep the FP32 core but exploit a proven exactness property instead of the clamp: every fp16/bf16 value is a multiple of the FP32 ulp at its magnitude, so the 2^23 magic is already exact for the whole 16-bit input domain and the magnitude clamp can be dropped for those dtypes. Combine that with a signed magic constant m = +-2^23 chosen by sign, which removes both tl.abs and the sign bit-restore, giving 6 op slots (input conversion, compare, select, add, sub, output conversion) instead of 9 for bf16/fp16, and keep the clamped 7-op FP32 path only for the fp32 dtype where the shape is memory-bound anyway.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On this backend 16-bit arithmetic is promoted to FP32 before execution: a 1024.0/128.0 magic therefore never rounds, and the extra promotion/demotion slots made the native kernel slower than the FP32 core. Any rounding scheme must use the 2^23 FP32 magic.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Native 16-bit arithmetic is closed off; remaining gains must come from reducing FP32 op slots in the 16-bit path, which is exactly 2 conversions plus the magic work.

plan.strategy: Establish the measured baseline for the seed implementation (flat cached-launch path for contiguous equal-shape operands, strided fallback otherwise) without modification.
plan.code_changes: None; the seed is submitted verbatim to record its authoritative correctness and latency on the full 30-workload suite.
plan.hypothesis: The seed reproduces its previously reported behaviour: the strided FP32 special-value cases expose non-finite mismatches while the contiguous timing cases pass, and per-workload latency is dominated by either host launch overhead (small shapes) or vector throughput (large shapes).

expected_effect.mechanism: No change; records the reference point for later comparisons.

conclusion.root_cause: Seed baseline establishes full 30/30 correctness and geo_mean 0.5458. The cached direct-launch path (compiled.run.launch) removed the previously dominant host cost: tiny-shape latency fell from ~0.161 ms (batch starting point) to ~0.023 ms. Remaining gap analysis from the authoritative per-workload numbers: the nine small timing workloads all sit at 0.0230-0.0246 ms against references of 0.0102-0.0120 ms (speedup 0.445-0.500), i.e. a roughly constant ~12 us deficit that is independent of N, which points to per-call host submission cost rather than device work. The three large workloads (timing-3 fp16 4096x4096 0.1530 vs 0.1148, timing-7 0.1525 vs 0.1247, timing-11 fp32 4096x4096 0.1762 vs 0.1600) are 0.75-0.91x; subtracting the same ~12 us host delta leaves the fp32 large case essentially at reference device cost while the fp16 4096x4096 case still carries a device-side gap.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline round, so no prior expectation exists. Observed geo_mean 0.5458 with min_speedup 0.4449 at worst_workload special_xlogy_-timing-6. The speedup distribution is bimodal: every workload with a small or medium element count is pinned near 0.47x with a near-constant absolute latency of ~23 us, while the three 4096x4096 workloads reach 0.75-0.91x. A constant absolute deficit across shapes as different as 1024 fp16 and 1048576 bf16 cannot be explained by device throughput, so the aggregate metric is currently controlled by host launch overhead, not by the device kernel.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Decompose the ~23 us per-call cost with a bounded debug job: measure submit-only cost of the cached raw launcher versus the full run() wrapper versus torch xlogy_, the cost of the current-stream query, and whether the raw launcher accepts a reduced runtime-argument list (constexpr N/BLOCK baked into packed_metadata). In parallel collect device-bound latency for 4096x4096 fp16/bf16/fp32 across BLOCK sizes to see whether the fp16 large case needs a tile change.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The batch starting point's 12x small-shape deficit was entirely host launch overhead, already removed by the seed's cached compiled.run.launch; the residual ~12 us gap versus the PyTorch reference is a pure submission-cost problem that must be measured by decomposition before any further device-side tuning.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Baseline recorded with the seed unmodified; next rounds target host submission cost first because it dominates 9 of 12 timing workloads and also contributes ~12 us to each large workload.

plan.strategy: Remove the two measured host-path costs (lazily imported triton.cdiv at ~4.7 us and the extra Python frames/grid derivation) by caching the launch tuple including grid, tile and device, and widen the flat tile from 4096 to a size-derived tile capped at 8192 for better large-tensor DMA.
plan.code_changes: run() now looks up a per-(dtypeA,dtypeB,n) tuple holding the launcher, function, packed metadata, precomputed grid, tile and device index, and calls the raw launcher from a single inlined fast path with no triton.cdiv and no _entry() indirection. Tile selection moved to compile time via _block_for(n): max(256, next_pow2(n)) capped at 8192 instead of a fixed 4096. The strided/broadcast fallback and the _xlogy_value NaN-priority semantics are unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: Measured debug evidence shows the seed spends 23.4 us per call on small shapes while its own raw cached launcher costs only 9.1 us and torch xlogy_ costs 10.0 us; a no-launch copy of the wrapper body costs 2.65 us and stream+cdiv alone costs 5.44 us, so triton.cdiv (a lazily-resolved module attribute) is the largest removable item. Independently, device-bound runs on 4096x4096 showed BLOCK 8192 at 92.3 us (fp16) and 147.2 us (fp32) versus 152.3/175.6 us at BLOCK 4096, and versus torch at 96.8/173.8 us.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing the lazily imported triton.cdiv call and the extra Python frames from the per-call path cuts a fixed ~6-10 us from every invocation, which dominates all nine small/medium workloads; the wider 8192-element tile gives larger contiguous DMA per program for the 4096x4096 workloads.

conclusion.root_cause: Confirmed the frozen hypothesis on both counts. The seed's fixed ~23 us per-call cost decomposed into ~9.1 us raw launch floor, ~4.7 us from the lazily resolved triton.cdiv, ~0.7 us stream query and the remainder in Python frames and per-call grid derivation; caching grid/tile/device in the entry tuple and inlining the fast path removed the removable part. The fp16/bf16 4096x4096 device deficit was tile width, not math precision: device-bound runs showed 152.3 us at BLOCK 4096 versus 92.3 us at BLOCK 8192 for fp16, with masked and unmasked loads and fp32 versus native-dtype math indistinguishable, so the larger contiguous DMA per program was the actual mechanism.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: remove ~6-10 us of fixed per-call host cost from all nine small/medium workloads and widen the flat tile to 8192 for the 4096x4096 workloads. Observed: geo_mean rose from 0.5458 to 0.8569 (+57% relative) and every one of the 30 workloads passes. Small/medium latency fell from 0.0230-0.0246 ms to 0.01454-0.01659 ms, a saving of 7.2-8.7 us, consistent with removing the ~4.7 us triton.cdiv lazy-import cost plus the extra Python frames and grid derivation. Their speedups moved from 0.445-0.500 to 0.780-0.830. The three 4096x4096 workloads crossed above parity exactly as the device-bound debug runs predicted: timing-3 fp16 0.0924 vs 0.0966 ms (1.0447x, predicted ~0.095), timing-7 0.0945 vs 0.0974 ms (1.0310x), timing-11 fp32 0.1467 vs 0.1553 ms (1.0587x, predicted ~0.136 at the debug ratio). Aggregate min_speedup improved from 0.4449 to 0.7800 at worst_workload timing-5. Residual gap: the nine small/medium workloads still sit 2.2-4.2 us above their references (0.01454-0.01659 vs 0.01155-0.01315 ms); measured separately, the raw cached launcher alone costs 9.07 us and torch's own xlogy_ submit is ~10.0 us, so the remaining wrapper overhead above the launch floor is roughly 5-6 us and is now the only source of loss.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Decompose the residual per-call cost precisely with lean-run variants on the 1024-element fp16 case: launch with tensor arguments instead of raw ints, removal of each guard (contiguity, shape equality, dict lookup, stream query), and a pure-launch floor, to identify which of the remaining ~3-4 us above the 9.1 us raw-launcher floor is removable. Also check whether the large-case tile can exceed 8192 now that the fp32 path is memory-bound.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On this backend triton.cdiv is not a free integer helper: it resolves through a module-level lazy import and cost ~4.7 us per call, which alone accounted for roughly a third of the seed's per-call latency. Caching the derived grid and tile in the compiled-entry tuple removes it entirely. Separately, a 8192-element flat tile is markedly better than 4096 for multi-megabyte tensors while masked loads cost nothing versus unmasked on this target.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 localized the deficit to a constant per-call host cost; round 2 removed the dominant removable term (lazy triton.cdiv) plus widened the tile, reaching 0.8569. The bottleneck has narrowed to the difference between our ~9.1 us raw launcher floor and the reference's ~10-12 us full call, so round 3 targets only the wrapper operations that sit above that floor.

plan.strategy: Trim the last removable interpreter work from the hot path: pre-bind the current-stream getter at import and use a bare subscript lookup with exception-based compile-on-miss.
plan.code_changes: Resolved the current-stream getter once at import into _GET_STREAM (probe: raw(0) accepted, else a no-arg/torch.npu fallback) so run() makes one call with no intermediate Python frame; replaced the _ENTRIES.get(...) + None branch with a subscript lookup inside try/except KeyError; kept the numel early return, the contiguity/shape guards, the alignment gate, the cached launch tuple and the 8192 tile cap unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The measured per-call budget on 1024-element fp16 is 9.0-9.2 us for the raw launcher, ~1.4 us for the contiguity/shape/pointer guards, ~0.8 us for the dtype/numel dict key and lookup, ~0.34 us for the stream query and the rest interpreter frame work, giving 13.4-14.6 us for run() overall. The guards and the launch cannot be removed, so only the stream indirection and the lookup form are available; a nested Python call was measured at ~1.5 us, so eliminating one frame should be visible.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing one Python call frame (_stream) and one LOAD_METHOD/CALL pair (dict.get) from every invocation trims a fixed fraction of a microsecond from the per-call cost, which shifts all nine launch-overhead-dominated workloads by roughly the same amount.

conclusion.root_cause: The hot path is already at its structural floor: the raw launcher alone costs 9.0-9.2 us while the reference's whole call costs ~12.7 us, and the remaining ~4.5 us is two data_ptr calls, two is_contiguous calls, a shape comparison, a numel call, two dtype reads, a dict lookup, the stream query and one interpreter frame. Only the last two were removable, worth roughly 0.3-0.5 us, and the measured result confirms that size. The large-case improvements relative to round 2 are reference drift, not candidate change.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: trimming one Python call frame (_stream) and one LOAD_METHOD/CALL pair (dict.get) plus the eager None branch would move all nine launch-bound workloads by a small constant. Observed: geo_mean 0.8569 -> 0.8768 (+2.3%) with 30/30 still passing, but the per-workload evidence does not cleanly support the mechanism. The nine small/medium latencies were 0.01454-0.01659 ms before and 0.01488-0.01653 ms after, i.e. unchanged inside noise, whereas timing-3 (0.0923 vs 0.0924), timing-7 (0.0944 vs 0.0945) and timing-11 (0.1671 vs 0.1467) moved substantially. The aggregate gain is therefore dominated by reference-side drift: timing-11's reference moved from 0.1553 to 0.1986 ms between rounds, and its speedup from 1.0587 to 1.1883 with our own latency getting worse in absolute terms. The honest reading is that the intended mechanism saved at most a few tenths of a microsecond, below the ~5% measurement noise, and the recorded improvement is partly luck.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Stop chasing host micro-optimisation and test the only remaining non-noise lever: a wider flat tile for the fp16/bf16 4096x4096 workloads. BLOCK 8192 beat 4096 by 40%, so test BLOCK 16384 with native-dtype math (96 KiB of buffers, which should fit the UB where the fp32-math variant overflowed) plus a max_contiguous/multiple_of offset hint at 8192, measuring device-bound totals against torch on both fp16 and bf16.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Both remaining cost centres are floors rather than defects: the raw NPU launcher costs 9.0-9.2 us per call (torch's own xlogy_ submit is 9.5-10.0 us) and the residual is interpreter call overhead for checks that cannot be dropped. Reference latencies for the large workloads also drift up to 28% between rounds on this shared device, so sub-microsecond host changes are not resolvable and the fp32 large-case speedup should not be read as a real step change.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Rounds 1-2 took geo_mean from 0.5458 to 0.8569 by removing the lazy triton.cdiv and widening the tile. Round 3 confirmed the host path is at its floor, so the remaining work shifts to the three wide workloads where tile width still shows a strong effect.

conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the tile-count cap instead of the mask: shorten the multi-buffer pipeline with num_stages=2 only in the n>=131072 regime and raise BLOCK to 16384 (16-bit, 32 KB per transfer) / 8192 (fp32, 32 KB per transfer), keeping grid capped at num_vectorcore, the unmasked hot loop, the single masked tail tile and the cached integer-address launch. This cuts sequential tiles per core from ~103 to ~26 for 16-bit and ~52 for fp32 while keeping UB inside 192 KB. Verify compilation by preflight (8192 elements alone overflows UB; only a reduced stage count makes it fit), and if num_stages does not shrink the footprint, fall back to the best measured tile and pivot to cutting the fixed ~6.5 us per-call host cost, which affects 9 of the 12 timing workloads.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A target-side debug sweep (n=16.7M) showed: num_vectorcore=40, num_aicore=20; torch.ops.aten.hardswish.out reaches 0.0430 ms (1561 GB/s) on fp16 and 0.0881 ms (1524 GB/s) on fp32, while our kernel gets 676/1167 GB/s. fp16 and fp32 take nearly the same time (0.0993 vs 0.1151) while moving 2x different bytes, and byte volume costs only 0.0158 ms for 67 MB (≈4.2 TB/s marginal, i.e. L2-resident), so the kernel is bound by the number of sequential tiles each vector core walks (N/(40*4096)=103), not by bytes. BLOCK is capped at 4096 elements by UB (8192 elements demands 262176 B against 196608 B available, ~32 B/element); grid=80/160 does not help because only one block is resident per core, and one-shot grid=4096 is far worse (0.170 ms). Raising the tile therefore requires shortening the compiler's multi-buffer pipeline.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Mask removal improved the many small/medium workloads (+3-4% each) and is kept as the new best, but the large-input regime needs fewer/larger tiles rather than better-shaped transfers; since UB caps a tile at 4096 elements per stage chain, the next lever is the multi-buffer depth (num_stages) rather than BLOCK alone.

Stream is still re-read every call.

plan.strategy: Native narrow-dtype vector arithmetic for the fp16 path
plan.code_changes: Added a constexpr H16 argument to _hardswish_stream. When H16 is true (input dtype is float16) both the hot loop and the masked tail keep the arithmetic in the operand dtype: the tl.full((1,), 3.0/0.0/6.0/1/6, x.dtype) constants and no .to(tl.float32), so no cast in and no cast out. fp32 and bfloat16 inputs keep the exact H16=false fp32 path. The plan list grew one field (index 11) carried into both the integer-address C launch and the JIT fallback. Host path, grid, BLOCK, vector-core cap and masked tail are unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The fp16 4096x4096 case is vector-arithmetic bound, not memory bound: at identical geometry the target sweep measured a pure copy at 0.0603 ms, one multiply at 0.0598 ms, fp32-emulated hardswish at 0.0994 ms and element-dtype hardswish at 0.0670 ms. Switching only the fp16 path to element-dtype math should take timing-3 from 0.098 to ~0.067 ms (speedup 0.431 -> ~0.63) and leave the ten already-faster small workloads and the bf16/fp32 large cases unchanged.

expected_effect.mechanism: Narrow-dtype vector math runs at twice the fp32 lane rate and drops the two cast operations per tile that the fp32 emulation pays, removing the vector-arithmetic saturation that dominates the 16.7M-element fp16 case.

conclusion.root_cause: The fp16 4096x4096 workload was saturated on fp32 vector arithmetic: emulating a 16-bit operand through fp32 costs a cast in and a cast out plus full-rate fp32 vector work over five operations per element, which the target isolates at 0.0994 ms against a 0.0603 ms copy floor. Element-dtype constants remove both casts and double the vector lane rate, taking that workload to 0.0648 ms. The aggregate metric moved the other way only because the ten CPU-bound workloads, now essentially at parity with the CANN call (our 0.0237 ms vs reference 0.0221 ms in the retest), are dominated by host-state variance that swamped a genuine 1.5x device-side gain on one of twelve workloads.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: timing-3 0.098 -> ~0.067 ms (0.431 -> ~0.63) with the small workloads and the bf16/fp32 large cases unchanged. Observed on the target workload: timing-3 0.0980 -> 0.0648 ms, speedup 0.431 -> 0.649, i.e. the mechanism and magnitude were both correct and the retest reproduced it at 0.0674 ms. timing-7 (bfloat16) was unchanged as predicted (0.1001 -> 0.1001). However the aggregate fell: geo_mean 0.9115 -> 0.8836, and the independent retest measured 0.8499. The cause is measurement drift, not the code: the ten CPU-bound small/medium workloads regressed in relative terms (timing-0 1.130 -> 0.996, timing-8 1.110 -> 1.002) although they run the byte-identical fp32 path and unchanged host path, and their CANN reference latency moved 0.0247 -> 0.0265 ms in this round and 0.0221 ms in the retest (-17% from this round) while the three device-bound large cases stayed stable (timing-7 0.1001 -> 0.1007, timing-3 0.0648 -> 0.0674). Net effect of the change itself, holding drift aside, is about +3.5% on geo_mean; the recorded aggregate does not show it.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Re-apply the float16 element-dtype path (it is a genuine 1.5x on timing-3 and was confirmed twice: 0.0980 -> 0.0648 ms in this round and 0.0674 ms in the retest) and evaluate it again for a clean draw, because the aggregate comparison was decided by host-side measurement drift on the ten CPU-bound workloads rather than by the code. While doing so, test whether genuinely narrow arithmetic frees enough on-chip buffer for a doubled float16 tile: with no fp32 intermediate the ~32 B/element footprint may fall, letting BLOCK=8192 (16 KB transfers) compile for float16 where it previously overflowed UB, which would move the fp16 case from 0.067 toward the 0.044 CANN level. Check compilation by preflight first, since an 8192-element tile failed UB before the narrow-math change. Do not pursue bfloat16 narrow math: bfloat16 is emulated in fp32 and a bfloat16->float16 encoding would silently overflow finite values above 65504.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The 16.7M-element fp16 case is vector-arithmetic bound, not memory bound: at identical geometry (BLOCK=4096, grid=40) the target ladder gave copy 0.0603 ms, copy+fp32-cast 0.0570, x*2 0.0598, fp32-emulated hardswish 0.0994 and element-dtype hardswish 0.0670 ms. Two further facts from the same measurements: bfloat16 element-dtype math gives no gain at all (0.1018 vs 0.1014 ms), so the backend emulates bfloat16 through fp32 and only float16 gets the doubled vector lane rate; and the residual gap between 0.0670 and the 0.0603 copy floor is the tile-granularity ceiling, since the ~32 B/element buffer footprint pins BLOCK at 4096 elements and no grid shape or num_stages setting changes that.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Element-dtype arithmetic is confirmed as the lever for float16 and confirmed useless for bfloat16. The remaining fp16 headroom is the 0.067 -> 0.060 copy floor, which requires a larger tile than the 4096-element UB cap currently allows; narrow arithmetic may itself lower that cap's binding, so the tile size becomes re-testable rather than settled.
